docs.title: Below the line
docs.text:
Real seams, worth building eventually, but the ratio does not justify going first:

Proposal Seam Why it waits drill-replay DrillFlowCore — the full state machine behind Tactics/Trap/Punish/Study/Endgame on both platforms The highest-leverage QA target in the Train module and the least JSON-Lines-natural: it is an interactive reducer, not a batch transform, so the command would test the script format as much as the kernel board-replay EBoardSessionCore.handle(event:game:orientationFlipped:) over a .replay script Turns a field diagnostic capture into a diffable effect trace. Real regression value, zero research value, and it needs three things the CLI does not have: a .replay-text-to-BoardEvent adapter, a GameView conformer to pass as game:, and a synchronous stand-in for the async resolution coordinator endgame-verify EndgameMiningV2ValidatedGeneration.validate(expectedCoverage:loadObjectJSON:), EndgameMiningValidatedGeneration.validate(loadShardJSON:) The validators are already pure functions over injected (String) -> String? load closures, so a directory-backed shim is the whole job — but EndgameMiningValidatedGeneration's initializer is fileprivate, so the V1 half is only reachable through a resolver. Fold into store as a verify-mining op rather than shipping alone material MaterialBalance.compute(from:) Self-contained and correct, but it is a starting-count subtraction over five piece types. The right artifact is a golden fixture, or an extra field on a command that already holds a Position clock-sim ClockCore.start(color:) / .stop() / .reset() / .switchTurn() / .advance(byElapsed:) Scriptable in principle, but the inputs only exist inside a running session driven by wall time. Niche game-logic QA, no research value

docs.title: Blocked by access level
docs.text:
Three seams the survey wanted and could not have. Each needs a one-word source change, and the CLI is a separate SPM package, so internal is as unreachable as private.

Seam Access What it would have enabled EloCalibrationData internal A calibration-dump command emitting coefficients, feature means and standard deviations, residual bands, and the Elo grid per (time control, model version). Tools/elo-calibration/generate_swift.py bakes these into Swift from JSON artifacts under a "DO NOT EDIT" header, and nothing currently re-reads the baked values to confirm they still match the source after a regen. This is the missing round-trip check for that generator StatsKernel.isOTBClassicalTC(tag:tc:) private An is_otb_classical field on classify. The rule is tc == .classical && estimatedSeconds(fromPGNTag:) >= 6000, and it selects a widened CI and a different estimate label TimeControlClass.estimatedSeconds(fromPGNTag:) internal The staged-clock duration behind both classifiers. classify can emit the resulting class but not the seconds that produced it, which is the field a mis-bucketing investigation actually wants

Note

Mirroring a non-public seam in the CLI is possible under the file:line citation convention the CLI index documents, but it is the wrong trade here: all three are load-bearing numeric logic, and a mirrored copy of numeric logic is a copy that can drift silently.

docs.title: Wire contracts for the top candidates
docs.text: All sketches follow the protocol the six shipped commands already implement: one JSON object per line in, one per line out, explicit snake_case CodingKeys, nil fields omitted rather than written as null, per-line failures emitted as {"id", "error"} without stopping the stream.

docs.title: chart
docs.text:
The strongest proposal on this page, because its bug class already shipped. The source comment on EloChartPresentation records the divergence verbatim: Apple's domain unioned the anchored intervals, the actual ratings, and the per-game evidence dots; Android's unioned only the intervals and ratings, so every dot outside that band drew flat against the chart edge — measured at 2.3% of points on the reference account and 7.1% on the worst. The dots are the varying series; the anchored line barely moves.

EloChartPresentation.domain(points:showsComparableRating:)

    values = for each point:
                 displayedInterval(for: point).lowerBound
                 displayedInterval(for: point).upperBound
                 point.actualRating          // ONLY if showsComparableRating
    no values at all                      -> 0...3_000

    performances = points.map(unclippedPerformance).sorted()
    count >= 20 -> lower = min(lower, performances[count / 20])
                   upper = max(upper, performances[count * 19 / 20])
    count <  20 -> lower = min(lower, performances.first)
                   upper = max(upper, performances.last)

    padding = max(30, (upper - lower) * 0.05)
    domain  = (lower - padding)...(upper + padding)

EloChartPresentation.clipped(_:to:)
    inset = max(1, (domain.upperBound - domain.lowerBound) * 0.01)
    min(upper - inset, max(lower + inset, value))

displayedInterval(for:)  / unclippedPerformance(for:)
    calibration == .chessComPersonalized && gameProjection != nil
        -> projection.interval68        / projection.mappedPerformance
    otherwise
        -> point.strengthCI             / point.performance.elo

The 5th/95th percentile trim is the load-bearing line: it is what stops one wild game rescaling the chart and flattening everything else, and it is exactly the kind of rule two independent implementations get subtly different.

{"id":"p1","date":"2026.03.01","calibration":"chessComPersonalized","actual_rating":1180,"performance":{"elo":1240.0,"ci_low":980.0,"ci_high":1500.0},"strength_ci":[1150.0,1280.0],"game_projection":{"mapped_performance":1305.0,"interval68":[1210.0,1400.0]}}

{"domain_high":1547.0,"domain_low":947.0,"point_count":1}
{"clipped_performance":1305.0,"displayed_interval_high":1400.0,"displayed_interval_low":1210.0,"id":"p1"}

let domain = EloChartPresentation.domain(
    points: points,
    showsComparableRating: showsComparableRating
)
for point in points {
    let interval = EloChartPresentation.displayedInterval(for: point)
    let raw = EloChartPresentation.unclippedPerformance(for: point)
    let drawn = EloChartPresentation.clipped(raw, to: domain)
}

Warning

unclippedPerformance must not itself be clipped to the domain — the domain is derived from it, and clipping first makes the derivation circular. A CLI that emits both values keeps that ordering visible in the output, which is the point.

docs.title: classify
docs.text:
Two classifiers deliberately disagree, and every mis-bucketed game silently changes which calibration artifact serves it and which provider rating pool it belongs to. The command emits both, plus the derived fields, one game per line.

TimeControlClass.classify(baseSeconds:incrementSeconds:)   // estimator artifact
    baseSeconds == nil -> .correspondence
    total = base + 40 * increment
    total <  180 -> .bullet        total < 1500 -> .rapid
    total <  480 -> .blitz         else         -> .classical

StatsKernel.classifySpeed(tags:event:)                     // provider rating pool
    TimeControl tag non-empty AND classifies .correspondence -> .daily
    event contains "bullet" / "ultrabullet"                  -> .bullet
    event contains "blitz"                                   -> .blitz
    event contains "rapid"                                   -> .rapid
    event contains "classical"                               -> .classical
    event contains "correspondence" / "daily" /
                   "let's play" / "lets play"                -> .daily
    tag empty                                                -> .rapid
    base = staged duration when the tag contains ":" or "/",
           else Int(text before "+"), else 0
    base <  180 -> .bullet        base <= 1800 -> .rapid
    base <  600 -> .blitz         else         -> .classical

A 300+5 game is .rapid to the estimator (300 + 40 × 5 = 500) and .blitz to the rating pool (base = 300). That is intentional, and it is exactly the pair a census wants to count. Three named failures are pinned by this pair: a Chess.com Daily clock spelled 1/86400 read as bullet by a naive + split, a - tag falling through to rapid, and a staged OTB control like 40/7200:3600+30 read as its first stage.

{"id":"g1","tags_json":"{\"TimeControl\":\"300+5\"}","event":"Rated blitz game"}

{"display_speed":"blitz","estimator_tc":"rapid","id":"g1","starts_with_white":true}

let tags = StatsKernel.parseTags(tagsJSON)
let estimatorTC = TimeControlClass.classify(
    fromPGNTag: tags["TimeControl"] ?? ""
)
let displaySpeed = StatsKernel.classifySpeed(tags: tags, event: event)
let startsWhite = StatsKernel.startsWithWhiteToMove(tags: tags)

docs.title: identity
docs.text:
Every cross-platform identity question and every corpus-dedup question reduces to "what keys does this game produce?", and there is no way to answer it today without launching the app.

GameIdentity.canonicalProviderID(_:)
    "lichess:<id>"      -> suffix (split on / ? #), 8...12 ASCII alphanumerics
                           -> "lichess:" + first 8 characters
    "chesscom:<id>" /
    "chess.com:<id>"    -> suffix (split on / ? #), all ASCII digits
                           -> "chesscom:" + suffix
    a recognized web location -> the same canonical form
    anything else             -> nil

GameIdentity.stableID(gameID:link:site:contentID:)
    first non-empty of:
        the persisted remote ID derived from gameID / link / site
        gameID itself, when it is already a content ID
        contentID()                            // autoclosure — computed last

Lichess's stable component is the first eight case-sensitive characters, so the canonical form is not the raw string, and the two representations are what a dedup pass across differently-sourced corpora has to reconcile.

{"id":"r1","game_id":"","link":"https://lichess.org/abcd1234/white","site":"lichess.org","white":"alice","black":"bob","date":"2026.03.01","result":"1-0","event":"Rated blitz game","opening":"B90","move_text":"1. e4 c5","tags_json":"{}"}

{"canonical_provider_id":"lichess:abcd1234","id":"r1","is_remote_id":true,"stable_game_id":"lichess:abcd1234"}

docs.title: combo
docs.text:
Stage 1 of combination mining is pure Foundation and ChessCore over stored annotation — no engine call at all. Both the admission gate and the ranking score are short enough to state completely, which is what makes offline threshold retuning practical.

CombinationMiningKernel.candidates(in:userIsWhite:)  — admission gate
    naiveCp <= sacrificeThresholdCp   (-150)   // looks like a sacrifice
    evalCp  >= winningThresholdCp     ( 150)   // actually winning
    evalCp  <= decidedBandCp          ( 900)   // not already decided

CombinationMiningKernel.score(naiveCp:seeCp:evalCp:sharpnessCp:foundIt:)
    total  = min(-naiveCp, 900)                     // how bad it looks
    total += min(max(0, seeCp - naiveCp), 900) / 2  // blind-spot gap
    total += min(evalCp, 600) / 2                   // winning, not runaway
    total += min(sharpnessCp ?? 0, 400) / 2         // uniqueness
    if foundIt { total -= 500 }                     // penalised, not filtered

CombinationMiningKernel.validateLine(startingFEN:uciMoves:)
    forcedReplies counts opponent turns with
        legalMoves.count <= forcedReplyMaxLegalMoves   (2)
    dipped     = maxDeficitCp <= minimumDeficitCp      (-150)
    longEnough = solverMoves  >= minimumSolverMoves    (3)

    endsInCheckmate && longEnough -> .combination
    !dipped || !longEnough        -> .notACombination
    netGain >= 0                  -> .combination
    otherwise                     -> .truncated   // re-probe deeper, do NOT discard

.truncated is the case that must not be treated as a rejection: the line dipped and ran out before recovering, so the resolution is past the probe horizon rather than absent.

{"id":"g1","white":"alice","black":"bob","username":"alice","move_text":"1. e4 c5","tags_json":"{}","annotation_evals_json":"[...]","second_best_evals_json":"[...]"}
{"id":"v1","mode":"verdict","fen":"...","moves":["d1h5","g7g6","h5e5"]}

{"candidates":[{"eval_cp":420,"move_number":14,"mover_is_white":true,"naive_cp":-400,"played_san":"Nf3","position_fen":"...","score":1085,"see_cp":100,"sharpness_cp":180,"engine_best_san":"Qxc8","engine_best_uci":"d1c8"}],"id":"g1"}
{"ends_in_checkmate":false,"final_material_cp":100,"forced_replies":2,"id":"v1","max_deficit_cp":-400,"opponent_turns":2,"outcome":"combination","solver_moves":3}

// Stage 1 from an annotated game — no engine, no async.
let candidates = CombinationMiningKernel.candidates(from: input)

// Or judge one hand-supplied line.
let verdict = CombinationMiningKernel.validateLine(
    startingFEN: fen,
    uciMoves: moves
)

Note

candidates(from:) returns [] for a game with no engine annotation, and for a game whose eval array length is not moves.count + 1. Both are honest answers rather than errors, so a CLI should report the empty result with its reason rather than emitting a per-line error.

docs.title: glyphs
docs.text:
annotate emits only white-POV evals, and accuracy derives only quality labels from them. Nothing exposes the glyph cascade users actually see, which depends on three inputs an eval array cannot carry: the rank-2 gap, the best-move match, and sacrifice detection.

AnnotationKernel.classifyGlyph(wpDrop:wpBefore:wpAfter:gap:playedBestMove:
                               opponentMissed:involvesSacrifice:absEvalCp:)

    wpDrop >= 0.20                                        -> .blunder
    wpDrop >= 0.10                          -> opponentMissed ? .miss : .mistake
    wpDrop >= 0.05                          -> opponentMissed ? .miss : .dubious

    wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.15 && absEvalCp < 50_000
                  && wpBefore < 0.75 && involvesSacrifice -> .brilliant
    wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.08 && wpBefore < 0.40       -> .great
    wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.08 && wpBefore < 0.55
                  && wpAfter > 0.60                       -> .great
    playedBestMove && gap >= 0.03                         -> .best
    wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.03                          -> .excellent
    wpDrop < 0.05 && gap >= 0.06                          -> .good
    otherwise                                             -> nil

    wpBefore       = winProbability(evals[i].bestCp)
    wpAfter        = 1 - winProbability(evals[i+1].bestCp)
    wpDrop         = max(0, wpBefore - wpAfter)
    gap            = winProbability(bestCp) - winProbability(secondBestCp),
                     0 when no rank-2 line was recorded
    opponentMissed = (prevWP - (1 - wpBefore)) >= 0.10 && wpBefore > 0.55

Sacrifice is the only non-eval predicate in the cascade and the sole gate on .brilliant, so a --sacrifice-only mode over {fen_before, uci} is worth having: it is board-only, needs no evals, and lets the brilliant precondition be measured over an arbitrary corpus.

let results = AnnotationKernel.computeAnnotations(
    inputs: inputs,   // [AnnotationComputeInput(positionBefore:positionAfter:move:)]
    evals: evals,     // [AnnotationEval]; evals[0] is the start position
    startIsWhite: true
)
for result in results {
    result.glyph          // MoveAnnotation?
    result.moveQuality
    result.moveAccuracy
    result.engineBestMoveUCI
    result.engineEval     // white-POV formatted string
}

Warning

computeAnnotations breaks at evals.count - 1 inputs. A caller supplying n moves must supply n + 1 evals, or the tail is silently dropped. The CLI should reject a length mismatch as a per-line error rather than emit a short array — the same discipline CombinationMiningKernel.candidates(from:) already applies internally.

docs.title: store
docs.text:
FileJSONBlobStore is the portable persistence substrate, and nothing in the six shipped commands inspects one. A store command makes a blob directory a debuggable artifact: enumerate keys by namespace, dump one key's raw JSON, snapshot the whole directory, or validate the routing invariants without decoding any progress schema.

namespaces routed by FileJSONBlobStore.fileURL(forKey:)
    flat                <root>/<key>.json
    authored heads      <root>/authored-heads/
    authored revisions  <root>/authored-revisions/
    authored index      <root>/authored-index/
    authored witnesses  <root>/authored-frontier-witnesses/
    import checkpoints  <root>/import-checkpoints/
    endgame mining      <root>/endgame-mining/<content address, 3-4 components>

enumeration ceiling  FileJSONBlobStore.maximumEnumeratedJSONKeys = 1_000_000
    Payload reads never begin after this bound is exceeded.

snapshotJSONByKey excludes, unconditionally:
    authored infrastructure keys
    endgame-mining infrastructure keys
    legacy flattened "personalEndgames_" keys
    and fails — rather than returning a partial map — if an enumerated file
    disappears between the listing and the read

let store = FileJSONBlobStore(directory: URL(fileURLWithPath: path))

switch store.storedJSONKeysReportingError() {
case .value(let keys):   // [String]
    for key in keys {
        switch store.loadJSONReportingError(forKey: key) {
        case .value(let json): break
        case .missing:         break
        case .failure(let message): break
        }
    }
case .failure(let message):
    break
}

let snapshot = store.snapshotJSONByKey(
    excludingKeys: [],
    includingAuthoredRecords: true
)

Note

The read APIs deliberately return three-case results rather than String?. A CLI must not collapse .failure into .missing: the whole reason the distinction exists is that an unreadable blob and an absent blob call for opposite recovery decisions.

docs.title: The storage seam makes every Codable store CLI-reachable
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because it changes what the stateful proposals cost: FileJSONBlobStore is a public struct conforming to JSONBlobStore, imports only Foundation, and has a public initializer that takes a directory. Every parameter after directory has a default, so a CLI constructs one in a line and gets the same persistence the app uses on any non-Apple platform.

let store = FileJSONBlobStore(directory: URL(fileURLWithPath: path))

var ratings = TacticsRatingStore.load(from: store)
let delta = ratings.recordAttempt(
    puzzleKey: key,
    difficulty: .medium,
    outcome: .correct,
    in: store
)

var srs = DrillSRS.load(from: store)
srs.recordCorrect(key: key, to: store)
srs.isDue(key: key, now: Date())

load(from:) and save(to:) come from a protocol extension on BlobBackedStore, so any conformer works with no per-store wiring. The public conformers, with their verified blob keys:

Store Blob key TacticsRatingStore tacticsRating TacticsPerformanceStore tacticsPerformance DrillSRS drillSRS RepertoireDrillStats repertoireDrillStats CombinationPuzzleStore combinationPuzzles VoiceTranscriptLog voiceTranscriptLog EBoardDiagnosticCapture eBoardDiagnosticCapture

Two more stores are stateless namespaces that read and write a blob directly rather than conforming: BlunderMasteryStore (key blunderMastery, masteryThreshold = 3) and TrainProgressCache (key trainProgress.<PracticeMode.rawValue>).

Six of these keys are semantically mergeable, which is what makes the merge-progress proposal testable at all:

ProgressBlobSemanticMerger.mergeableKeys
    tacticsRating          tacticsPerformance     drillSRS
    repertoireDrillStats   blunderMastery         endgameHistory

mergedResult(forKey:candidates:)
    candidates sorted by (updatedAt descending, json ascending)
        — the json tiebreak is what makes the choice independent of fetch order
    only consumer-decodable candidates contribute
        — a syntactically valid but wrong-schema sibling cannot lend its
          newer timestamp to the merged union

The consequence for this page: progress, merge-progress, and the stateful half of authored need no new persistence design. They need a directory path and a flag.

Note

FileJSONBlobStore also has an init(subdirectory:) that resolves against the user's document directory. That is the app-shaped initializer; a CLI should use init(directory:) so the store location is an explicit argument rather than an environment-dependent default.

docs.title: What is deliberately not worth exposing
docs.text:
Being able to wrap a seam is not a reason to. Four classes should stay out of the CLI permanently.

Presentation policies whose only consumer is a view. StatsChartPresentationPolicy.servingPathLabel(for:) returns "Move-quality model", "Exact-opponent Maia", or "Neutral-1500 Maia (provisional)". EstimatedStrengthServingCoverage.label assembles a sentence like "Maia-refined: 12 of 40 games (9 exact, 3 neutral-1500 provisional)". TacticsExtractionMode.displayName and .prompt return "Punish" and "Your opponent erred — find the punishing move.". BoardCatalog.displayName(key:) names a hardware brand. These are real cross-platform contracts and they are worth pinning — as fields inside a command that already computes the underlying value, never as a command of their own. This is why coverage is proposed around estimatedStrengthServingCoverage(for:), which returns counts, and not around the label that formats them. A subcommand whose entire output is a noun phrase is a string table with a process around it.

Mode and selection policies that exist to keep a control populated. StatsChartPresentationPolicy.normalizedMode(_:) and .effectiveMode(storedMode:canShowEstimated:) map a persisted string onto one of two segmented-control values, failing safely to the rating chart. normalizedEstimatedSpeed(_:) folds any speed outside estimatedStrengthSpeeds down to .rapid. Correct, portable, and completely uninteresting outside a view that has a segment to select.

Anything that needs live hardware. The BLE transports and the live half of the e-board stack cannot run in a batch process at all: they need a radio, a paired board, and a human moving pieces. Only the pure kernels underneath are proposed — BoardCatalog's static tables, and BoardDiffResolver / BoardTakebackDetector driven from synthetic occupancy arrays. That split is deliberate: board-catalog and board-diff are in tier 2, and board-replay, which needs a captured session transcript and a Game conformer, is below the line.

Anything that mutates an object graph. AnnotationKernel.computeAnnotations is pure and returns value types; applyAnnotations writes onto MoveNode through a Game. The CLI wants the pure half. The rule generalizes: when a kernel splits into a pure compute and a thin write pass, the CLI wraps the compute and stops. The same reasoning keeps drill-replay and board-replay below the line — both are reducers that expect a caller owning mutable board state.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • fianchetto-cli — the six shipped commands, the JSON-Lines protocol, and the four-requirement CLICommand seam a new subcommand implements

docs.title: maia
docs.text: Runs the app's Maia backfill inference path headless: for one player in one game, it emits the 11-point Elo-grid log-likelihood vector that the v4.1 ensemble consumes as evidence. Policy and math are linked kit code; only the Core ML transport is mirrored.

docs.title: stdin
docs.text:
One JSON object per line.

Field Type Required Default Meaning id String yes — echoed on the response line uci_moves [String] one of the two — moves from the standard start position pgn String one of the two — a PGN game; headers optional color String yes — "white" or "black" — which side is the scored player provider String yes — e.g. "lichess", "chesscom"; decides opponent conditioning opponent_rating Int or null no null the opponent's provider rating

Both input kinds are normalized to SAN move text before parsing, so they ride the identical path: uci_moves are replayed through UCIParser.uciToMove + Game.apply and re-emitted as their recorded SAN notations; pgn goes through PGNParser.parse and then parseMainLineSnapshot.

The parsed start position must equal Position.initial(). Non-standard starts are rejected, matching the kit's SetUp / FEN / variant eligibility gate.

docs.title: stdout
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning id String the request id maia_log_likes [Double] 11 entries, one per grid point — or [] when no owner move qualified positions_scored Int qualifying owner positions; 0 in the empty case opponent_conditioning String "exact-lichess-opponent" or "neutral-lichess-1500" opponent_elo Double the elo_oppo value actually fed to the network

The terminal empty shape mirrors the app's "no qualifying owner moves" receipt: an empty vector with count 0, not an error. The conditioning fields are still reported, because they are resolved from the provider and rating before any position is scored.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning Default --model-path <path> the Maia3CoreML.mlpackage to load <repo>/Fianchetto/Resources/Maia3CoreML.mlpackage, located by walking five parents up from #filePath --compute-units <u> cpuOnly | cpuAndNeuralEngine | all | gated; any other value is a hard error cpuOnly, chosen for determinism

gated mirrors the app's MaiaComputeUnitGate: load a candidate model under cpuAndNeuralEngine, run the sanity probe, use the ANE only on a pass and fall back to cpuOnly otherwise, logging the verdict to stderr. Unlike the app, the CLI re-probes fresh on every run instead of caching a verdict in UserDefaults — a CLI process should not write the app's persisted verdict. The app's own default is that gated verdict; the CLI's is cpuOnly so repeated runs are bit-identical.

docs.title: Decision rules
docs.text:
Three policy decisions determine the output, and all three are kit calls.

The grid. MaiaBackfillPolicy.eloGrid is 11 points read at runtime from the v4.1 ensemble calibration artifact, falling back to the literal [600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2400, 2600].

Opponent conditioning. The exact opponent rating is used only under one narrow condition:

MaiaBackfillPolicy.scoringContext(...)
    normalized provider == "lichess"
      AND opponent rating present
      AND rating in trainedOpponentEloRange = 400...3200
        -> elo_oppo = that rating,  conditioning = exact-lichess-opponent
    every other case
        -> elo_oppo = neutralOpponentElo = 1500,
           conditioning = neutral-lichess-1500

That is not a provider preference; the v4.1 collector only ever admitted Lichess opponent ratings, so a Chess.com rating would be a number from a different scale. The conditioning label travels with the evidence and decides which serving path estimate reports.

Which positions count.

MaiaBackfillPolicy.qualifiesForInference(plyIndex:legalMoveCount:)
    plyIndex >= 8  AND  legalMoveCount > 2

the player-color overload additionally requires the scored side to be to move

Before any inference, two encoding guards must hold for every qualifying position, or the whole game is rejected: tokens.count == 768 (64 × 12) and policyIndex in 0..<4352.

The sweep. One batch-1 inference per (grid point × position), accumulated in grid order:

for eloSelf in eloGrid:                 // 11 outer steps
    for each qualifying position:
        logits = model(tokens, elo_self: eloSelf, elo_oppo: contextElo)
        sums[gridIndex] += logSoftmaxAt(logits, idx: policyIndex)

a single non-finite value aborts the ENTIRE vector — partial evidence is never
emitted

The whole sweep runs inside a detached userInitiated task, like every Core ML call in the app.

docs.title: The always-on sanity oracle
docs.text:
maia has no --self-test, because it does something stronger: a fail-closed probe runs on every invocation, against the resolved model path, before any game is scored.

one inference on the initial position at elo_self = elo_oppo = 1200
    top decoded move must be e4 or d4          with probability > 0.30
    when a value head is present:              win < 0.85 and loss < 0.85

Decoding goes through the linked Maia3Encoding.decodeOutput. A missing model file, a failed probe, an invalid encoding, or a missing logits_move output each raise a named error and stop the run — a wrong or silently mis-compiled model can never produce evidence.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"id":"italian-white-lichess","uci_moves":["e2e4","e7e5","g1f3","b8c6","f1c4","f8c5","c2c3","g8f6","d2d4","e5d4","c3d4","c5b4","b1c3","f6e4"],"color":"white","provider":"lichess","opponent_rating":1650}' \
  '{"id":"italian-black-chesscom","uci_moves":["e2e4","e7e5","g1f3","b8c6","f1c4","f8c5","c2c3","g8f6","d2d4","e5d4","c3d4","c5b4","b1c3","f6e4"],"color":"black","provider":"chesscom","opponent_rating":1650}' \
  '{"id":"too-short-no-qualifying","uci_moves":["e2e4","e7e5","g1f3","b8c6","f1c4","f8c5"],"color":"white","provider":"lichess","opponent_rating":2000}' \
  | .build/debug/fianchetto-cli maia

{"id":"italian-white-lichess","maia_log_likes":[-15.068658736499842,-13.45112097051431,…,-13.165787875335432],"opponent_conditioning":"exact-lichess-opponent","opponent_elo":1650,"positions_scored":3}
{"id":"italian-black-chesscom","maia_log_likes":[-16.71934077426711,-15.244745311102697,…,-8.88329170726237],"opponent_conditioning":"neutral-lichess-1500","opponent_elo":1500,"positions_scored":3}
{"id":"too-short-no-qualifying","maia_log_likes":[],"opponent_conditioning":"exact-lichess-opponent","opponent_elo":2000,"positions_scored":0}

Three things to read off that output. The same 14-ply game scores 3 positions for either side, because only plies ≥ 8 with more than two legal moves qualify and only the scored side's moves count. The identical game conditions differently by provider: Lichess keeps the exact 1650, Chess.com falls back to the neutral 1500 prior. And the six-ply game produces the terminal empty shape rather than an error, while still reporting the conditioning it would have used.

Model load and the probe verdict are written to stderr, so stdout stays a clean JSONL stream:

maia: loading model at …/Maia3CoreML.mlpackage (compute units: cpuOnly)
maia: model loaded; resolved-path sanity probe passed; grid [600.0, 800.0, …]

docs.title: project
docs.text:
Replays one account pool's chronological game sequence through the serving-side strength projection — the Kalman tracker, the personalized offset calibrator, and the Chess.com anchored per-game projection — wired in exactly the order StatsKernel.eloPoints wires them. This is the command that reproduces the number the app charts.

One run models exactly one account pool

A pool is one provider × account × speed group. The app never shares a tracker or a calibrator across pools, and neither should you: feed one pool per process, oldest game first. Grouping — and the app's decision to skip correspondence pools entirely — stays with the caller.

docs.title: stdin
docs.text:
One JSON object per line, in chronological order.

Field Type Required Default Meaning id String yes — echoed on the response line performance object or null no absent the game's Elo estimate; absent or null marks an unannotated game actual_rating Int or null no null the provider's rating tag for this game

performance members:

Member Type Required Default Meaning elo Double yes — the point estimate ci_low / ci_high Double yes — must satisfy ci_low <= elo <= ci_high accuracy Double yes — 0–100; part of the projection validity gate sample_moves Int yes — this side's move count; sets the evidence weight used_maia Bool no false keys which residual bucket this game calibrates

The five required members are exactly the fields estimate emits, so building the request is a rename and a wrap.

docs.title: stdout
docs.text:
Only annotated games produce a line. An unannotated game emits nothing at all; it still advances the anchor through projectionCalibrator.observe(actualRating:), and only when the pool personalizes to Chess.com.

Field Type Meaning id String the request id strength_mean Double the charted number for this game strength_ci68 [Double] [lo, hi] strength_ci95 [Double] [lo, hi] calibration String "lichessEquivalent" / "chessComCalibrating" / "chessComPersonalized" calibration_sample_count Int labels behind the offset uses_empirical_intervals Bool whether the interval came from conformal errors rather than the propagated form projection object the anchored per-game dot — the key is absent until the calibrator warms up

projection members: anchor, mapped_performance, evidence_weight, mean, interval68 [lo, hi], interval95 [lo, hi], offset, sample_count, used_maia.

strength_mean is the slow posterior for the account; projection.mean is this game's "played like" dot, anchored on the most recent strictly earlier rating. They are different numbers answering different questions, and the command emits both.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning Default --source <s> the provider for this pool; lowercased before comparison "chesscom"

Only chesscom enables personalization: personalizesToChessCom = (source == "chesscom"). Any other value disables both Chess.com paths, which means the personalized offset is never applied, no projection is ever emitted, no label is ever observed, and every line reports calibration: "lichessEquivalent".

docs.title: Wiring order
docs.text:
The order is the whole point of the command, and step 6 must come last:

per pool
    tracker  = StrengthTracker(priorMean: 1500, priorSigma: 300)
    local    = PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator()
    proj     = ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator()

per game (strict prequential)
    unannotated -> proj.observe(actualRating:) only; NO output line
    1. projection = proj.projection(for: performance)      // strictly earlier ratings
    2. tracker    = tracker.updated(with: performance)
    3. personalized = local.prediction(baseStrength: tracker.posteriorMean,
                                       baseSigma:    tracker.posteriorSigma)
    4. select displayed mean / CI68 / CI95 / calibration label
    5. emit the point
    6. local.observe(baseStrength:actualRating:personalizedPrediction:)
       proj.observe(actualRating:rawPerformanceElo:usedMaiaRefinement:projection:)

Neither projection(for:) nor prediction(baseStrength:baseSigma:) takes a current-rating parameter, so this game's label physically cannot leak into its own estimate. Observing before emitting would silently turn an honest forecast into a fit.

Step 4 is a two-branch selection:

Condition mean / intervals calibration calibration_sample_count uses_empirical_intervals a personalized prediction exists its mean, interval68, interval95 chessComPersonalized the prediction's count the prediction's flag Chess.com pool, still warming up tracker.posteriorMean, tracker.ci, mean ± 1.96σ chessComCalibrating the local calibrator's sampleCount false any other provider the same tracker values lichessEquivalent the same false

docs.title: Calibrator constants
docs.text:
Constant PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator residual window 20 20 minimum samples before answering 20 20 forecast-error window 50 100 minimum samples for empirical intervals 20 20

The 20-label warm-up is directly observable in the output: calibration flips from chessComCalibrating to chessComPersonalized at exactly the 20th observed label.

Projection-specific constants:

weight            = 0.60 * sample_moves / (sample_moves + 15.0)    // 30 moves -> 0.40
mappedPerformance = clamp(elo + pathOffset, 100, 3500)
weightedDelta     = weight * (mappedPerformance - anchor)
cappedDelta       = clamp(weightedDelta, -250.0, +250.0)
mean              = clamp(anchor + cappedDelta, 100, 3500)

propagated interval arms (fewer than 20 strictly earlier projection errors)
    offsetStandardError = 1.2533 * max(50.0, 1.4826 * MAD) / sqrt(n)
    lowerSigma = sqrt((elo - ci_low)² + offsetStandardError²)
    upperSigma = sqrt((ci_high - elo)² + offsetStandardError²)
    bound      = mean ± multiplier * weight * sigma      // 1 for 68%, 1.96 for 95%

empirical interval arms (>= 20 strictly earlier projection errors) — conformal
    half = the finite-sample quantile of the sorted absolute errors

Residuals and forecast errors are kept in separate buckets keyed on used_maia, so a partially backfilled pool can never calibrate one serving path with the other path's residuals.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A performance violating ci_low <= elo <= ci_high emits {"id", "error"} and is skipped without disturbing any state. Unparseable lines emit an id-less error and the stream continues.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A pool of identical games — every one estimated at 1600 ± 100 over 30 moves, against a steady Chess.com rating of 1520 — isolates what the calibrators do:

for i in $(seq 1 22); do
  printf '{"id":"g%d","performance":{"elo":1600,"ci_low":1500,"ci_high":1700,"accuracy":79.8,"sample_moves":30,"used_maia":false},"actual_rating":1520}\n' "$i"
done | .build/debug/fianchetto-cli project --source chesscom

The first game, with the pool at its 1500/300 prior:

{"calibration":"chessComCalibrating","calibration_sample_count":0,"id":"g1","strength_ci68":[1495.2471117358514,1685.2406931421974],"strength_ci95":[1404.0501926608056,1776.4376122172432],"strength_mean":1590.2439024390244,"uses_empirical_intervals":false}

No projection key: the anchored calibrator has no residual window yet. After the 20th label, both change:

{"calibration":"chessComPersonalized","calibration_sample_count":20,"id":"g21","projection":{"anchor":1520,"evidence_weight":0.4,"interval68":[1479.609218653262,1560.390781346738],"interval95":[1440.8340685603935,1599.1659314396065],"mapped_performance":1520,"mean":1520,"offset":-80,"sample_count":20,"used_maia":false},"strength_ci68":[1438.8188876120516,1601.3024517274134],"strength_ci95":[1360.826776836678,1679.2945625027871],"strength_mean":1520.0606696697325,"uses_empirical_intervals":false}

evidence_weight is exactly 0.60 × 30 / (30 + 15) = 0.4, and offset is −80 — the median residual of a pool whose estimates ran 80 Elo above its Chess.com ratings. Because mapped_performance lands on the anchor, mean does too.

docs.title: Seam provenance
docs.text:
Linked — StrengthTracker, PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator, ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator, and the EstimatedStrengthCalibration label enum are all the app's own types, called directly.

Mirrored — only the wiring order above, which lives in StatsKernel.eloPoints in the kit's stats pass. The CLI reproduces the sequence line-cited; it does not reimplement any calculation.

var tracker = StrengthTracker(priorMean: 1500, priorSigma: 300)
var trend = PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator()
var projections = ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator()

let projection = projections.projection(for: performance)
tracker = tracker.updated(with: performance)
let personalized = trend.prediction(
    baseStrength: tracker.posteriorMean,
    baseSigma: tracker.posteriorSigma
)
// … emit the point here, and only then observe this game's label.
trend.observe(
    baseStrength: tracker.posteriorMean,
    actualRating: actualRating,
    personalizedPrediction: personalized
)
projections.observe(
    actualRating: actualRating,
    rawPerformanceElo: performance.elo,
    usedMaiaRefinement: performance.usedMaiaRefinement,
    projection: projection
)

docs.title: track
docs.text: Runs the app's Bayesian StrengthTracker over an ordered sequence of per-game Elo estimates and emits the posterior after each game. It is the smallest of the six commands: a Kalman update, a JSON line, no calibration.

docs.title: stdin
docs.text:
One JSON object per line, in game order. The output of estimate is directly pipe-compatible — its extra keys are ignored by the decoder.

Field Type Required Default Meaning id String yes — echoed on the response line elo Double yes — this game's point estimate ci_low Double yes — must satisfy ci_low <= elo ci_high Double yes — must satisfy elo <= ci_high

Accuracy and move count are not read by the update, so they need not be supplied; the command fills the carrier with zeros for them.

docs.title: stdout
docs.text:
One JSON object per line — the posterior after that game.

Field Type Meaning id String the request id posterior_mean Double the strength estimate after this game posterior_sigma Double the posterior standard deviation ci68_low / ci68_high Double mean ± 1σ

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Meaning Default Where the default comes from --prior-mean <x> initial Elo belief 1500 the app's per-pool prior in StatsKernel --prior-sigma <x> initial uncertainty 300 the same seeding call --process-tau <x> process noise per game 50 StrengthTracker's own default

Each value must parse as a Double or the command errors. τ = 50 corresponds to roughly 150 Elo of drift over 9 games, which is the app's assumption about how fast real strength moves.

docs.title: The update
docs.text:
predVariance      = posteriorSigma² + processTau²
ciHalfWidth       = (ci_high - ci_low) / 2
obsVariance       = max(1.0, ciHalfWidth²)                 // guards a zero-width CI
posteriorVariance = 1 / (1/predVariance + 1/obsVariance)
posteriorMean     = posteriorVariance * (mean/predVariance + elo/obsVariance)
posteriorSigma    = sqrt(posteriorVariance)
ci68              = posteriorMean ± posteriorSigma

The observation variance is the squared CI half-width, which is why nothing else needs a weighting scheme: everything that widens an interval upstream — few moves, OTB classical, a below-floor estimate — automatically shrinks that game's influence on the posterior. A game with a ±400 interval moves the mean far less than one with a ±100 interval, without either command knowing about the other.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A row violating ci_low <= elo <= ci_high emits {"id", "error"} and is skipped without disturbing the posterior. Unparseable lines emit an id-less error and the stream continues.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Two identical games, from the default 1500 / 300 prior:

printf '%s\n' \
  '{"id":"g1","elo":1600,"ci_low":1500,"ci_high":1700}' \
  '{"id":"g2","elo":1600,"ci_low":1500,"ci_high":1700}' \
  | .build/debug/fianchetto-cli track

{"ci68_high":1685.2406931421974,"ci68_low":1495.2471117358514,"id":"g1","posterior_mean":1590.2439024390244,"posterior_sigma":94.9967907031729}
{"ci68_high":1668.6391902089251,"ci68_low":1522.2956539837098,"id":"g2","posterior_mean":1595.4674220963175,"posterior_sigma":73.17176811260755}

Working the first line by hand: predVariance = 300² + 50² = 92 500, obsVariance = 100² = 10 000, so posteriorVariance = 1 / (1/92 500 + 1/10 000) = 9 024.39… and posteriorMean = 9 024.39… × (1500/92 500 + 1600/10 000) = 1590.2439…. The posterior sits far closer to the observation than to the prior because the prior is much more diffuse; the second game moves it only 5 more Elo, while sigma keeps falling.

The whole point of --prior-mean / --prior-sigma is replaying a pool that is already warm: seed with a previous run's posterior_mean and posterior_sigma and the continuation is identical to having processed the earlier games in the same run.

docs.title: Seam provenance
docs.text:
Fully linked to StrengthTracker.updated(with:). The tracker is a value type with pure value semantics — updated(with:) returns a new tracker and leaves the receiver alone — so the command's entire state is one var. The only CLI-original code is constructing the GamePerformance carrier, where accuracy, sampleMoves, and belowCalibrationFloor are inert placeholders because the Kalman update reads only elo and ci.

var tracker = StrengthTracker(priorMean: 1500, priorSigma: 300, processTau: 50)

for performance in performancesInGameOrder {
    tracker = tracker.updated(with: performance)
    tracker.posteriorMean
    tracker.posteriorSigma
    tracker.ci              // 68%: mean ± 1σ
}

docs.title: Analysis Math
docs.text: The pure-logic layer over the model: accuracy aggregation, procedural endgame generation, and streak math.

docs.title: AccuracyAggregator
docs.text:
AccuracyAggregator computes per-side, per-phase accuracy from a white-POV centipawn array. It is a set of pure functions, so accuracy can be aggregated across many games off the main actor.

public enum AccuracyAggregator {
    public enum Phase: String, CaseIterable, Sendable { case opening, middlegame, endgame }

    public struct GameAccuracy: Sendable {
        public let overall: Double?
        public let overallSampleCount: Int          // moves represented by `overall`
        public let phases: [Phase: Double]
        public let phaseSampleCounts: [Phase: Int]   // moves represented by each phase average
        public let moveBuckets: [Int: Double]
        public let moveBucketSampleCounts: [Int: Int]   // moves represented by each bucket average
    }

    public static let moveBucketSize: Int   // 5
    public static func bucketStart(forMoveNumber: Int) -> Int
    public static func bucketLabel(start: Int) -> String      // "6–10"
    public static func accuracy(evalsJSON: String, startIsWhite: Bool, color: PieceColor) -> GameAccuracy?
    public static func winProbability(cp: Double) -> Double
    public static func moveAccuracy(wpBefore: Double, wpAfter: Double) -> Double
}

let acc = AccuracyAggregator.accuracy(
    evalsJSON: game.evalsJSON,    // a JSON array of white-POV centipawns
    startIsWhite: true,           // active color at move 1
    color: .white                 // the side you want accuracy for
)

The two formulas are shared across FianchettoKit (the same constants ChessCore uses for engine evaluations):

  • winProbability(cp:) is the logistic 1 / (1 + exp(-0.00368208 * cp)) — the same constant as UCIInfo.Score.winProbability; EngineAnalysis.Evaluation.whiteWinProbability delegates to this single constant rather than holding its own copy.
  • moveAccuracy(wpBefore:wpAfter:) maps the win-probability drop to a 0–100 accuracy: min(100, max(0, 103.1668·exp(-0.04354·drop) − 3.1668)).

Note

GameAccuracy is a public type with directly readable public let fields — overall, phases, and moveBuckets, each paired with a sample-count field (overallSampleCount, phaseSampleCounts, moveBucketSampleCounts) giving the actual move count behind that average. Obtain a value from accuracy(...) and read the fields directly. The standalone winProbability(cp:) and moveAccuracy(...) helpers are also fully public.

docs.title: EndgameArchetype
docs.text:
EndgameArchetype generates random legal endgame FENs for a trainer — each case produces a fresh position matching its theme, for unlimited replay value.

public enum EndgameArchetype: String, Hashable, Codable, Sendable, CaseIterable {
    case kqVsK, krVsK, k2bVsK, kbnVsK, kpVsK, kqVsKp, lucena, philidor

    public var displayCategory: String   // "K+Q vs K", "Lucena", ...
    public func randomFEN() -> String
    public var fallbackFEN: String
}

let fen = EndgameArchetype.kbnVsK.randomFEN()   // a fresh, legal K+B+N vs K

"Legal" means playable: the side not to move isn't in check, the side to move has a legal move, the kings aren't adjacent, and so on. The position uses stockfishSafeFEN; if random generation can't satisfy the constraints after ~200 attempts, it falls back to a known-good static FEN.

docs.title: Custom endgames
docs.text:
CustomEndgameConfig lets a user pick how many of each non-king piece each side has:

public struct CustomEndgameConfig: Hashable, Sendable, Codable {
    public var white: PieceCounts
    public var black: PieceCounts
    public var totalPieces: Int
    public var summary: String           // "K+R+P vs K+B+N"
    public var isValid: Bool             // totalPieces <= 32
    public func randomFEN() -> String?   // nil if 200 retries can't satisfy it
    public var fallbackFEN: String
}

Positions with more than 7 pieces fall outside the Lichess tablebase, so the trainer skips win verification for them.

docs.title: StreakMath
docs.text:
Consecutive-correct streak math, shared by the drill stat stores. Callers map attempts to [Bool] (most-recent last):

public enum StreakMath {
    public static func current(_ flags: [Bool]) -> Int   // trailing run of `true`
    public static func best(_ flags: [Bool]) -> Int      // longest run anywhere
}

let outcomes = [true, true, false, true, true, true]
StreakMath.current(outcomes)   // 3
StreakMath.best(outcomes)      // 3

EvalJSON.decode(jsonString)               // [Double]   white-POV centipawns
PieceColor.mover(ply: 2, startIsWhite: true)   // .white
