docs.title: Authored History & the Mutation Journal
docs.text: How user-authored notes and board marks survive concurrent edits across devices, backup/restore, and legacy migration — a small causal CRDT kernel (Sources/FianchettoKit/Authored), not generic last-write-wins.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Everything else in the library — imported games, engine evaluations, cached analysis — can be recomputed or re-fetched. A user's notes and board-mark annotations cannot, so they're reconciled by a purpose-built kernel instead of the ordinary "newest updatedAt wins" merge that suffices for everything else. The kernel tracks causality with a bounded vector clock per (logicalGameID, field) pair, never a timestamp: two edits are either causally ordered (one observed the other) or concurrent (neither did), and concurrent edits are never silently discarded, only surfaced as a conflict. The two independently reconciled fields are AuthoredField.notes and .boardMarks.

The rest of this page follows data through five layers: the causal model (vector clock, immutable revision, canonical values); the reconciliation algorithm, AuthoredReconciler, called by every platform and every backup/restore path; the edit path, turning one keystroke into a crash-safe committed revision; backup, restore, and recovery; and supporting infrastructure — the frontier cache, promotion-stable game identity, and retention/migration policy.

docs.title: AuthoredReplicaID and AuthoredVectorClock
docs.text:
AuthoredReplicaID is a validated installation identity — commonly a lowercase UUID, though the format isn't UUID-specific so a legacy importer can own a separately-namespaced synthetic head. It's capped at maximumUTF8Bytes = 96 bytes, ASCII charset [0-9A-Za-z\-._].

AuthoredVectorClock is a [AuthoredReplicaID: UInt64] map bounded at maximumReplicaEntries = 32 replicas. Its relation(to:) is the whole of CRDT causality for this kernel:

relation(lhs, rhs):
    for each replica present in lhs OR rhs:
        hasGreater |= lhs[replica] > rhs[replica]
        hasLess    |= lhs[replica] < rhs[replica]
        if hasGreater && hasLess: return .concurrent   // short-circuits
    if hasGreater: return .dominates
    if hasLess:    return .dominated
    return .equal

A zero counter is invalid, not normalized away

validate() rejects any counter of 0 outright instead of dropping the entry. Silently dropping a zero-valued replica entry would make a real concurrent edit look like dominance.

docs.title: AuthoredHead — the immutable per-replica revision
docs.text:
AuthoredHead<Value> is the causal fact itself: schemaVersion, logicalGameID, authorReplicaID, clock, value, authoredAtMilliseconds. currentSchemaVersion = 1, maximumLogicalGameIDBytes = 512, and maximumEncodedBytes = 900 * 1_024 — deliberately under CloudKit's 1 MiB record ceiling, checked after JSON escaping (encoded()), not estimated from raw text length.

New heads are never built directly by editors — authoring(observing:) is the one place a new clock entry gets minted:

authoring(logicalGameID, authorReplicaID, value, observing: heads, authoredAtMilliseconds):
    guard heads.count <= 32                              // maximumReplicaHeads
    guard every head.logicalGameID == logicalGameID
    guard heads have distinct (replicaID, logicalGameID, field) storage keys
    joined = merge(heads.map(\.clock))                   // per-replica max()
    clock  = joined.incrementing(authorReplicaID)         // +1 for this replica
    → the resulting head causally dominates every branch the editor actually saw

Every head also carries a revisionProof, a stable SHA-256 tie-break for otherwise-indistinguishable candidates — explicitly documented as "never used as a substitute for the vector clock":

revisionProof = SHA256(length-prefixed concat of:
    logicalGameID, field.rawValue, authorReplicaID.rawValue,
    value.sha256, String(authoredAtMilliseconds),
    "replica=counter" for each clock entry, sorted by replica)
Type Kind Key facts AuthoredReplicaID validated string 96-byte ceiling, [0-9A-Za-z\-._] AuthoredVectorClock bounded map 32 replicas max, zero counters rejected AuthoredHead<Value> immutable fact schema 1, 512-byte game ID, 900 KiB encoded ceiling AuthoredHeadStorageKey (replicaID, logicalGameID, field) identity of one mutable compact-head row AuthoredHeadCandidate<Value> {copyID, isAnnotatedCopy, head} one physical copy's context; annotation never affects dominance AuthoredFieldIdentity Comparable (logicalGameID, field) the coarser identity one field's entire causal history is grouped under — ordered by logicalGameID, then field.rawValue, so backup, health, and restore adapters share one grouping instead of each inventing their own

AuthoredNotesHead and AuthoredBoardMarksHead are the two field-specialized typealiases actually threaded through the reconciler and edit path — AuthoredHead<AuthoredNotesValue> and AuthoredHead<AuthoredBoardMarksValue> respectively. AuthoredMutationPlanner.makeIntent and the edit-path examples below traffic in these, not the bare generic AuthoredHead<Value>.

docs.title: Canonical values
docs.text:
AuthoredCanonicalValue is the protocol every reconciled payload implements: a static field, a static maximumPayloadBytes, a canonicalPayload, and a sha256. Two conformers exist today:

Value type Field Ceiling Canonicalization AuthoredNotesValue .notes 256 * 1_024 (256 KiB) exact UTF-8 bytes; U+0000 rejected AuthoredBoardMarksValue .boardMarks 768 * 1_024 (768 KiB) BoardMarkDocument.decodeStrict(source).encoded()

Notes preserve Unicode normalization and whitespace exactly — the proof is over the exact bytes shown to the user. U+0000 is rejected on every platform because Apple's SwiftData/SQLite bridge truncates strings at that scalar; rejecting it everywhere keeps the portable value lossless instead of allowing a snapshot an Apple store can't reproduce. Board marks decode/re-encode through BoardMarkDocument before hashing, so two physically different JSON strings meaning the same marks hash identically; their 768 KiB ceiling is a raw parser bound, while the authoritative CloudKit safety net is AuthoredHead's 900 KiB encoded-bytes ceiling (nesting this JSON inside a head can expand quotes and control characters substantially).

let notes = try AuthoredNotesValue(text: "Missed 23...Qxh7+ here.")
let marks = try AuthoredBoardMarksValue(source: boardMarksJSON)

notes.sha256            // hex SHA-256 over the exact UTF-8 bytes
notes.canonicalPayload   // the exact text

docs.title: AuthoredReconciler — the reconciliation algorithm
docs.text: AuthoredReconciler<Value> is the one piece of logic every platform, both backup paths, and restore all call, so replica capacity, conflict classification, and tie-break ordering can never drift between adapters. Causality always outranks annotation quality: isAnnotatedCopy only ever selects a projection representative among causally maximal, SHA-equivalent copies — never dominance, never a divergent branch.

docs.title: selectSameReplicaHistory
docs.text:
Collapses one replica's own head history down to its causal maximum:

selectSameReplicaHistory(heads, limit: 64):
    guard heads.count <= limit                     // maximumCandidates
    guard all heads share one AuthoredHeadStorageKey
    dedupe by revisionProof
    detect corruption: two heads with an *identical* clock but different
        values → hasRelationFailure = true (independent of scan order)
    reduce to the causally-maximal subset (drop anything another head dominates)
    if maximal.count != 1 OR hasRelationFailure:
        hasCausalConflict = true
        active = lexicographically-least maximal head,
                 ordered by (revisionProof, then full encoded JSON bytes)
    else:
        active = the sole maximal head
    → {active, alternates: other maximal heads, superseded, hasCausalConflict}

docs.title: reconcile
docs.text:
Reconciles across replicas — answers "what is this field's value right now, across every device":

reconcile(candidates):
    guard candidates.count <= 64                   // maximumCandidates
    guard all candidates share one logicalGameID, distinct copyIDs
    drop dominated candidates → causally-maximal set
    group the maximal set into AuthoredValueBranch<Value>s by SHA-equivalence
        (sha256 AND canonicalPayload both match)
    each branch's representative: isAnnotatedCopy wins first,
        then stable (copyID, storageKey, revisionProof) ordering
    preferred = first branch's representative (display choice only)
    hasConcurrentConflict = branches.count > 1

AuthoredValueBranch<Value> is just {representative, equivalentCandidates} — one causally-maximal, SHA-equivalent value plus every physical copy that carries it, so a branch is a projectable value, not a single head. Every branch stays in valueBranches even when hasConcurrentConflict is true — nothing is discarded; the caller decides whether to surface a conflict-resolution UI.

docs.title: planDirectProjection — the witnessed-value rule
docs.text:
What a live app or a restore actually applies to a visible row. Its central invariant: every direct value must be historically witnessed by a known compact head or immutable revision, or the call fails with .unexplainedDirectValue rather than accepting an unexplained byte string as fact.

planDirectProjection(frontierCandidates, historicalWitnesses, directCopies):
    guard directCopies have distinct copyIDs
    guard frontierCandidates.count <= 64     // maximumDirectProjectionFrontierCandidates
    guard historicalWitnesses.count <= 512   // maximumDirectProjectionHistoricalWitnesses
    guard every directCopy.value is witnessed by some known head's value
          (else: .unexplainedDirectValue)

    select each replica's active frontier head (selectReplicaHistories)
    historical witnesses NOT causally covered by that compact frontier
        rejoin reconciliation instead of being hidden
    reconcile the union →
        .noCausalState        (no history at all for this field)
        .converge(value:, changedCopyIDs:)   (unique non-conflicting branch)
        .concurrentConflict   (more than one branch survives)

Each element of directCopies is an AuthoredDirectValueCopy<CopyID, Value> — {copyID, value, isAnnotatedCopy}. It plays the same role as AuthoredHeadCandidate above but for a physical row that carries a value with no causal head of its own yet, which is exactly the shape a live import or a restored backup copy starts from.

The "rejoin" step matters: a physical copy can legitimately still show an older value after another copy advances the shared compact head — export retains that copy's exact immutable revision, and if the compact frontier doesn't causally cover it, that older fact stays part of the live decision instead of being quietly overwritten.

let candidates = try [headFromPhone, headFromDesktop].map {
    try AuthoredHeadCandidate(
        copyID: $0.authorReplicaID.rawValue,
        isAnnotatedCopy: false,
        head: $0
    )
}
let reconciliation = try AuthoredReconciler<AuthoredNotesValue>.reconcile(candidates)

if reconciliation.hasConcurrentConflict {
    // present reconciliation.valueBranches for the user to pick a winner
} else if let preferred = reconciliation.preferred {
    display(preferred.head.value.canonicalPayload)
}

docs.title: Storage key grammar — AuthoredBlobRecordCodec
docs.text:
Two namespaces exist because a single generic row can't support both "what does this replica currently say" (mutable, rewritten in place) and "prove exactly what was ever said" (append-only, never overwritten):

compactHeadNamespace       = "authoredHead.v1."
immutableRevisionNamespace = "authoredRevision.v1."

compact head key (one row per replica, rewritten on every edit):
  authoredHead.v1.<field>.<base64url(logicalGameID)>.<base64url(replicaID)>

immutable revision key (one row per revision, never rewritten):
  authoredRevision.v1.<field>.<base64url(logicalGameID)>.<base64url(replicaID)>.
      <20-digit zero-padded authorCounter>.<valueSHA256>.<revisionProof>

Tokens are base64url (+→-, /→_, = stripped). decodeToken() bounds any incoming key token to 683 UTF-8 bytes before decoding — the exact base64url expansion of the 512-byte logicalGameID ceiling — so a hostile or corrupted key can't amplify parsing cost. maximumCompactHeadCandidates = 64 bounds how many same-key compact siblings any adapter reconciles at once; a backup sidecar excludes the active row, so its ceiling is maximumCompactHeadAlternates = 63.

DecodedRecord case Storage role Mutable? .notesHead / .boardMarksHead compact per-replica projection yes — replaced on edit .notesRevision / .boardMarksRevision append-only causal fact no — write-once

Because both shapes wrap the identical AuthoredHead<Value> payload, AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.relation(_:_:) compares any two decoded records regardless of role. immutableRevisionProjection(for:) derives the canonical immutable row for any validated compact head, and rekeying(_:to:) losslessly moves a causal fact from a deterministic pre-marker alias key to its promoted canonical logicalGameID — clock, author, value, and timestamp stay byte-identical; only the key and proof regenerate. That's what lets game identity promotion fold a duplicate copy's causal history into its canonical lineage losslessly.

docs.title: The edit path
docs.text:
One user edit becomes a durable, causally-sound revision through four cooperating pieces, each owning one safety property:

AuthoredMutationPlanner.makeIntent   → builds the CAS intent (pure, no I/O)
AuthoredSemanticCAS.plan             → decides commit / repair / conflict
AuthoredMutationBlobWriter           → the actual two-phase durable write
AuthoredMutationIntentJournal        → single-slot WAL bridging the two writes

AuthoredMutationPlanner.makeIntent builds a LibraryData.PendingAuthoredMutation from an expected/desired field projection plus the visible causal frontier. Ordinary edits advance exactly the value branch the editor's own direct row showed (expected); if another copy already advanced past that branch, the planner falls back to the exact witnessed historical revision instead of manufacturing a precursor, and if the local replica's own head diverged onto a branch not superseded by this edit, planning fails with .localReplicaBranchWouldBeLost rather than clobbering it. An explicit conflict resolution instead passes resolvingFrontierToken — a PortableSHA256 hash over the exact reviewed frontier rows, sorted by (key, dataJSON) — proving the resolution applies to precisely that state; a changed frontier throws .directValueChanged.

let intent = try AuthoredMutationPlanner.makeIntent(
    incarnation: incarnation,
    logicalGameID: logicalGameID,
    replicaID: replicaID,
    field: .notes,
    expected: expectedProjection,
    desired: desiredProjection,
    frontierRows: frontierRows,
    authoredAtMilliseconds: Int64(Date().timeIntervalSince1970 * 1_000)
)

try AuthoredMutationIntentJournal.admit(intent, to: blobStore)
try AuthoredMutationBlobWriter.writeImmutableFacts(intent, to: blobStore)
try AuthoredMutationBlobWriter.writeCompactHead(intent, to: blobStore)
try AuthoredMutationIntentJournal.clear(intent, from: blobStore)

AuthoredSemanticCAS.plan is the exact decision table every storage adapter applies to a direct-value write — persistence-neutral, no I/O:

plan(current, expected, desired, mode):
    if current == desired:
        if mode == .resolveKnownFrontier AND current != expected:
            → .conflict(currentValue: current)
        → .repairMetadata(base: mode == .ordinaryEdit ? desired : expected)
    else if current != expected:
        → .conflict(currentValue: current)
    else:
        → .commitDirectValue

AuthoredMutationBlobWriter writes in two phases and read-back-verifies every byte — no last-write-wins. Immutable rows first: a pre-existing row at the same key with a different decoded value throws .immutableFactConflict; a byte-different but semantically identical row is rewritten to canonical bytes so SHA manifests don't retain two physical representations of one fact. The compact head second, and only if AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.relation(desired, existing) == .lhsDominates and the existing head's own immutable revision is already among the intent's own immutable rows from phase one — writeCompactHead checks this, it does not backfill; an intent that omits that revision fails closed with .compactHeadConflict instead.

AuthoredMutationIntentJournal is the single-slot WAL bridging those two writes (blobKey = FileJSONBlobStore.pendingAuthoredMutationKey). admit(_:to:) refuses to overwrite a different pending intent — only the byte-identical intent may be rewritten, to re-prove durability after an uncertain prior write. clear(_:from:) only removes the slot when the caller's expected intent still matches what's stored, then verifies removal. Android's replica identity is guarded the same way: AuthoredReplicaIdentity.loadOrCreate(in:key:) generates a fresh UUID().uuidString.lowercased() only when the blob is entirely absent, and returns .failure for anything malformed or unreadable rather than silently regenerating it — two devices sharing one compact replica head would erase history.

fianchetto-cli does not drive this edit surface: its annotate subcommand produces per-ply engine evaluations from a live Stockfish session, not authored notes or board marks, and none of the CLI's six implemented subcommands (annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project, track) touch this pipeline. An authored subcommand appears in the CLI's expansion proposals for offline inspection and fuzzing of the reconciler, but it is unimplemented and, even as proposed, reads and replays history rather than editing it — a scripted note or board-mark edit still has to go through this exact planner/CAS/writer/journal pipeline on a real platform shell.

docs.title: AuthoredBackupReconciler — the mutation-free merge kernel
docs.text:
AuthoredBackupReconciler.plan(_:) produces one complete merge plan from live rows, an existing backup envelope, and/or an incoming backup, without writing anything. Input combines primaryRows: [BlobRow] (duplicate keys intentional — the kernel merges them), conflictSidecars, and allowedLogicalGameIDs; any decoded record outside that ID set throws .orphanedLogicalGameID, fencing orphans out of a category-limited backup. Physical duplication is bounded at maximumPhysicalCandidatesPerKey = 256 per key before any semantic decoding, so repeated identical payloads can't become a CPU/memory amplification vector.

The output Plan holds immutableRevisionRows (every compact candidate becomes an immutable fact first, so a dominated compact projection can never be discarded without a permanent record) and compactHeadGroups — causally maximal compact rows per key, {active, alternates}.

syncedBlobs is not exclusively authored data

A backup's syncedBlobs array is the same progress-category row list every ordinary BlobBackedStore rides in — combinationPuzzles (CombinationPuzzleStore), tacticsRating, drillSRS, and the rest sit in it beside the authored compact-head and immutable-revision rows. plan(_:) decodes every primaryRows entry as an authored record and throws .invalidRecord on the first one that isn't, so a real caller must pre-filter with AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.isAuthoredKey(_:) before calling in — never pass a raw syncedBlobs array through unfiltered. Those non-authored progress rows reconcile very differently on conflict: they have no vector clock at all, so two offline replicas are folded with a plain typed union instead of causal reconciliation. That union's return value is a ProgressBlobMergeResult — the merged json plus the exact contributors that fed it, so a caller can derive backup precedence without re-deciding which rows counted. See the file store guide for the merge rules themselves; it isn't this page's kernel.

let plan = try AuthoredBackupReconciler.plan(.init(
    primaryRows: (backup.syncedBlobs ?? []).compactMap { row in
        guard AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.isAuthoredKey(row.key) else { return nil }
        return .init(key: row.key, dataJSON: row.dataJSON)
    },
    conflictSidecars: (backup.syncedBlobConflicts ?? []).compactMap { conflict in
        guard AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.isAuthoredKey(conflict.key) else { return nil }
        return .init(
            key: conflict.key,
            // Each alternate `Candidate` carries only `dataJSON`; it repeats
            // the parent conflict row's key rather than owning one itself.
            alternates: conflict.alternates.map {
                .init(key: conflict.key, dataJSON: $0.dataJSON)
            }
        )
    },
    allowedLogicalGameIDs: allowedIDs
))

A DirectProjectionIndex(from:) built once over a validated Plan gives O(1) per-game notesDirectProjection(logicalGameID:directCopies:) / boardMarksDirectProjection(...) lookups without re-decoding history for every game — the same witnessed-value rule above, applied per field.

docs.title: AuthoredRestoreJournal — the four-slot crash-safe handoff
docs.text:
Android library restore spans several durable phases; AuthoredRestoreJournal (currentSchemaVersion = 2) survives a crash between them. Four fixed large payload keys hold the prepared targets — targetLibraryBlobKey, targetBackupBlobKey, restoreWriteSetBlobKey, recoverySnapshotBlobKey — and one small canonical head, headBlobKey = "local.authoredRestoreJournal.v1" (maximumHeadBytes = 16 * 1_024), is written last and is the sole active-transaction marker:

prepare(...)                        → build + validate every byte, no writes
installBeforeCausalPublication(_:)  → write 4 payloads (read-back-verified),
                                        recheck ownership, THEN write the head
recoveryRead()                      → startup: read head, decide AggregateState
clearIfCommitted()                  → retire the journal once everything durable

Because the head is written last and the four payload slots are fixed and reused rather than accumulated, a crash at any point leaves at most four inactive, overwriteable payloads. Recovery compares the durable aggregate library's ExactByteProof against head.expectedLibrary (unchanged since prepare → AggregateState.needsCommit) or head.targetLibrary (already replaced → .targetCommitted) — the only two AggregateState cases. Any other observed value is never overwritten: it surfaces as RecoveryReadResult.stale, not as an AggregateState case, and the journal is retained rather than risking an unrelated newer library getting clobbered.

let journal = AuthoredRestoreJournal(store: blobStore)
switch journal.prepare(
    restoreCategoryRawValue: LibraryBackupCategories.games.rawValue,
    authoredPublicationMode: .completeFrontier,
    restoreWriteSet: writeSet,
    targetLibrary: targetLibrary,
    targetBackupJSON: incomingBackupJSON
) {
case .value(let prepared):
    _ = journal.installBeforeCausalPublication(prepared)
case .failure(let message):
    break   // targets rejected; nothing was written
}

docs.title: AuthoredRestoreProjector
docs.text: AuthoredRestoreProjector.project(_:onto:boardMarksProjectionExclusions:) applies one validated AuthoredBackupReconciler.Plan onto a live LibraryData snapshot. It installs the identity marker (AuthoredGameIdentity.installingMarker) on every physical copy of a logical game, but overwrites a field's bytes only on the copies named in decision.changedCopyIDs. A move-sequence-incompatible copy is excluded from board-mark projection but still receives notes and identity.

docs.title: AuthoredRecoveryPlanner — the inverse of restore
docs.text:
A normal restore projects the causal winner into direct storage. AuthoredRecoveryPlanner.plan(reconciling:to:authorReplicaID:authoredAtMilliseconds:) is the inverse: after observing every current causal branch, it authors an explicit new revision converging to a target backup value. It never manufactures tracking for a field with no existing causal state; recovery only touches fields already represented.

When a game's target copies disagree, recovery authors one concurrent branch per distinct value, each on a deterministic sub-replica ID:

recoveryReplicaID = "recovery.v1." + SHA256(seed head's encoded bytes)

so re-running the same recovery advances the same branches instead of consuming new vector-clock slots on every retry.

docs.title: The frontier inventory cache — AuthoredBlobInventory
docs.text:
Rescanning every append-only immutable revision to answer "what does this field currently say" would make routine reads scale with history depth. AuthoredBlobInventory sits in front of AuthoredReconciler as a bounded, resumable cache with two tiers, bound together by a SHA-256/byte-count proof:

generation (a UUID)
  → FrontierCatalog (schemaVersion 2): sorted indexKeys, isComplete flag
      → per-(logicalGameID, field) FrontierManifest (schemaVersion 4,
        maximumRows = maximumCompactHeadCandidates * 2 = 128)

A complete, proof-bound catalog that omits a field's key is itself proof that field has no causal state — the first edit on a brand-new game is O(1) instead of a full rescan. frontierRows(...) returns one field's rows; allFrontierRows(...) returns everything for backup export, falling back to a full rebuild only if the catalog is missing, incomplete, or unbound.

Full rebuilds (the exceptional path) checkpoint via FrontierRebuildCheckpoint (schemaVersion 1), keyed on a rolling SHA-256 digest of the exact sorted authored-key sequence (sequenceSHA256) plus the backup envelope's own SHA-256, so an interrupted rebuild resumes per already-completed field group. The actual per-field reduction, one AuthoredHistoricalReducer<Value, Element> per (logicalGameID, field), streams that field's immutable revision rows in storage-key order and folds them down to the retained frontier — capped at AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.maximumCompactHeadCandidates — without ever materializing every decoded revision at once, which is what keeps a rebuild's memory footprint independent of how deep a game's edit history runs.

garbageCollectInfrastructure only deletes a manifest or witness proven unreachable from a fully validated, complete generation; on any doubt — an unreadable manifest, an unbound catalog — it leaks the row rather than guessing ownership.

docs.title: Game identity — AuthoredGameIdentity
docs.text:
Every storage key above is keyed on logicalGameID, a promotion-stable identity distinct from any platform row ID. It lives inside game tags under reservedTagKey = "_FianchettoAuthoredLogicalID" — deliberately not a valid PGN tag name, stripped at every generic PGN import/export boundary (externalTags(from:)) so it never leaks into a shared or exported game.

A marker is markerPrefix ("stable.v1.") + 64 lowercase hex characters (isValidMarker). Before any marker exists, the deterministic alias is AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.logicalGameID(forIdentitySource:) = "stable.v1." + SHA256(identitySource). The first authored write on an unmarked game stamps that deterministic value as an explicit marker:

let resolution = try AuthoredGameIdentity.resolveOrCreate(
    tagsJSON: game.tagsJSON,
    identitySource: game.authoredIdentitySource
)
game.tagsJSON = resolution.tagsJSON
let logicalGameID = resolution.logicalGameID   // stable across future promotion

Once a marker exists on one physical copy, ownership resolution (ownership(for:) / replayingOwnership(...)) propagates it to every other copy sharing the same content seed or semantic remote game ID — so promoting an imported game to a synced one doesn't orphan its existing notes. Two different valid markers on the same seed or remote ID is a hard failure, .conflictingMarkers, thrown before any adapter mutates a row.

docs.title: Why AuthoredRevisionRetentionPolicy retains everything today
docs.text: AuthoredRevisionRetentionPolicy.currentGarbageCollectionDecision is hardcoded to .retainAll(blocker: .acknowledgedEpochUnavailable), and permitsDeletion is hardcoded false for every case that exists. The kernel's reasoning: an old vector-clock counter, a dominated value, elapsed time, or total row count are all observations, not deletion authority. Safe reclamation needs a sync-visible checkpoint epoch that every active replica has acknowledged, plus proof each candidate revision is covered by it — records that don't exist yet in the persistence protocol. The policy is deliberately one-sided: a deletion-authorizing case is meant to arrive as part of a future acknowledged-epoch protocol, not a local heuristic that quietly widens this API.

docs.title: AuthoredStorageMigration — restartable legacy-file migration
docs.text:
Migrates Android's original flat authored filenames into the routed authoredHead.v1. / authoredRevision.v1. hierarchy, bounded at maximumEntriesPerLaunch = 512 entries per pass. Discovery uses BoundedCandidateSelection, a capacity-bounded max-heap retaining only the lexicographically smallest capacity sortTokens seen across an unbounded directory scan — O(directory entries × log budget) time, O(budget) memory.

Each candidate is migrated verify-copy-then-delete: the legacy source is never removed until the exact same bytes are durable and directly readable at the canonical path, and both paths are re-read and re-compared immediately before the delete call.

The checkpoint is diagnostic-only, not the safety mechanism

Unlike the frontier rebuild checkpoint above, every migration pass re-enumerates every physical legacy candidate regardless of what an earlier checkpoint claims was .complete. If an Android system restore brings back old legacy rows alongside a checkpoint saying migration finished, the next pass still finds and repairs them — the checkpoint only rotates the resume cursor for a bounded per-launch batch.

let result = blobStore.migrateLegacyAuthoredStorage()
result.migratedCount
result.retainedCount
result.isComplete   // remainingCandidateCount == 0 && failureDescription == nil

docs.title: Drill Flow, SRS & Tactics Mining
docs.text: How FianchettoKit decides what a drill does next: the shared drill state machine, the engine-probe contracts it issues, the spaced-repetition and Elo math that scores an answer, and the pure functions that mine and select tactics puzzles from a game.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Train module splits along one line: the shell (SwiftUI on Apple, Compose on Android) owns the item pool, the board, and the pixels; every type documented on this page owns the decision — what counts as an answer, when to ask the engine, how strict to be, when a position is due again, and which puzzles a drill hands out. Every type here imports only Foundation and ChessCore — no SwiftUI, no UIKit, no platform concurrency. DrillFlowCore in particular never suspends: it is a pure event in → [Effect] out state machine, and every asynchronous step (an engine probe, a paced auto-advance, a scripted reply) is requested as an effect and reported back later as an event, never awaited inside the core.

Five drills (Tactics, Traps, Punish, Study, Endgames) and the game-review quiz sit on this shared spine. TacticsRatingStore, TacticsPerformanceStore, BlunderMasteryStore, TrainProgressCache, and PracticeMode are covered from the persistence side in Stores & the storage seam; this page covers the algorithms and flow/selection logic layered on top.

docs.title: DrillFlowCore: the drill state machine
docs.text: DrillFlowCore is a Sendable struct that walks a pool of Items against the moves a user plays. It keeps score, owns every generation counter, and returns the exact board/engine work the shell must perform as [Effect].

docs.title: Item and Goal
docs.text:
An Item is one drill question: a FEN, a board orientation, the ply the answer is expected at (answerPly, 0 for a freshly loaded root), and a Goal that says what answers it:

public struct Item: Equatable, Sendable {
    public enum Goal: Equatable, Sendable {
        case knownAnswer(expectedUCI: String, expectedDisplay: String)
        case discoveredBestMove
        case mateIn(Int)
        case keepTheWin(playOutToMate: Bool)
    }
}
Goal Used by How it grades .knownAnswer(expectedUCI:expectedDisplay:) Tactics, Traps, Punish; Study's replay/find-better drills Instant exact-UCI accept; a miss runs the two-FEN leniency probe .discoveredBestMove Study's best-move puzzles The engine's best move at the item FEN, probed once and cached per item load; a terminal position after the played move is an instant solve .mateIn(Int) Study's mate-in-N puzzles Mid-line moves are budget-checked against the remaining mover moves; on-track earns a scripted opponent reply and the line continues with no verdict .keepTheWin(playOutToMate:) the Endgame trainer The composite endgame probe is the whole grade — membership, leniency, and (with playOutToMate) the defense continuation all arrive in one transport hop; only a delivered checkmate is graded by the core alone

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Sampled once when the core is created for a run:

public struct Configuration: Equatable, Sendable {
    public let marginBase: Int              // base cp margin before DrillStrictness scales it
    public let autoAdvance: Bool
    public let missRetriesSameItem: Bool    // default false
    public let dynamicItemSupply: Bool      // default false
    public let endlessSupply: Bool          // default false — forces dynamicItemSupply = true
}

marginBase is the drill's unscaled acceptance margin before DrillStrictness scales it — 50cp for Tactics/Trap/Punish, 80cp for Study, 150cp for the Endgame trainer (see Grading primitives below). endlessSupply implies dynamicItemSupply in init regardless of what the caller passes — a custom endgame drill that never exhausts also, necessarily, deals each item's FEN itself.

docs.title: The flow: boardChanged → beginGrading → probe → commit
docs.text:
Every cursor change on the board — including ones the drill caused itself, like a scripted reply landing — goes through boardChanged(_:strictness:). Filtering echoes is the core's job, not the caller's: it only reacts when board.cursorPly == answerPly, i.e. exactly the ply it is waiting on for a user answer.

boardChanged(board, strictness)
  ├─ cursorPly != answerPly, or a verdict is already showing → [] (ignored echo)
  ├─ .knownAnswer && played == expectedUCI → instant .correct, no engine hop
  └─ else: capture PendingAttempt (uci, afterFEN, afterSafeFEN, isCheckmate,
           isStalemate, marginCp, requiresExact, showsCloseEnough)
       → beginGrading(attempt, item, restoreFirst: false)

beginGrading dispatches on item.goal:
  .knownAnswer         requiresExact ? commitRejected : runProbe (leniency)
  .discoveredBestMove  terminal position → commitAccepted (instant)
                       cachedBaselineUCI present → gradeAgainstBaseline
                       else → runBestMoveProbe, then cache the result
  .keepTheWin          isCheckmate ? commitAccepted (instant) : runEndgameProbe
  .mateIn(N)           isCheckmate ? commitAccepted (instant)
                       isStalemate || remaining <= 0 → runBestMoveProbe
                         (hint only — the grade is already .wrong)
                       else → runMateProbe

*ProbeFinished handlers → commitAccepted / commitRejected / surfaceUnavailable
  .onTrack / .continueLine → scheduleLineContinuation → .scheduleReply effect
    → scriptedReplyPlayed(_:) commits the line advance (answerPly += 2,
      userMovesPlayed += 1, no verdict shown)

gradeAgainstBaseline is the one place an exact match short-circuits a second engine query: matching the cached baseline commits immediately, so an unavailable redundant probe can never reject the engine's own best move.

docs.title: The Effect vocabulary
docs.text:
Effect is Equatable on purpose — golden tests assert the exact array a transition returns. Every case is a command the core issues; the shell never asks the core anything, it only reports events back (boardChanged, probeFinished, bestMoveProbeFinished, mateProbeFinished, endgameProbeFinished, scriptedReplyPlayed, itemSupplied, beatElapsed, retryProbe, advance, skip, effectFailed, suspend/resume, exit).

Effect What the shell must do .loadItem(index:fen:flipped:ticket:) Load a fresh drill board. Failable — report ticket via effectFailed on failure .supplyItem(index:) Generate the FEN for item index (dynamic supply) and answer with itemSupplied(index:fen:flipped:) synchronously .restoreAttempt(ply:uci:ticket:) Put the captured attempt back on the board ahead of a probe verdict. Failable .runProbe(DrillProbeRequest, ProbeTicket) Run the leniency probe; report probeFinished(ticket:verdict:) .runBestMoveProbe(fen:ticket:) Ask the engine's best move at fen; report bestMoveProbeFinished(ticket:uci:) .runMateProbe(DrillMateProbeRequest, ProbeTicket) Run the composite mate-line check; report mateProbeFinished(ticket:verdict:) .runEndgameProbe(DrillEndgameProbeRequest, ProbeTicket) Run the composite endgame grade; report endgameProbeFinished(ticket:verdict:) .scheduleReply(attemptPly:attemptUCI:replyUCI:delayNs:ticket:) After delayNs, restore the attempt, play replyUCI, report scriptedReplyPlayed(ticket:) (or effectFailed) .cancelReply Cancel the outstanding scripted-reply task .presentMissComparison(playedUCI:expectedUCI:) Draw played-vs-expected arrows (expectedUCI nil when it could not be discovered) .clearMissComparison Remove the comparison — emitted explicitly on every transition that leaves one presented .recordOutcome(DrillOutcome) Persist the result (SRS / mastery / rating / hub progress) .scheduleBeat(delayNs:ticket:) Start the auto-advance timer; report beatElapsed(ticket:) .cancelBeat Cancel the outstanding beat .reportUnavailable(message:) Surface a probe/board failure — an explicit, assertable effect twinned with the .unavailable verdict .completed(score:attempts:) The run finished — payload matches the completion card

DrillOutcome is the persisted record: DrillOutcome(kind: .correct \| .wrong \| .skipped, itemIndex: Int), emitted exactly once per completed verdict — and always after that verdict's board-work effects (see effect ordering below).

docs.title: Probe seams
docs.text:
The core mandates only the shape of each engine question; how a shell transports it (broker one-shots, resilient retries, movetime vs. depth) is its own business.

Leniency probe — DrillFlowProbe = @Sendable (DrillProbeRequest) async -> DrillProbeVerdict. DrillProbeRequest(puzzleFEN:afterPlayedFEN:marginCp:) is a two-FEN question: is afterPlayedFEN within marginCp centipawns of puzzleFEN's best line? POV contract: puzzleFEN is evaluated from the side to move (the drill mover); afterPlayedFEN is evaluated from the opponent of that side, so both scores land oriented to the mover. Both FENs are stockfishSafeFEN — the request shape itself forces the sanitization, so no transport can forget it at the engine boundary.

Mate-line probe (Study's .mateIn) — one composite question per move. DrillMateProbeRequest(questionFEN:afterPlayedFEN:remainingMateBudget:) asks whether the position still forces mate within remainingMateBudget mover moves (always ≥ 1 — the core grades exhausted budgets itself and never asks the engine about them). DrillMateProbeVerdict answers with .onTrack(replyUCI:) (still forces mate; the scripted reply to play), .offTrack(expectedUCI:) (a nil hint degrades the miss copy to "?", never the grade), or .unavailable.

Endgame probe (.keepTheWin) — the endgame's "probe" is its grader; the shell's transport holds the tablebase/engine evidence and answers the whole chess question in one hop:

public struct DrillEndgameProbeRequest: Equatable, Sendable {
    public let questionFEN: String
    public let playedUCI: String
    public let afterPlayedFEN: String       // engine-safe
    public let isStalemate: Bool            // a certain miss, no engine consult needed
    public let playOutToMate: Bool          // end-to-end: a kept win continues with a defense
    public let marginCp: Int
    public let requiresExactBestMove: Bool  // strict can't short-circuit — the accepted set
                                             // itself IS the transport evidence
}

public enum DrillEndgameProbeVerdict: Equatable, Sendable {
    case won(dtm: Int?)
    case wonSuboptimal(dtm: Int?, bestDisplay: String?)
    case lostWin(expectedUCI: String?, expectedDisplay: String?)
    case continueLine(replyUCI: String)
    case voidItem                          // never winnable — withdraw, zero score movement
    case unavailable(message: String?)
}

.voidItem is not a grade — the shell supplies a replacement item through the same itemSupplied path dynamic supply uses, and score/attempts don't move.

docs.title: Opaque tickets over one monotonic counter
docs.text:
ProbeTicket, AutoAdvanceTicket, and EffectTicket are each a one-field wrapper (let generation: UInt64) around a RunGeneration — a small Sendable counter (begin() -> UInt64, invalidate(), owns(_:) -> Bool) that the core keeps three independent copies of: probeGeneration, beatGeneration, effectGeneration. The field isn't public, so a shell can never construct or inspect a ticket — it can only hold the one the core handed it and pass it back unchanged. Any transition that invalidates in-flight work calls invalidate(), so a late-arriving result from a retired generation is silently dropped by the owns(_:) check at the top of every event handler. probePurpose (.leniency, .baseline, .mateCheck, .endgame, .hint) rides alongside probeGeneration so a probe launched for one reason can never be misinterpreted as another's answer, even while sharing the same counter.

NO SILENT FALLBACK

An unavailable probe is never converted into a grade, a failure never auto-skips, and .checking is never left unrecoverable. Probe failure, probe interruption mid-flight, an unplayable scripted reply, and a failed board effect all surface as the typed, retryable .unavailable(message:) verdict plus .reportUnavailable — score, attempts, and the item cursor move only when a completed verdict lands.

docs.title: The V4 rollback/retry channel
docs.text: Every batch that contains failable board work (.loadItem, .restoreAttempt, .scheduleReply) arms an internal Rollback: a captured token, the provisional scoreDelta/attemptsDelta, a failureMessage, a RetryAction (.grade re-runs the retained attempt; .reload re-issues the item load), and the pending/missShown state to restore. Effect ordering is load-bearing — every emitted batch places its failable board effects before .recordOutcome — so a shell that applies effects in order and calls effectFailed(ticket) on the first failure un-does the provisional commit exactly, re-arming the same retry retryProbe() triggers. An outcome can therefore never be persisted for a verdict whose board presentation never actually landed.

docs.title: Pacing constants
Usage: driving a single-move drill
docs.text:
var core = DrillFlowCore(configuration: .init(marginBase: 50, autoAdvance: true))

let items = puzzles.map {
    DrillFlowCore.Item(
        fen: $0.fen, expectedUCI: $0.correctMoveUCI,
        expectedDisplay: $0.correctMoveSAN, flipped: $0.userColor == .black
    )
}
var effects = core.start(items: items)          // apply(effects): shell loads item 0

// The user plays a move; the shell reports the resulting board facts.
effects = core.boardChanged(
    DrillFlowCore.BoardFacts(cursorUCI: playedUCI, cursorSAN: playedSAN,
                             cursorPly: core.answerPly, position: afterMove),
    strictness: .normal
)

for effect in effects {
    switch effect {
    case .runProbe(let request, let ticket):
        let verdict = await probeTransport(request)              // DrillFlowProbe
        effects += core.probeFinished(ticket, verdict: verdict)
    case .recordOutcome(let outcome):
        persist(outcome)                                         // SRS / mastery / rating
    default:
        apply(effect)
    }
}

docs.title: Grading primitives (DrillTypes.swift)
docs.text:
DrillTypes.swift is the platform-free grading vocabulary shared by every puzzle drill (extracted 2026-06-16 from the app's DrillKit.swift).

DrillVerdict — the per-attempt result:

public enum DrillVerdict: Equatable, Sendable {
    case checking
    case correct
    case closeEnough(expected: String, played: String)
    case wrong(expected: String, played: String)
    case unavailable(message: String)
    case done
}

DrillProbeVerdict — the three-state lift of an optional completed decision (nil means no reliable chess judgment was made):

public enum DrillProbeVerdict: Equatable, Sendable {
    case accepted, rejected, unavailable
    public init(completed decision: Bool?)   // true→.accepted, false→.rejected, nil→.unavailable
    public var completedAttemptDelta: Int    // 1 for accepted/rejected, 0 for unavailable
}

DrillStrictness — the Settings → Practice knob, @AppStorage key "drillStrictness":

marginScale:  lenient = 2.0   normal = 1.0   strict = 0.3
scaledMargin(base) = max(1, Int((Double(base) * marginScale).rounded()))
showsCloseEnough        == (self == .normal)
requiresExactBestMove    == (self == .strict)

Lenient accepts generously (a winning-but-imperfect move still reads "Correct"); Normal is the only strictness with a "Close enough" middle ground; Strict demands the engine's exact rank-one move and — critically — requiresExactBestMove lets DrillFlowCore.beginGrading reject a miss without ever issuing a probe, so a smaller-margin probe can never relabel a near-best move as correct under Strict.

DrillMastery — aggregate counts against the shared BlunderMasteryStore history map:

public static func counts<Item>(
    _ items: [Item], history: [String: Int],
    threshold: Int,
    key: (Item) -> String
) -> (total: Int, due: Int, mastered: Int)

public static func distinctCounts<Item>(
    pools: [[Item]], history: [String: Int],
    threshold: Int,
    key: (Item) -> String
) -> (total: Int, due: Int, mastered: Int)

threshold has no default, deliberately. It used to be = BlunderMasteryStore.masteryThreshold, and that expression was a trap: the Apple app separately declares its own enum literally named BlunderMasteryStore whose masteryThreshold reads the user's "Mastery streak" setting out of UserDefaults, so the character-identical source text BlunderMasteryStore.masteryThreshold meant the user's chosen streak in Fianchetto/Views and meant the kit's floor of 3 in FianchettoAndroid/Sources/Fianchetto — and, because a Swift default argument is evaluated in the module that declares it, any call that simply omitted the argument got 3 on both faces regardless of what the user had chosen. Nine live defects came out of that one construct kit-wide, including two that wrote disagreeing mastered/due counts into the synced TrainProgressCache. The floor now lives on MasteryStreak, which nothing shadows; a caller without the user's stored preference gets it through MasteryStreak.resolve(stored:) so the fallback is visible at the call site instead of hidden in a default argument:

let threshold = MasteryStreak.resolve(stored: storedMasteryThreshold)
let counts = DrillMastery.counts(items, history: history, threshold: threshold) { $0.masteryKey }

distinctCounts exists because tactics pools overlap — one position can be nominated by several TacticsExtractionModes (an opponent blunder that is also a critical position) — so summing per-mode counts would inflate the Train hub's total by however much the modes happen to overlap. It counts each distinct mastery key once, regardless of pool iteration order.

docs.title: Spaced repetition: DrillSRS
docs.text:
DrillSRS is the repertoire drill's SRS state, a Codable, BlobBackedStore keyed by blobKey = "drillSRS". Per key it tracks nextReview, interval (days), and streak:

correct → streak += 1;  interval = min(interval * 2, 30)   // days, doubling, capped
wrong   → streak  = 0;  interval = 1                        // days
nextReview = mutation.timestamp + interval days   (UTC Gregorian calendar,
                                                     secondsFromGMT: 0)
isDue(key) == entries[key] == nil  ||  entry.nextReview <= now

A key with no entry at all counts as due — an unseen position is always served. There is no partial credit and no separate "ease factor": the interval only ever doubles or resets, so the entire schedule is captured by interval and streak.

var srs = DrillSRS.load(from: blobStore)

if srs.isDue(key: position.positionKey) {
    // serve this position in today's drill
}

srs.recordCorrect(key: position.positionKey, to: blobStore)
// srs.recordWrong(key: position.positionKey, to: blobStore)

let entry = srs.entry(for: position.positionKey)
entry?.interval    // Int, days
entry?.streak      // Int
entry?.nextReview  // Date

recordCorrect/recordWrong persist through save(to:) themselves — no separate save call is needed.

Android migration

DrillSRS.load(from:migrationStore:) is an Android-only convenience: if the canonical "drillSRS" blob decodes with empty entries, it falls back to the legacy "repertoireDrillSRS" key, and on a successful migration immediately re-saves under the canonical key so every subsequent load takes the normal path. The old key and the new key share the identical algorithm and JSON shape — this is a rename, not a format migration.

docs.title: Cross-replica mutation ledgers
docs.text:
ConsecutiveCorrectProgress (backing BlunderMasteryStore), DrillSRS, and TacticsRatingStore all persist through the same pattern, so that two devices syncing the same CloudKit-mirrored blob can union their concurrent answers instead of one whole-blob write clobbering the other's:

1. First write:  legacyBaseline := current materialized state
                 mutations := []
2. Each answer:  append an immutable Mutation { id: UUID, timestamp, key, correct }
3. Rebuild:      state := legacyBaseline
                 replay mutations where timestamp > mutationCompactedAt
                   ordered by (timestamp asc, then id.uuidString asc)
4. Compaction:   once mutations.count >= 1,000 (maxRetainedMutations):
                   legacyBaseline := current materialized state
                   mutations := []
                   mutationCompactedAt := now

A wrong answer is therefore an ordinary ordered operation — one more Mutation — not a destructive whole-blob reset. record(key:correct:) / recordCorrect/recordWrong / recordAttempt all follow the same four steps: prepareMutationLedgerIfNeeded(), compactMutationLedgerIfNeeded(), append, rebuildFromMutationLedger(). Two replicas that both append a mutation and later merge just get a longer, still-deterministically-sorted list — timestamp order, with the UUID string as a tiebreaker for same-instant concurrent writes.

ConsecutiveCorrectProgress.decode(_:) also accepts a pre-ledger legacy shape directly — a raw [String: Int] — and lifts it into legacyBaseline with an empty mutations array, so an older build's blob decodes exactly like a freshly-compacted one.

reset() only tombstones the future

TacticsRatingStore.reset(in:) does not just wipe the ledger: it tombstones only mutations with a future timestamp into discardedMutationIDs — a defense against a replica whose wall clock runs ahead — then sets clearsLegacyBaseline = true and resetAt = now. The replay lower fence becomes max(mutationCompactedAt, resetAt), so a concurrent mutation with a badly skewed earlier clock can still land on the wrong side of it — the ledger is a bounded, best-effort merge window, not an unbounded event log. TacticsPerformanceStore.reset(in:) guards its own capped attempt array the same way, tombstoning only future-timestamped attempts into discardedAttemptIDs.

docs.title: Tactics puzzle mining: TacticsExtractor
docs.text: TacticsExtractor is a pure PGN + eval arrays → [TacticsPuzzle] function over Sendable value types — no Game/MoveNode traversal, so extraction can run from a Task.detached without blocking the main actor.

docs.title: The four extraction modes
docs.text:
public enum TacticsExtractionMode: String, Sendable, CaseIterable, Codable {
    case opponentBlunders   // "Punish"   — the opponent erred; find the punishing reply
    case userBlunders       // "Improve"  — you erred; find what you should have played
    case criticalPositions  // "Critical" — either side; any sharp eval swing
    case missedMate         // "Mates"    — you had a forced mate and let it slip
}

extract(from:mode:mateMaxN:swingThreshold:) requires mainline.count >= 4 and evals.count == moves.count + 1; anything short of that yields []. Neither mateMaxN nor swingThreshold has a default — each used to (mateMaxN: Int = 5, swingThreshold: Int = 150), and Android's Tactics view called this exact overload with the arguments left off, so it silently graded every account at the kit's floor no matter what the user had chosen in Settings (mateMaxN) or a value that had never actually been correct at extraction time in the first place (swingThreshold — see TacticsSensitivity). A caller without the user's mate-cap preference reaches the floor through MissedMateCap.resolve(stored:); both shipping Tactics views extract at TacticsSensitivity.minimum — the kit's loosest offered sensitivity — and apply the person's actual preference afterward with TacticsSensitivity.filteredPools, rather than varying swingThreshold per call. extractAll(from:modes:mateMaxN:swingThreshold:) parses the PGN and decodes the three eval JSON arrays exactly once and fans them out across every requested mode — the dominant cost (the PGN token walk plus three JSON decodes) is paid once regardless of how many modes are requested. Every mode's result list is sorted descending by |evalAfter - evalBefore|.

swingForUser = white user:  evalAfterCp - evalBeforeCp
               black user:  evalBeforeCp - evalAfterCp

.opponentBlunders  qualifies:  !isUserMove  &&  swingForUser >= swingThreshold
.userBlunders      qualifies:   isUserMove  &&  swingForUser <= -swingThreshold
.criticalPositions qualifies:  |swingForUser| >= swingThreshold
.missedMate        qualifies:   isUserMove
                    && a forced mate favoring the user existed before the move
                       (|mateDistance| <= mateMaxN)
                    && that forced mate is gone after the move

.opponentBlunders poses the puzzle after the blunder (find the punishing reply, taken from the engine's recommendation at the next node); the other three modes pose it before the erring move (find what should have been played there).

docs.title: isHighQuality and the difficulty ladder
docs.text:
puzzleEvalCp = mode == .opponentBlunders ? evalAfter : evalBefore
contested    = |puzzleEvalCp| <= 600                    // contestedBandCp
isHighQuality = contested && (bestVsSecondGapCp ?? nil) >= 100   // uniquenessThresholdCp
                                                          // nil gap => false

A decisively-won or decisively-lost position makes a poor puzzle — many moves "win" and the recorded best is arbitrary — so isHighQuality requires the position to still be genuinely contested (within ±600cp) and to have a clear best move (at least 100cp ahead of the second-best alternative). A nil gap — a legacy game annotated before second-best tracking shipped — is never high-quality, but stays eligible at lower priority rather than being dropped.

swing = |evalAfter - evalBefore|
isSharp = (bestVsSecondGapCp ?? nil) >= 100, or true when the gap is nil (legacy fallback)

swing >= 500  →  isSharp ? .easy   : .medium
swing >= 250  →  isSharp ? .medium : .hard
otherwise     →  .hard

docs.title: cacheFingerprint
docs.text:
TacticsInput.cacheFingerprint is a 64-bit FNV-1a-style hash — offset basis 14_695_981_039_346_656_037, prime 1_099_511_628_211 — folded over ["tactics-cache-v4", white, black, username, moveText, startingPositionFEN, annotationEvalsJSON, secondBestEvalsJSON, mateDistancesJSON]. Swift's built-in Hasher is process-randomized and unsuitable for a persisted cache key, so each component is explicitly length-framed (its UTF-8 byte count folded in 8 bytes at a time) before its own bytes are mixed in — without that framing, ["ab", "c"] and ["a", "bc"] would hash identically at the component boundary.

annotate feeds this directly

fianchetto-cli's annotate subcommand emits exactly the per-ply, white-POV centipawn array (white_pov_evals, forced mates flattened to the ±100000 sentinel) that TacticsInput.annotationEvalsJSON expects and that MissedMateCandidate's offline scan checks against (mateMarker = 100_000.0). Puzzle mining over an arbitrary PGN can therefore run entirely headless downstream of annotate, with no app involved.

docs.title: TacticsDrillSelection
docs.text:
Which puzzles a tactics drill serves, and in what order — extracted because both shells had independently written the same ranking and disagreed on exactly one edge case.

ranked(subset):
  unmastered = subset.filter { history[key] < masteryThreshold }
  source = unmastered.isEmpty ? subset : unmastered   // fallback, not a filter
  sort source by:
    1. mastery count ascending      (fewest attempts first)
    2. |evalAfter - evalBefore| descending

prioritized(from: pool, count):
  high = ranked(pool.filter { $0.isHighQuality })
  low  = ranked(pool.filter { !$0.isHighQuality })
  return (high + low).prefix(max(1, count))

The mastered-drop in ranked is a fallback, not a filter: a player who has mastered every puzzle in a tier still gets that tier back, rather than an empty pool. prioritized's max(1, count) is the same never-empty discipline one level up — Settings' "puzzles per drill" picker defaults to 20, but if it were ever read as 0 (a fresh key, a bad restore, a foreign value), a naive prefix(count) would start a drill with no puzzles. max(1, count) guarantees a user who asked to drill always gets at least one.

let byMode = TacticsExtractor.extractAll(
    from: input,
    modes: [.opponentBlunders, .criticalPositions, .missedMate],
    mateMaxN: MissedMateCap.resolve(stored: storedMateMaxN),
    swingThreshold: TacticsSensitivity.minimum
)
let pool = byMode[.opponentBlunders] ?? []

let drill = TacticsDrillSelection.prioritized(
    from: pool,
    count: 20,
    masteryHistory: BlunderMasteryStore.history(in: blobStore),
    masteryThreshold: MasteryStreak.resolve(stored: storedMasteryThreshold)
)

docs.title: ReviewQuizKernel
docs.text: The shared review-quiz selection engine: which mainline plies become quiz questions, and what answer choices each one offers. Lifted from Android's ReviewQuizView, which handled a case iOS's pre-set node.moveQuality check missed entirely — batch-annotated library games that carry evals but no per-node quality labels.

docs.title: Annotations-first, eval-derived fallback
docs.text:
public static func quizMoveQuality(
    plyIndex k: Int, evalCps: [Double], mainLineCount: Int,
    annotations: [Int: MoveAnnotation], startIsWhite: Bool
) -> MoveQuality?

startIsWhite reflects who moves first — a FEN-setup / black-to-move game flips ply parity, and therefore flips who the quiz is about. It carried = true until 2026-08-08, and that default is exactly what let the Android quiz view drop the argument entirely: for a black-to-move game Android inverted the mover on every ply and quizzed the user on the opponent's mistakes, while its own entry-button count — which did pass the flag — advertised a different set of questions than the quiz actually asked (divergence register C8). A defaulted correctness argument makes "forgot to pass it" indistinguishable from "meant true", so the only durable fix was to make the compiler ask every caller.

A non-empty annotations dictionary means the caller has authoritative per-ply labels: the eval path is disabled entirely, and only a stored .blunder or .mistake at ply k qualifies (this is what reproduces the interactive-review behavior exactly). When annotations is empty — the batch-annotated library path — quality is derived instead from the win-probability drop across evalCps (both before/after probabilities oriented to the mover via AccuracyAggregator.winProbability, then classified with AccuracyAggregator.classifyMoveQuality(wpDrop:playedBestMove:)); only a resulting .blunder/.mistake qualifies.

quizablePlies(mainLine:evalCps:annotations:moveText:startIsWhite:) walks every mainline ply, keeps the ones quizMoveQuality accepts, and resolves each one's best move — engineBestMoveUCI first, else a PGN-embedded snapshot built lazily (at most once, only on the first miss, and only kept if it aligns 1:1 with the mainline) — dropping any ply whose best move still can't be resolved. QuizablePly { index, quality, bestUCI } is the result element.

docs.title: choices() distractor assembly
docs.text:
public static func choices(
    bestUCI: String, bestSAN: String,
    actualUCI: String, actualSAN: String,
    legalMoves: [Move], positionBefore: Position,
    limit: Int = 4
) -> [Choice]

The engine's best move always appears first. The move actually played is added only when it differs from best — the whole point of the question is to contrast the two, so a quiz that omits the played move teaches nothing. Remaining slots up to limit are filled with legal-move distractors, shuffled and deduplicated by UCI. The result is returned unshuffled — best (and maybe played) first, then the distractors in their shuffled order — so the caller decides presentation order; both shells shuffle again themselves before display, which keeps this function deterministic and directly testable:

let plies = ReviewQuizKernel.quizablePlies(
    mainLine: game.mainLine, evalCps: evalCps,
    annotations: perPlyAnnotations, moveText: pgn.moveText
)
let options = ReviewQuizKernel.choices(
    bestUCI: plies[0].bestUCI, bestSAN: bestSAN,
    actualUCI: actualUCI, actualSAN: actualSAN,
    legalMoves: legalMoves, positionBefore: positionBefore
).shuffled()   // caller owns presentation order

docs.title: StudyPuzzleCatalogue
docs.text:
A fixed, data-only, 51-position reference set shared verbatim by both shells — extracted because the FEN sets had been hand-maintained in two files with no test to notice a divergence, and at extraction time they were still, in fact, identical.

public enum Goal: Equatable, Sendable {
    case mateIn(Int)
    case bestMove
}

public struct Spec: Equatable, Sendable {
    public let fen: String
    public let goal: Goal
}
Category Count Goal pieceCheckmates 10 K+Q, K+R, K+2B, K+B+N basic mates, .mateIn(1...4) checkmatePatterns 17 named patterns — back-rank, hook, Anastasia's, smothered, Boden's, Arabian, Morphy's, Pillsbury's, Damiano's, Lolli's, and more — all .mateIn(1) mateInTwo 6 combinational mates, .mateIn(2) or .mateIn(3) forks 6 .bestMove pins 6 .bestMove pawnEndgames 6 key squares and opposition, .bestMove

10 + 17 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 51. The opening traps Study also drills are not here — those load from a bundled resource, and bundle lookup is shell-specific.

docs.title: Combination puzzles: CombinationDrillCore
docs.text:
A combination — a multi-move tactic with a scripted opponent reply after each solver move — cannot be graded against a single expected UCI the way DrillFlowCore grades a puzzle, because the "answer" is a tree: several solver moves can be equally correct, and the opponent's reply differs by branch. CombinationDrillCore is that tree's own Sendable state machine, lifted out of CombinationDrillView for the same reason DrillFlowCore was extracted from the shells — every bug it had shipped was an ordering bug (an undo re-triggering the check it was undoing from; a move scored before its consequence was known playable; a completion written one line before another assignment overwrote it), and none of the three was reachable by any test that had to go through a SwiftUI view to exercise them. It owns no board: every board mutation comes back as an Effect the shell applies, and every board fact it needs arrives as a BoardSnapshot — the same input/output split this page's other cores use.

var core = CombinationDrillCore(puzzle: puzzle)
apply(core.start())                       // [.loadPosition(fen:), .setBoardFlipped(_)]

// On EVERY cursor change — including the ones the drill caused itself.
let effects = core.boardChanged(CombinationDrillCore.BoardSnapshot(
    cursorUCI: cursorUCI,     // the move under the cursor; nil at the start position
    cursorPly: cursorPly,     // its ply index; -1 at the start position
    position: livePosition    // WITH cursorUCI already on the board
))
apply(effects)

core.solved; core.wrongAttempts; core.attempts; core.totalSolverMoves; core.isFinished

Its re-entrancy guard is the same shape as DrillFlowCore's: a board change only counts as an answer when board.cursorPly == waitingPly + 1, a value recorded when the core decides, before the shell has applied anything — so the scripted reply landing at waitingPly, a take-back returning the cursor there, or the user browsing the move list all grade nothing, regardless of what order the shell delivers them in. Effect is loadPosition(fen:), setBoardFlipped(Bool), takeBack(TakeBackReason), playReply(uci:move:), and completed(solved:attempts:); TakeBackReason distinguishes a scored .wrongMove from an unscored .replyUnplayable (a malformed or exhausted tree), so a shell can eventually word the two differently without the core tracking anything more than it already does.

The tree CombinationDrillCore walks is built by CombinationPuzzleKernel from engine lines, fed by two small value types:

  • NodeEvaluation — engine evaluations for the legal moves at one position, mover-POV centipawns: moveEvals: [String: Int] plus a computed bestCp (the max). buildPuzzle's evaluations parameter is keyed by FEN; a solver node accepts every move within dualSolutionToleranceCp (50cp) of bestCp, not only the engine's top pick, because a drill that accepted just one of two winning moves would reject a correct dual solution. A position with no entry falls back to accepting only the move the supplied line actually played — conservative rather than wrong.
  • UnresolvedBranch — an opponent reply a real player might choose that the tree has no scripted continuation for: the FEN, the solver-relative UCI path to it, the reply itself, lossVsBestCp, an optional humanProbability from a Maia policy, and reachProbability (the product of the opponent choices above it in the tree). Its expectedFrequency ((humanProbability ?? 1) * reachProbability), not lossVsBestCp alone, is what decides whether a gap is worth scripting — a reply nobody plays costs nothing to leave unresolved. A non-empty unresolvedBranches list does not block drilling: CombinationDrillCore always plays a scripted reply, so the walk can never strand on one; it is reported so the miner can go probe the gap, not so the solver refuses to start.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Stores & the storage seam — TacticsRatingStore, TacticsPerformanceStore, BlunderMasteryStore, TrainProgressCache, and PracticeMode from the persistence/seam side: blob keys, capacity limits, and the query surface each store exposes. This page covers the algorithms and the flow/selection logic layered on top of that storage — the two pages are complementary, not overlapping.
  • Analysis math — AccuracyAggregator.winProbability and classifyMoveQuality, which ReviewQuizKernel's eval-derived path calls directly.

docs.title: Persistence DTOs
docs.text:
Sendable, SwiftData-free Codable value types. They carry game and repertoire data across the actor boundary and let heavy parsing happen on a detached task, without depending on SwiftData or CloudKit.

All are Sendable, Codable, Equatable.

docs.title: PreparedGameData
docs.text:
A portable, Sendable snapshot of a game ready for storage. PGN tokenization and Elo parsing happen in the PGNGame constructor, so a batch built on a detached task does the heavy work off-main.

public struct PreparedGameData: Sendable, Codable, Equatable {
    public let orderIndex: Int
    public let white, black, date, event, result, opening: String
    public let moveText: String        // via PGNExporter.tokenText
    public let tagsJSON: String        // via GameTagCodec.encode
    public let gameID: String
    public let cachedMoveCount: Int    // sentinel -1 when unknown
    public let cachedWhiteElo: Int
    public let cachedBlackElo: Int
    public let cachedIsAnnotated: Int  // 0 for fresh imports
    public let annotationEvalsJSON: String     // per-ply white-POV best eval; "" for fresh imports
    public let secondBestEvalsJSON: String?    // per-ply second-best eval; nil for fresh imports

    public init(from pgnGame: PGNGame, orderIndex: Int)
}

let games = PGNParser.parse(pgnString)
let prepared = games.enumerated().map { i, g in
    PreparedGameData(from: g, orderIndex: i)
}

It also exposes the portable parsing contract as static helpers:

PreparedGameData.normalizedGameID("?")               // ""  (empty/"?"/"-" collapse)
PreparedGameData.parseSanitisedElo("?")              // nil (empty/"?"/non-positive)
PreparedGameData.computeIsAnnotated(evalsJSON: e, moveText: m)   // Bool
PreparedGameData.toPGNGame(moveText: m, tagsJSON: t, result: r)  // PGNGame

stableGameID: String (computed) is the runtime canonical identity for a PreparedGameData — a decoded legacy DTO or a freshly prepared game alike. It prefers an explicit PGN Link/Site-derived remote reference and falls back to GameDedup.compositeKey(...) over the DTO's own fields, so a generic-Site game still converges on the same deterministic content key new imports use.
