docs.title: E-Board Integration: Session Core, Diff Resolution, and Diagnostics
docs.text: Sources/FianchettoKit/Boards/ (17 files) turns a raw physical-board event stream into game state, shared by the iOS/macOS app and the Android (Skip/SkipFuse) port from one decision core. Every type here except EBoardSessionCore — a plain class that deliberately holds non-Sendable stored state and is never sent across an actor boundary — is Sendable, and all but three files carry no @MainActor — the whole desync-resolution and promotion-disambiguation state machine is a plain value/reference-type decision core a unit test (or a future CLI) can drive with zero UI and zero Bluetooth.

docs.title: Overview: BoardKit's primitives vs. what FianchettoKit's Boards layer adds
docs.text:
BoardKit (extracted from FianchettoKit 2026-07-03, a sibling package) owns the wire-level kernel — BoardEvent, BoardCommand, BoardTransport, BoardTransportState, BoardAdapter, BoardCapabilities, BoardExecutionGate, OccupancyMoveInference, BoardDiffResolver, BoardCorrectionPlanner, BoardTakebackDetector, ChessBoardGeometry, BoardReconnectPolicy, BoardSyncGate — plus the four brand codecs (SquareOffAdapter, ChessnutAdapter, ChessUpAdapter, MillenniumAdapter). FianchettoKit re-exports BoardKit and SquareOffAdapter (@_exported import), so import FianchettoKit alone resolves every board kernel type. FianchettoKit's Boards/ layer adds the product decisions BoardKit deliberately doesn't own:

Concern Type(s) Which physical brand is this, and how do I find/name it BoardCatalogKey, BoardCatalog, BoardGATTSpec, BoardBrand Is it safe to scan / swap adapters right now BoardTransportLifecyclePolicy Who owns this async BLE callback BoardConnectionGeneration Deterministic write pacing BoardWriteQueue<Owner> Turning BoardEvent into game effects EBoardSessionCore, EBoardEffect Running the diff search off-main, applying its result EBoardDiffResolutionCoordinator One shared effect-application + orientation re-feed EBoardShellKernel, EBoardShellKernelContext UCI (re-)validation, takeback log lines EBoardMoveResolution App-to-board write-back move search EBoardPositionTransition Sync-sheet/OTB copy BoardSyncPresentation Field-bug capture and replay EBoardDiagnosticCapture, EBoardDiagnosticPersistenceCoordinator

The iOS and Android EBoardSession shells used to hand-mirror this logic in Swift and Kotlin/Skip separately; every type here exists because that mirroring drifted.

docs.title: Board identity and the catalog
docs.text:
BoardCatalogKey is the closed identity every board is keyed by, shared by both platforms' local BoardType enums (a FianchettoKit type can't be a Compose @State on Android, so each app maps its own thin BoardType to this key with an exhaustive switch):

public enum BoardCatalogKey: String, CaseIterable, Sendable {
    case squareOffPro
    case chessnutAir
    case chessUp2
    case millenniumEONE
}

BoardBrand.displayName(rawValue:) is the single source of truth for what a board is called: squareOffPro → "Square Off Pro", chessnutAir → "Chessnut", chessUp2 → "ChessUp 2", millenniumEONE → "Millennium eONE" (BoardBrand.pgnEventTag(rawValue:) currently mirrors this).

docs.title: GATT identity
docs.text:
BoardGATTSpec is the platform-neutral BLE contract for one brand — plain String UUIDs, no CoreBluetooth import, so it stays Linux/Android-compilable. BoardCatalog.gattSpec(key:) returns the real values:

Key scan filter TX service / char RX service / char dual-service aux notify squareOffPro D804B643-…, NUS 6e400001-… 6e400001…/6e400003… 6e400001…/6e400002… false — chessnutAir boardStateService, commandService boardStateService/boardStateChar commandService/commandWriteChar true commandResponseChar, fileChar chessUp2 NUS 6e400001-…, Device Info 0000180a-… 6e400001…/6e400003… 6e400001…/6e400002… false — millenniumEONE MillenniumGATT.serviceUUID serviceUUID/notifyCharUUID serviceUUID/writeCharUUID false —

Note

ChessnutGATT.*/MillenniumGATT.* resolve to literal UUIDs inside BoardKit, not FianchettoKit — cited here by symbolic name, not hex this package can't verify.

BoardGATTSpec.auxiliaryNotifyEndpoints subscription is best-effort: a missing auxiliary endpoint never fails the connection. Chessnut is the only brand that populates it — commandResponseChar (stored-game download replies) and fileChar (the archive itself) — and neither is the primary board-state notify channel, so losing one costs a feature (stored-game import), not the connection.

serviceUUIDs — a computed property, distinct from scanServiceUUIDs — is the narrower set of services the transport discovers characteristics on: a case-insensitively de-duped [txServiceUUID, rxServiceUUID, advertisedServiceUUID].compactMap { $0 }. It deliberately excludes ChessUp's 0000180a Device Information service even though that UUID is in scanServiceUUIDs (an advertising filter only) — discovering characteristics there costs a round trip for a service the protocol never touches.

docs.title: Name and scan matching
docs.text:
BoardCatalog.matchesScan(key:name:advertisedServiceMatches:) =
    !excludes && (serviceMatch || includes)

Exclusion wins. For .chessnutAir, excludes = ChessnutGATT.isMoveProfile(name:) — the Chessnut Move shares every GATT UUID with the Air/classic profile, so a service-UUID match alone must never pull a Move into .chessnutAir. The other three keys have no shared-UUID sibling: advertisedServiceMatches || matchesName(key:name:).

scansByName(key:) is false for squareOffPro/chessUp2 (they advertise their service UUID directly) and true for chessnutAir (two 128-bit service UUIDs don't fit a 31-byte advertising packet) and millenniumEONE (advertises only the Local Name "MILLENNIUM CHESS", no service UUID). A scansByName == true board must run a broad withServices: nil scan and filter every discovered peripheral through matchesScan in the callback.

import FianchettoKit
import BoardKit

let key = BoardCatalogKey.chessnutAir
let adapter = key.makeAdapter()          // ChessnutAdapter()
let spec = key.gattSpec                  // BoardGATTSpec

if key.scansByName {
    let belongsHere = key.matchesScan(
        name: advertisedLocalName,
        advertisedServiceMatches: sawOneOf(spec.scanServiceUUIDs)
    )
}

key.displayName            // "Chessnut"
key.kotlinManagerClass     // "fianchetto/module/ChessnutBleManager"

BoardCatalog.chessnutBeepData(frequency:durationMs:) forwards to ChessnutAdapter.beepData(frequency:duration:) so the app can drive the one beeper in the fleet without importing ChessnutAdapter directly.

docs.title: Transport lifecycle policy and connection ownership
docs.text:
BoardTransportLifecyclePolicy centralizes "is it safe to touch the transport right now" so the iOS and Android radios can't drift into one platform tearing down an adapter the other is still using:

allowsScan(from:) / allowsBoardTypeChange(from:) — true only for:
    .idle, .disconnected, .poweredOff, .unauthorized
                                        — false for:
    .scanning, .connecting, .connected, .reconnecting

isTerminalConnectionAvailabilityState(_:) — true only for:
    .poweredOff, .unauthorized

statePoweredOn(reconnectIsRunning:attempt:) =
    reconnectIsRunning ? .reconnecting(attempt: attempt) : .idle

resolvesDeferredScanOnPowerOn(reconnectIsRunning:) = true   // always

.poweredOff/.unauthorized are deliberately allowed for scan/type-change so the platform can still run its native retry/permission flow; any state with a connection attempt in flight blocks both. statePoweredOn keys off whether a reconnect task is alive rather than the last-written state value — a radio bounce during a reconnect loop can otherwise write .poweredOff over .reconnecting, and "don't clobber .reconnecting" can't fire on the way back up if it's reading a state the bounce already overwrote.

docs.title: Connection ownership
docs.text:
BoardConnectionGeneration is the monotonic token guarding a delayed async BLE callback against mutating state after its connection attempt is obsolete:

begin():            current &+= 1; isActive = true      // returns the new token
activate(token):     current  = token; isActive = true   // process-wide token (Android JNI)
invalidate():        isActive = false
accepts(g):          isActive && g == current

activate(_:) exists because Android's singleton JNI bridge can outlive and retarget multiple transport instances — a per-instance begin() counter starting at 1 isn't sufficient there, since two transports would both start at the same value.

docs.title: Write pacing
docs.text:
BoardWriteQueue<Owner: Equatable & Sendable> is a deterministic FIFO for physical writes, combining a per-command delay with the adapter's minimum write interval:

nextAction(activeOwner:now:):
    drop every queued entry whose owner != activeOwner
    if queue empty: .none
    if first write since reset():  required = delayBefore;                          anchor = enqueuedAt
    else:                          required = max(delayBefore, minimumWriteInterval); anchor = lastWriteAt
    if (now - anchor) < required: .wait(required - elapsed)
    else: dequeue; .write(payload, owner)

The caller performs the write, then calls didWrite(at:) to record the timestamp nextAction paces off next. reset() drops queued entries and forgets lastWriteAt, for when the transport swaps links.

docs.title: The session state machine (EBoardSessionCore, EBoardEffect)
docs.text:
EBoardSessionCore is a final class, not @Observable, never crossing an actor boundary — called synchronously from whichever @MainActor shell owns it:

public final class EBoardSessionCore {
    public init()
    public private(set) var pendingOutbound: BoardExecutionGate?
    public private(set) var awaitingPromotionFromUCI: String?
    public private(set) var lastReportedOccupancy: [Bool]?
    public private(set) var boardPromotionPick: PieceType?
    public private(set) var lastReportedIdentity: [Piece?]?

    public func clearPendingOutbound()
    public func handle(event: BoardEvent, game: GameView, orientationFlipped: Bool) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func completeBoardDiffResolution(
        _ resolutions: [BoardDiffResolver.Resolution],
        for request: EBoardDiffRequest,
        game: GameView
    ) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func present(move: Move, positionBefore: Position) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func forceApply(uci: String, game: GameView) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func applyResolution(_ resolution: BoardDiffResolver.Resolution, game: GameView) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func syncAfterPromotion(game: GameView) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func completePromotion(pieceType: PieceType, game: GameView) -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func cancelPromotion(game: GameView) -> [EBoardEffect]
    @discardableResult public func resetInference() -> [EBoardEffect]
    public func occupancyMismatches(game: GameView) -> [String]
    public func corrections(game: GameView) -> [BoardCorrectionPlanner.Correction]
}

Every call takes a GameView — a closure-free value snapshot the shell builds fresh each cycle, which keeps the core testable without a live Game or a SwiftUI host:

public struct GameView {
    public let position: Position
    public let currentNodeUCI: String?             // for promotion-completion detection
    public let ancestorPositions: [Position]        // up to 6 plies back, shell-precomputed
    public let legalCastlingRookHomes: Set<String>  // e.g. ["a1", "h1"]
    public init(position:currentNodeUCI:ancestorPositions:legalCastlingRookHomes:)
}

EBoardEffect is the closed, Equatable vocabulary of everything the core can decide — the shell iterates the returned array and applies each case, which is what lets a golden test assert the exact effect sequence a BoardEvent produces:

Group Cases Observable mirrors setLiftedSquare, setLastAppliedMove, setLastReportedOccupancy, setPendingResolutions, setPendingOutbound, setAwaitingPromotionFromUCI, adoptOrientationFlip Deferred reconciliation resolveBoardDiff, scheduleStateConfirmation(afterMilliseconds:) Game mutations applyMove(uci:), applyResolution(moves:), retractPlies(_:) Physical counters bumpPhysicalMoveApplied, bumpTakeback Promotion picker showPromotionPicker(from:to:legalUCIs:), dismissPromotionPicker Board hardware indicateSquares(_:)

handle(event:game:orientationFlipped:) is the single entry point; each call re-binds OccupancyMoveInference.isCastlingStillLegal from game.legalCastlingRookHomes, then switches on BoardEvent. The cases the core acts on: .squareSensed, .occupancySnapshot, .disconnected, .promotionPick, .identitySnapshot. .ready, .connected, .raw, .battery, .storedGameImported are no-ops here — the last is a side-channel import result the app session handles before it reaches the move-inference core at all.

docs.title: Execution-gate routing
docs.text:
While an app-dictated move (an engine reply, a tap-move) awaits physical execution, pendingOutbound: BoardExecutionGate? reroutes field events away from OccupancyMoveInference entirely:

if let gate = pendingOutbound {
    switch gate.feed(square: square, isLift: isLift) {
    case .inProgress: return []
    case .executed:   /* clear gate, reset inference, clear LEDs */
    case .deviated:   /* clear gate, LEDs, fall into the diff resolver */
    }
}

present(move:positionBefore:) arms the gate — the shell must guard transport.state == .connected first, or arming while disconnected blocks inference forever. It snapshots pre-move occupancy into pendingOutboundPreOccupancy; tryResolveAgainstSnapshot treats the board still showing that exact pre-move state as the expected wait state rather than a desync (the "Go auto-takeback fix" — without it, a streaming board's heartbeat frame kept re-running stash/confirm/BFS and eventually retracted the app's own move).

docs.title: Lift/place inference
docs.text: Outside a gated move, field events go to OccupancyMoveInference.handle(square:isLift:), returning .pieceLifted(square), .moveCandidates([String]), or .noChange. .moveCandidates is matched against MoveGenerator.legalMoves(for:) in tryApply; .noChange (a lift returned to its own square) still re-runs the diff resolver so a stale pendingResolutions clears the instant the board re-agrees. A committed move that doesn't consume the triggering lift square gets that lift re-fed, so the opponent's next pickup isn't swallowed.

docs.title: Promotion disambiguation
docs.text:
tryApply collects the inference candidates that resolve to a legal promotion move, deduplicated by promotion piece type:

2+ distinct legal promotion pieces:
  1. boardPromotionPick already reported (BoardEvent.promotionPick, e.g. a
     ChessUp 0x97 frame) -> auto-commit to that piece, no picker
  2. else, an identity-sensing board's latest identitySnapshot shows a piece
     on the promotion square whose type ∈ {queen, rook, bishop, knight} AND
     whose color equals the promoting side's game.position.activeColor
     -> auto-commit to that piece, no picker
     (a still-standing pawn, a king, or a wrong-color spare piece falls
     through — those are the player's own captured pieces set aside)
  3. else -> .showPromotionPicker(from:to:legalUCIs:), awaitingPromotionFromUCI = from+to

Exactly 1 legal promotion piece survives the candidate filter:
  -> auto-promote directly, no picker

The identity-consult branch runs after the boardPromotionPick check — a hardware-reported pick always wins. A .promotionPick arriving while the picker is already open (the 0x97 frame can race the pawn-placement events either way) auto-completes the promotion and emits .dismissPromotionPicker so the shell closes its UI without a tap.

docs.title: Auto-orientation
docs.text:
An .identitySnapshot on a 64-square identity-sensing board (Chessnut Air family) can prove the board is physically rotated relative to the app's orientationFlipped flag:

on .identitySnapshot(pieces) where pieces.count == 64:
    expected = identityArray(for: game.position)
    adjusted = orientationFlipped ? pieces.reversed() : pieces
    reversed = adjusted.reversed()

    if adjusted != expected && reversed == expected:
        adopt `reversed`; emit .adoptOrientationFlip(!orientationFlipped)

identityArray(for: position):
    out[file * 8 + rank] = position.board[rank * 8 + file]   // rank-major -> file-major, a1..h8

A position can never equal its own 180°-reversal (the two kings alone forbid it), so "matches un-reversed" and "matches reversed" are mutually exclusive — once adopted, every following frame matches directly and the flip cannot re-fire, closing the "stale persisted flip" class where a leftover flip silently misread every move 180° with no UI surface to discover it.

.adoptOrientationFlip must not trigger a re-feed

The core has already stored the corrected arrays for the frame that produced .adoptOrientationFlip. The shell must persist the new flag without running its normal orientation-change re-feed (EBoardShellKernel.orientationRefeed, below) — re-feeding would reverse an already-reversed array a second time.

docs.title: Diff resolution and correction flow
docs.text:
tryResolveAgainstSnapshot(game:fromSnapshot:) is the core's desync classifier, run on every .squareSensed, .occupancySnapshot, and .identitySnapshot, in order:

1. pendingOutbound != nil && occupancy == pendingOutboundPreOccupancy
       -> expected pre-move wait state; clear stash; []

2. gameOccupancy == occupancy
       -> in sync; clear stash; [.setPendingResolutions([])]

3. lift-in-progress guard (occupancy is a strict subset of gameOccupancy —
   squares only vacated, none newly filled)
       -> pure lift; clear stash; [.setPendingResolutions([])]
       (defer to OccupancyMoveInference, fed by the same frame's deltas)

4. stability gate: occupancy != unconfirmedMismatch
       -> stash it; [.scheduleStateConfirmation(afterMilliseconds: 500)]

5. occupancy == unconfirmedMismatch but !fromSnapshot
       -> still waiting; [.scheduleStateConfirmation(afterMilliseconds: 500)]

6. occupancy == unconfirmedMismatch && fromSnapshot
       -> clear stash; [.resolveBoardDiff(EBoardDiffRequest(position, occupancy))]

The stability gate (4–6) exists because continuously-streaming boards (Chessnut Go) emit frames during a move — a piece slid across the board, or resting off-centre and crosstalking an adjacent square — producing a one-frame mismatch that is neither in-sync nor a pure lift. It requires the same mismatched occupancy on two consecutive snapshot-originated observations before the depth-3 BFS runs.

A delta-path re-entry cannot self-confirm

fromSnapshot distinguishes a full snapshot from a delta-path re-entry (a deviation, a no-change, a failed-candidate fallback) — both observe lastReportedOccupancy, so without this gate a delta-path call re-observing the same physical frame would confirm the stash against itself. This happened once: hand-shadowing crosstalk during 1...e6 self-confirmed and the resolver fabricated [e7e5, d4e5], silently corrupting the game.

The lift-in-progress guard (3) exists separately because occupancy-only boards (Millennium eONE) auto-report a full frame on every sensor change, including the transient "lifted, not yet placed" instant at the start of a move — occupancy-indistinguishable from a completed capture. Without it, the BFS can fabricate a spurious multi-ply capture chain and auto-apply it: a c7 lift mid 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 once resolved to the unique [c7c5, c4d5, c5c4], leaving white pawns on both d4 and d5.

docs.title: Resolving and applying
docs.text:
EBoardDiffResolutionCoordinator moves the BFS off @MainActor:

public init(resolver: @escaping Resolver = { request in
    BoardDiffResolver.resolve(
        from: request.position,
        targetOccupancy: request.targetOccupancy,
        maxDepth: 3,
        limit: 8
    )
})

It runs the search on a Task.detached, keeps a one-entry (cachedRequest, cachedResolutions) memo so an identical request served twice is free, and tags every request with a generation counter (generation &+= 1 on every invalidation) so a completed-but-stale search can never publish over newer game state. completeBoardDiffResolution re-validates the request against the current position and occupancy first — defense-in-depth layer one, independent of the coordinator's own generation check:

resolutions.count == 1:
    if first.moves.count > 1 && resolutionContainsCapture(first, from: request.position):
        -> [.setPendingResolutions(resolutions)]     // demoted for user confirmation
    else:
        -> applyResolutionEffects(first)             // auto-applied

resolutions.count > 1:
    -> [.setPendingResolutions(resolutions)]

resolutions.isEmpty:
    if pendingOutbound == nil: try BoardTakebackDetector.pliesToUndo(boardOccupancy:ancestorPositions:)
    else:                      -> [.setPendingResolutions([])]   // gate still armed; not a takeback

resolutionContainsCapture walks the resolution's UCI moves against a scratch position; a move counts as a capture if its destination is occupied before the move, or it is en passant. An unparseable UCI counts as a capture too, failing toward the safer, user-confirmed path.

Multi-ply capture chains are demoted, not blocked

A single-resolution quiet multi-ply catch-up (moves played while the app looked away) still auto-applies. Only a multi-ply resolution containing a capture is demoted — a capture is the only way the BFS can "explain away" a sensor-dropout-vacated square, so a fabricated chain and a genuine quiet catch-up need different defaults.

Takeback detection only runs when pendingOutbound == nil — while a gate is armed, the board showing an ancestor position is the expected pre-execution state, not proof of a physical takeback.

docs.title: Correction-instruction text
docs.text:
BoardSyncPresentation supplies the shared strings both platforms' sync sheet and OTB status strip render:

public enum SummaryState: Equatable, Sendable {
    case noSnapshot
    case inSync
    case outOfSync(count: Int)
    public init(hasSnapshot: Bool, mismatchCount: Int)
    // !hasSnapshot -> .noSnapshot; mismatchCount == 0 -> .inSync; else .outOfSync(count:)
}
public static func syncStripMessage(hasPendingResolutions: Bool, mismatchCount: Int) -> String
public static func otbResult(for state: GameState, activeColor: PieceColor) -> String?

SummaryState's title/subtitle are the sync sheet's summary card copy:

State Title Subtitle .noSnapshot "No board snapshot yet" "Tap Refresh to fetch the board's current occupancy." .inSync "In sync" "The app and the physical board agree on every square." .outOfSync(n) "n square(s) out of sync" "Highlighted squares disagree between the app's game and the physical board."

syncStripMessage is the OTB status strip's tap-to-fix line: "Choose how to apply the board's move" while hasPendingResolutions, else "n square(s) out of sync — tap to fix".

otbResult(for:activeColor:) is deliberately distinct copy from GameResultPresentation.text(for:activeColor:) — that serves the analysis surfaces ("Checkmate — Black wins"); this serves both platforms' OTB views ("Black wins by checkmate"). Nil while the game is still live:

GameState otbResult .checkmate "White wins by checkmate" / "Black wins by checkmate" .stalemate "Draw by stalemate" .draw "Draw" .insufficientMaterial "Draw — insufficient material" .repetition "Draw by threefold repetition" .playing, .check nil

BoardCorrectionPlanner.Correction.instruction (an extension added here) formats one physical-correction step using FianchettoKit's own Piece.descriptiveName — defined in Voice/AccessibilityPhrasing.swift for VoiceOver/TalkBack labels, not ChessCore, and reused here so the wording matches what a sighted user sees and what a screen-reader user hears:

for correction in core.corrections(game: gameView) {
    print(correction.instruction)
    // "Move the piece on e2 to e4 (White Pawn)"
    // "Place the White Queen on d1"
    // "Remove the piece on h5"
}
corrections.placeSquares    // expected occupied, board empty
corrections.removeSquares   // board occupied, expected empty

docs.title: Cross-platform shell glue: EBoardShellKernel
docs.text:
EBoardShellKernelContext is the @MainActor protocol both platform EBoardSession shells conform to — observable mirrors named to match each shell's @Observable stored properties (conformance is automatic), bridged internals (sessionCore, diffResolution, suppressRefeedFlag, …), and platform services (sendBoardCommand, kernelLogNotice, persistDiagnostics, …).

EBoardShellKernel.apply(_:context:) is an exhaustive switch over EBoardEffect — a new case fails compilation here, in exactly one place, preserving the parity the shells' hand-mirrored switches used to provide only by discipline. Nine cases are applied directly (setLiftedSquare, setLastReportedOccupancy, setPendingResolutions, resolveBoardDiff, scheduleStateConfirmation, setPendingOutbound, setAwaitingPromotionFromUCI, adoptOrientationFlip, indicateSquares); eight are platform-divergent and return false: setLastAppliedMove, applyMove, applyResolution, retractPlies, bumpPhysicalMoveApplied, bumpTakeback, showPromotionPicker, dismissPromotionPicker.

.setLastReportedOccupancy and .setPendingResolutions are equality-gated before the @Observable write — streaming boards emit identical heartbeat frames continuously, and an ungated assignment fired Observation per BLE frame (the resolver bookkeeping underneath still runs unconditionally). A non-empty .setPendingResolutions only logs/annotates when EBoardDiagnosticDeduplication.desyncKey(positionFEN:occupancyHex:resolutions:) differs from the last-logged key — the same content-key mechanism the diagnostic capture uses to collapse repeated frames.

docs.title: Orientation re-feed
docs.text: EBoardShellKernel.orientationRefeed(context:) replaces ~56 hand-mirrored lines per shell. On an orientation flag change it reverses the shell's lastReportedOccupancy/liftedSquare mirrors (via ChessBoardGeometry.flippedSquare(_:)), then re-feeds the core a synthetic, already-corrected snapshot — .identitySnapshot if core.lastReportedIdentity is non-nil, else .occupancySnapshot — with orientationFlipped: false since the arrays are pre-corrected. Any .adoptOrientationFlip the core would compute on that synthetic feed carries wrong flag semantics, so it (and the fed-back .setLastReportedOccupancy) is filtered from the applied effects: a manual toggle stays manual, and the next real frame still auto-corrects.

docs.title: EBoardDiagnosticCapture — always-on ring buffer
docs.text:
EBoardDiagnosticCapture is a BlobBackedStore (blobKey = "eBoardDiagnosticCapture") that starts recording as soon as a board session exists — no opt-in toggle, since its content is board-protocol data only (no player names, no device UUID), so always-on is safe by construction.

cap = 500 entries

appendRaw(bytes:):
    hex = space-separated lowercase hex of the bytes
    if last entry is .rx AND sameState(last.data, hex, keyByteCount: stateKeyByteCount):
        merge: repeatCount += 1; lastOffsetMs = now      // collapse the run in place
    else: append a new EBoardDiagnosticEntry(kind: .rx)

stateKeyByteCount(forBrand:):
    "chessnutAir" -> 34
    everything else -> nil    // compares the WHOLE frame (always safe, never over-merges)

An entry is a run of identical frames, not one slot per frame. The 34 came from a field capture: a Chessnut Air frame changed only at bytes 21 and 25, byte 34 was a free-running counter cycling through 55 distinct values, and every other trailing byte was static — collapsing on the full 38-byte frame yielded 57 ring entries for 500 raw frames; collapsing on the leading 34 yielded 3. The ring buys state changes, which is what a desync investigation actually reads.

EBoardDiagnosticEntry.Kind is rx | lifecycle | comment; appendLifecycle(_:) records "connected"/"disconnected", annotate(_:) records free text (FEN, UCI, desync notes — never player names). asReplayText() renders .replay format text, valid input for ReplayScript.parse(text:) and replayable with zero live hardware:

var capture = EBoardDiagnosticCapture()
capture.startSession(boardBrandRawValue: "chessnutAir")
capture.appendRaw(bytes: frame)
capture.annotate("desync fen=\(fen) choices=\(resolutions.count)")
let text = capture.asReplayText()
// "# board: chessnutAir"
// "# privacy: content-only (board frames + moves; no player names, no device ID, relative timestamps)"
// "rx 4d 43 ..."
// "# repeated x12 over 1100ms"

let steps = try ReplayScript.parse(text: text)
let replay = ReplayTransport(adapter: SquareOffAdapter(), parsedScript: steps)
let events = replay.runSync()
// Feed `events` through EBoardSessionCore.handle(event:game:orientationFlipped:)
// for deterministic decision replay of a field bug.

docs.title: Desync deduplication
docs.text:
A board parked in one persistently-mismatched state would otherwise fill the ring with the same annotation on every frame. EBoardDiagnosticDeduplication keys on content, not time, so re-observing the same mismatch is a no-op:

EBoardDiagnosticDeduplication.desyncKey(
    positionFEN: String, occupancyHex: String,
    resolutions: [BoardDiffResolver.Resolution]
) -> String
// "\(positionFEN)|\(occupancyHex)|" + resolutions
//     .map { $0.moves.joined(separator: ",") }
//     .joined(separator: ";")

EBoardShellKernel compares this key against context.desyncDedupKey on every non-empty .setPendingResolutions and, only when it differs, logs

squareoff desync: fen=<fen> choices=<n> board=<hex>

via context.kernelLogNotice(_:) and annotates desync fen=<fen> choices=<n> into the diagnostic capture — so a board stuck in one mismatched state produces one ring entry, not five hundred.

docs.title: EBoardDiagnosticPersistenceCoordinator — debounced writes off-main
docs.text:
Encoding a 500-entry capture and atomically replacing its file is delegated to this @MainActor coordinator plus a private, non-MainActor Worker actor:

public init(debounceNanoseconds: UInt64 = 250_000_000)   // 250ms
public func schedule(
    _ capture: EBoardDiagnosticCapture,
    immediate: Bool = false,
    writer: @escaping @Sendable (String) -> Bool
)

let persistence = EBoardDiagnosticPersistenceCoordinator()
persistence.schedule(capture) { json in
    (try? json.write(toFile: diagnosticsPath, atomically: true, encoding: .utf8)) != nil
}
persistence.schedule(capture, immediate: true, writer: writeToDisk)   // lifecycle/takeback boundaries

Each call bumps a revision counter; the Worker actor only acts on a call whose revision is still the newest it has seen, and skips re-encoding entirely when capture == lastPersisted — an unchanged snapshot never touches JSONEncoder. immediate: true still performs the encode/write on the worker actor; it only collapses the coalescing delay to zero, for boundaries that should survive an abrupt app exit.

docs.title: Headless surfaces and CLI opportunities
docs.text:
Everything through "Diff resolution and correction flow" — BoardBrand, BoardGATTSpec, BoardCatalogKey/BoardCatalog, BoardConnectionGeneration, BoardTransportLifecyclePolicy, BoardWriteQueue, EBoardEffect, EBoardSessionCore, EBoardMoveResolution, EBoardPositionTransition, BoardSyncPresentation, EBoardDiagnosticCapture — is headless: no @MainActor, no SwiftUI, no Compose. Only EBoardShellKernelContext/ EBoardShellKernel, EBoardDiffResolutionCoordinator, and the outer EBoardDiagnosticPersistenceCoordinator class are @MainActor-bound (its nested Worker actor is not) — they exist specifically to bridge into each shell's @Observable view state.

fianchetto-cli's existing subcommands (annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project, track) all operate on completed games — PGN, FEN, engine analysis — rather than a live BLE session, so none of them currently drive this subsystem. But EBoardDiagnosticCapture's .replay export plus BoardKit's ReplayScript/ReplayTransport already form a complete, deterministic, hardware-free path from a captured field session back through EBoardSessionCore's exact decision code — the same handle(event:game:orientationFlipped:) entry point a live shell calls. A .replay file captured in the field is a natural fit for a future headless CLI regression command: parse the script, replay it through a fresh EBoardSessionCore, and assert the resulting [EBoardEffect] sequence against a golden file — reproducing (and guarding against a regression of) a desync bug without a phone, a physical board, or a UI in the loop.

See also the storage seam's BoardSyncGate (the board-agnostic clock-pause/haptic kernel, covered in Stores & the storage seam) for the smaller, adjacent state machine that reacts to a desync once EBoardSessionCore has already reported one.

docs.title: Elo Estimation & Strength Tracking
docs.text:
Turns engine-annotated games into an Elo number, in two senses. A GamePerformance is per-game evidence — what one game's move quality implies about the player's strength, with a deliberately wide confidence interval. A StrengthTracker posterior integrates many games into one tighter estimate via a Kalman filter. Chart domains, provider-scale personalization, and serving-coverage labels are all built from that pair.

Layering: pure domain logic over Foundation + ChessCore only. No SwiftUI, no SwiftData, no CoreML, no Skip imports — every type here is a value type or a nonisolated enum namespace.

This is not all of Engine/

EloEstimator and StrengthTracker are the strength-and-rating slice of Sources/FianchettoKit/Engine/, not the whole directory. A dozen other files there — AnnotationStaleness, GuessEloPolicy, MoveAnnotationSeverityBand, and others covering engine identity, search budgets, and live-analysis publication — have no page in either the reference or superseded set yet. Don't infer their behavior from this page; they need their own pass.

docs.title: Two time-control classifiers
docs.text:
TimeControlClass picks the calibration artifact (Lichess-style); TimeSpeed picks the display/rating pool (Chess.com-style). They can disagree.

TimeControlClass.classify(baseSeconds:incrementSeconds:)
  estimatedSeconds = baseSeconds + 40 × incrementSeconds
  < 180 → .bullet   < 480 → .blitz   < 1500 → .rapid   else → .classical
  baseSeconds == nil → .correspondence

StatsKernel.classifySpeed(tags:event:)          // different thresholds
  1. definitive correspondence TimeControl tag  → .daily  (wins over stale Event)
  2. Event keyword: bullet/ultrabullet/blitz/rapid/classical/
     correspondence|daily|"let's play"          → matching TimeSpeed
  3. empty tag + no keyword                      → .rapid  (NOT .daily —
                                                    no signal ≠ correspondence)
  4. base < 180 → .bullet  base < 600 → .blitz  base ≤ 1800 → .rapid  else classical

TimeControlClass.classify(fromPGNTag:) parses staged PGN clocks ("40/7200:3600+30") via estimatedSeconds(fromPGNTag:): each :-stage contributes base + moveCount × increment, moveCount defaulting to 40 when no moves/ quota is given, then classifies with incrementSeconds: 0 (the weighting already happened). A lone "1/seconds" single-stage tag is Chess.com's Daily serialization and returns nil.

Chess.com rates 5|5 as Blitz (300 < 600); the Lichess formula computes 300 + 40×5 = 500, landing in rapid. StatsKernel.estimateEloHistory carries both per candidate — displaySpeed (grouping/chart key, from classifySpeed) and timeControl (artifact selection, from TimeControlClass) — computed once, never re-derived from each other.

Daily is its own rating pool

.daily/.correspondence games are excluded from estimated-strength history entirely. Folding Daily into Rapid was tried: on the reference account, 378 Daily games (627–1,225) interleaved chronologically with 2,529 live games (202–1,048) on one axis, reading as "erratic and counterfactual." There is also no v4.1 model for correspondence.

docs.title: Accuracy formulas
docs.text:
AccuracyAggregator is the sole home of every accuracy/win-probability constant; EloEstimator and the WinProbability.swift ChessCore extensions delegate here rather than holding their own copy.

winProbability(cp:)             = 1 / (1 + exp(-0.00368208 × cp))
moveAccuracy(wpBefore:wpAfter:)   drop = max(0, wpBefore−wpAfter) × 100
accuracy(fromMeanLoss:)           raw  = 103.1668 × exp(-0.04354 × loss) − 3.1668
                                   return clamp(raw, 0, 100)

moveAccuracy and accuracy(fromMeanLoss:) share the same constants but differ in when they're applied: moveAccuracy runs per-move and is then averaged (dashboard, RecentAccuracyKernel); accuracy(fromMeanLoss:) runs once on a pre-aggregated mean loss (EloEstimator, matching the Python calibration pipeline's filter.py). By Jensen's inequality, averaging per-move accuracy yields slightly higher values — a dashboard tile and an EloEstimator accuracy for the same game can differ by a point or two.

let acc = AccuracyAggregator.moveAccuracy(wpBefore: 0.58, wpAfter: 0.51)

Move-quality classification, Stockfish-native and Maia-native:

classifyMoveQuality(wpDrop:playedBestMove:)
  playedBestMove → .best
  wpDrop >= 0.20/0.10/0.05/0.02 → .blunder/.mistake/.inaccuracy/.good
  else → .excellent

maiaMoveQuality(rank:probability:)      // rank -1 = outside Maia's top-K
  rank == 0                              → .best
  rank 0...2                             → .excellent
  rank 0...5  || probability >= 0.05     → .good
  rank 0...15 || probability >= 0.02     → .inaccuracy
  rank 0...30                            → .mistake
  else                                   → .blunder

maiaMoveAccuracy(rank:probability:) = clamp(sqrt(probability) × 100, 0, 100)

Both return ChessCore's MoveQuality. The sqrt curve keeps mid-probability moves from collapsing to near-zero the way a linear scale would.

docs.title: The 12-feature move-level vector
docs.text:
EloEstimator's v3, v4.1-ensemble, and v4.1-no-Maia models all consume the same 12-element vector (assembleV3Features), mirroring the Python pipeline's filter.py exactly:

# Feature Computation 0 accuracy accuracy(fromMeanLoss:) of this player's win-% losses 1–3 blunder/mistake/inaccuracy_rate share of moves with win-% loss ≥ 20 / 10 / 5 4 acpl_capped mean per-move cp loss, each move capped at 500 5 eval_volatility population std-dev (÷n) of win-% after every ply, not just this player's moves 6 opp_punish_rate share of opponent blunders (win-% swing ≥ 20) where the player's next loss ≤ half the gift; 0.5 if the opponent never blundered 7 mean_abs_eval mean \|win% − 50\| across every ply 8 n_moves this player's move count 9 plies total plies 10 is_checkmate always 0.0 — coefficient is 0 in every fitted model 11 is_time 1.0 from PGN Termination via isTimeEnding(_:), else 0.0

isTimeEnding treats Lichess's normalized "time"/"time forfeit" and Chess.com's prose ("won on time") as time endings, while explicitly excluding "timeout vs insufficient material" first. Computing the vector needs ≥ 3 of the player's own moves — stricter than the v2 path's ≥ 1.

docs.title: Calibration artifacts (EloCalibrationData)
docs.text:
internal (not public) — generated by Tools/elo-calibration/generate_swift.py from the Lichess Open Database (CC0, May 2026); its header says "DO NOT EDIT." That generator does not live in this package: its header is explicit that it lives in the Fianchetto (Apple app) repository, because regenerating needs a 1 MB research corpus and an SSH compute target that have no business being a dependency consumers resolve. FianchettoKit's own Tools/ directory holds only FianchettoMaiaBackupTool. Because EloCalibrationData is internal, fianchetto-cli cannot read these constants directly today, only through EloEstimator.estimate.

Quota balancing differs by time control

Bullet, blitz and rapid were fit with rating-band quota balancing (≤ 15k rows per band) for better sub-1200 coverage. Classical is an unbalanced fit — its corpus was too small to support quotas. That shows up in the fitted numbers: classical's Maia lift is the largest of the four classes (see below), and its ensemble residual bands are tighter than bullet's everywhere except the bottom band (0–800: classical 270.5 vs. bullet 257.6) — exactly where an unbalanced, quota-free corpus would be thinnest on very-low-rated games.

Version Features Selected when v2 (TCModel) accuracy only correspondence, or any TC with no v4.1 model v3 (V3TCModel) 12 superseded by v4.1 in production; kept for parity tests v4.1 ensemble (V41EnsembleTCModel) 16 (12 + 4 Maia) a valid 11-point Maia log-likelihood vector is available v4.1 no-Maia (V3TCModel refit) 12 Maia evidence missing or wrong length — the production fallback 
v2: binnedLookup(accuracy:model:)          // monotone binned-median, linear interpolation
  accuracy <= centers[0]      → ratings[0]              (clamp low)
  accuracy >= centers[last]   → ratings[last]            (clamp high)
  between centers[i], [i+1]   → linear interpolation
  degenerate table (<2 bins)  → evalPoly(polyCoefficients, accuracy)  // cubic Horner

v3 / v4.1: prediction = intercept + Σᵢ coefficients[i] × (feature[i] − featureMeans[i]) / featureStds[i]

v4.1 Maia features 12–15, from an 11-point log-likelihood vector over
eloGrid = [600,800,...,2600] (step 200):
  llSpread = max(logLikes) − min(logLikes)        // ORIGINAL values
  weights  = softmax(logLikes)                     // stable: subtract max before exp
  meanElo  = Σ eloGrid[i]×weights[i]
  stdElo   = sqrt(Σ weights[i]×(eloGrid[i]−meanElo)²)
  argmaxElo = eloGrid[argmax(weights)]

v4.1-ensemble cross-validated MAE by TC: bullet 226.5, blitz 200.4, rapid 189.2, classical 159.0. Classical's fit documents a +115.6 Elo contribution from the Maia features versus the no-Maia fallback — the largest lift of the four classes.

Both v4.1 variants also carry five residualBands used by EloEstimator.estimate's CI walk (below), banded identically at 0–800/800–1200/1200–1600/1600–2000/2000+:

Band Bullet Blitz Rapid Classical ensemble, 0–800 257.6 260.4 233.4 270.5 ensemble, 800–1200 228.4 198.8 187.4 155.7 ensemble, 1200–1600 167.0 173.2 151.2 147.0 ensemble, 1600–2000 170.1 177.9 157.6 150.5 ensemble, 2000+ 266.8 197.0 203.5 168.9 no-Maia, 0–800 400.8 426.4 377.2 457.2 no-Maia, 800–1200 363.0 362.7 320.8 274.7 no-Maia, 1200–1600 238.8 257.8 231.3 199.5 no-Maia, 1600–2000 296.7 287.1 264.0 234.4 no-Maia, 2000+ 536.0 497.9 425.5 353.0

Every no-Maia band is worse than its ensemble counterpart — the Maia features are not just a classical-only win. The no-Maia 2000+ bands are the single worst cells in either table (bullet 536.0, blitz 497.9), which is why a high-rated player without Maia evidence gets the widest CI the estimator ever produces. v2 and v3 use a different, coarser banding (0–1200/1200–1400/1400–1600/1600–1800/1800–2000/2000–2200/2200+); v2 correspondence's worst band is its lowest one — 1200–1400 has an MAE of 591.4, the reason the stats pipeline withholds daily games from the chart entirely (see estimateEloHistory, below).

docs.title: EloEstimator.estimate — routing and confidence intervals
docs.text:
public static func estimate(
    evalsJSON: String, startIsWhite: Bool, color: PieceColor, tc: TimeControlClass,
    isOTBClassical: Bool = false, maiaLogLikes: [Double]? = nil,
    maiaEvidence: MaiaBackfillPolicy.TargetEvidence? = nil, termination: String? = nil
) -> GamePerformance?

(A whitePovEvals: [Double] overload skips re-decoding an already-parsed eval array.)

bullet/blitz/rapid/classical
  + valid maiaEvidence (11 finite log-likes, eligibleMoveCount > 0)
      → v4.1 ensemble   servingPath = .exactOpponentMaiaEnsemble
                                    or .neutral1500EvidenceExactArtifact
                                       (per maiaEvidence.opponentConditioning)
  + legacy bare maiaLogLikes (11 doubles, no metadata)
      → v4.1 ensemble   servingPath = .exactOpponentMaiaEnsemble  (always)
  + no usable Maia evidence
      → v4.1 no-Maia    servingPath = .moveQualityFallback
correspondence (or any TC with no v4.1 model)
      → v2 binned lookup   servingPath = .moveQualityFallback

EloEstimatorServingPath.usesMaiaRefinement is true for every case except .moveQualityFallback. The two Maia paths currently share identical v4.1 coefficients — the split exists so a future neutral-conditioned artifact has somewhere to route without touching today's behavior.

The four dispatch functions in EloCalibrationData disagree on purpose about the raw value their switch doesn't name — in practice always "correspondence", since TimeControlClass has only five cases and the other four are named explicitly. model(forRawTC:) — the v2 lookup — falls back to rapid as the nearest calibrated neighbor, never returning nil. v3model(forRawTC:), v41ensembleModel(forRawTC:) and v41noMaiaModel(forRawTC:) all return nil instead: for those three, nil is the routing signal that sends estimate down to the v2 lookup, so returning a guessed model there would silently defeat the correspondence fallback in the routing table above.

servingPathLabel(for:) on StatsChartPresentationPolicy renders exactly three strings, one per EloEstimatorServingPath case — "Exact-opponent Maia", "Neutral-1500 Maia (provisional)", "Move-quality model" — with no "pending" or default case, because a move-quality estimate is a valid result in its own right, not a placeholder for missing Maia evidence. estimatedStrengthServingCoverage(for:) tallies a batch of GamePerformance values into an EstimatedStrengthServingCoverage, which carries exactOpponentMaiaCount and neutral1500MaiaCount as separate fields rather than one merged count. Its init(maiaRefinedCount:gameCount:) compatibility initializer exists for callers written before that split was observable: it files every historical Maia-refined count under exactOpponentMaiaCount and leaves neutral1500MaiaCount at zero, which is the correct backward reading since the legacy API had no conditioning field to have gotten it wrong from.

belowFloor (v4.1)  = rawElo < 100.0            pointElo = clamp(rawElo, 100...3500)
belowFloor (v2)    = accuracy < binnedCenters[0]   // e.g. 26.0 for blitz

baseHalfWidth = belowFloor ? 2×(floor-band MAE)
              : residual-std band whose bandLow <= pointElo (walk ascending, last match wins)

uncertaintySampleMoves = min(nMoves, maiaEligibleMoveCount ?? nMoves)   // v4.1 path;
                          // v2/correspondence uses sampleMoves directly instead
sampleFactor = min(3.0, sqrt(max(1.0, 20.0 / uncertaintySampleMoves)))
otbFactor    = isOTBClassical ? 1.5 : 1.0
halfWidth    = baseHalfWidth × sampleFactor × otbFactor
ci           = pointElo ± halfWidth

belowCalibrationFloor fires only for very low accuracy (< 26% for blitz) — most beginners stay inside the calibrated range even though the estimate may overshoot, because the Lichess accuracy formula yields ≥ 60% even for 800-rated players. maiaEligibleMoveCount (positions Maia actually scored, after excluding the opening and forced moves) is smaller than raw move count, so a Maia-refined CI uses that tighter count.

isOTBClassical should be true only for a genuine over-the-board long control mapped into Lichess's .classical bucket — StatsKernel's isOTBClassicalTC flags this when TimeControlClass.estimatedSeconds(fromPGNTag:) >= 6000 (90+30 → 6600s, 120+0 → 7200s), because the Lichess-classical corpus is dominated by 30+0 (1800s) games.

let tc = TimeControlClass.classify(fromPGNTag: tags["TimeControl"] ?? "")
guard let performance = EloEstimator.estimate(
    evalsJSON: game.annotationEvalsJSON, startIsWhite: true, color: .white, tc: tc,
    isOTBClassical: false, maiaEvidence: maiaTargetEvidence,   // nil → v4.1 no-Maia
    termination: tags["Termination"]
) else { return }
print(performance.elo, performance.ci, performance.servingPath)

docs.title: StrengthTracker — the Kalman filter
docs.text:
Value-semantic: updated(with:) returns a new tracker, the receiver is unchanged.

predVariance      = posteriorSigma² + processTau²
obsVariance        = max(1.0, ciHalfWidth²)     // ciHalfWidth = (ci.upper − ci.lower)/2
posteriorVariance = 1 / (1/predVariance + 1/obsVariance)
posteriorMean      = posteriorVariance × (posteriorMean/predVariance + performance.elo/obsVariance)
posteriorSigma      = sqrt(posteriorVariance)

public init(priorMean: Double, priorSigma: Double = 300.0, processTau: Double = 50.0)

priorSigma = 300 starts "very uncertain"; processTau = 50 lets the posterior drift ~±150 Elo over 9 games even absent new evidence, so genuine improvement is followed rather than smoothed away. A wider GamePerformance CI (fewer moves, OTB widening) contributes proportionally less to the update. StatsKernel seeds every tracker at priorMean: 1_500, priorSigma: 300 and the processTau default.

var tracker = StrengthTracker(priorMean: 1_500, priorSigma: 300)
for performance in performancesInDateOrder {
    tracker = tracker.updated(with: performance)
}
print(tracker.posteriorMean, tracker.ci)   // 68% interval

docs.title: Personalizing onto a provider scale
docs.text:
Two causal calibrators sit downstream of the tracker, both prequential: predict using only strictly-earlier labels, emit, then observe(...) the current game's rating. observe is a separate call from the prediction, so no code path can let today's label leak into today's estimate.

PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator (the slow trend) is offset-only — a single account rarely spans enough of a rating pool to fit a slope reliably.

offset = median(residuals)     // residuals: actualRating − baseStrength, window 20
                                // available once residuals.count >= minimumOffsetSamples (20)
mean = baseStrength + offset

fallbackHalfWidth: robustScale = max(50.0, 1.4826 × MAD(residuals))
                    offsetSE    = 1.2533 × robustScale / sqrt(n)
                    = sqrt(baseSigma² + robustScale² + offsetSE²)
conformalHalfWidth(coverage):    // once forecastErrors.count >= minimumConformalSamples (20), window 50
  rank = clamp(ceil((n+1)×coverage), 1, n);  return max(1, sorted(forecastErrors)[rank-1])

half68 = conformalHalfWidth(0.68) ?? fallbackHalfWidth
half95 = conformalHalfWidth(0.95) ?? (1.96 × fallbackHalfWidth)

prediction(baseStrength:baseSigma:) returns a PersonalizedStrengthPrediction (nil during the offset warm-up): mean, interval68/interval95, the offset that produced mean, calibrationSampleCount/forecastSampleCount (how many residuals/forecast errors the calibrator has banked), and usesEmpiricalIntervals — whether the intervals above came from the split-conformal branch or the warm-up fallback formula.

ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator (the current-game projection) keeps entirely separate residual/forecast-error state per serving path (usedMaiaRefinement) — Maia-refined evidence and the move-quality fallback have different bias and spread, so mixing them would let fallback noise corrupt Maia calibration.

offset (per path) = median(residualsByPath)     // needs >= minimumSampleCount (20)
mappedPerformance   = clamp(performance.elo + offset, 100...3500)

weight = ceiling × sampleMoves / (sampleMoves + prior)
  Maia path:     ceiling 1.00 (maiaMaximumEvidenceWeight), prior 5.0 (maiaMoveCountPrior)
  fallback path: ceiling 0.60 (fallbackMaximumEvidenceWeight), prior 15.0 (fallbackMoveCountPrior)

cappedDelta = clamp(weight × (mappedPerformance − anchorRating), ±250.0)  // maximumAnchorDelta
mean        = clamp(anchorRating + cappedDelta, 100...3500)

A 30-move Maia game reaches weight ≈ 30/35 ≈ 0.86; the same game on the fallback path reaches only 0.60×30/45 ≈ 0.40 — the noisier estimator is trusted less relative to the account anchor. Interval construction: propagated (offsetSE combined in quadrature with the performance CI's model sigma, × 1 or × 1.96) during warm-up, or a split-conformal order statistic (finiteSampleQuantile: sorted[clamp(ceil((n+1)×coverage)-1, 0, n-1)]) once ≥ minimumIntervalSampleCount (20) strictly-earlier forecast errors exist for that path. Its forecastErrorWindow is 100 (vs. 50 for the slow-trend calibrator) — the per-game projection sees more raw observations per account, so it can hold a wider window.

projection(for:) returns an AnchoredGamePerformanceProjection — the "played like" number, distinct from both GamePerformance.elo (evidence-only) and StrengthTracker.posteriorMean (the slow pool-wide posterior). It carries anchorRating and mappedPerformance (the two inputs to mean above), performanceWeight (the weight computed above), mean with its interval68/interval95, the path's offset/offsetStandardError, sampleCount/intervalSampleCount (residual/forecast-error occupancy for that path), usesEmpiricalInterval, and usedMaiaRefinement — the path key, so a caller can tell which calibration state produced a given projection without re-deriving it from the input GamePerformance.

tracker = tracker.updated(with: performance)
let gameProjection = projectionCalibrator.projection(for: performance)
let personalized = localCalibrator.prediction(
    baseStrength: tracker.posteriorMean, baseSigma: tracker.posteriorSigma
)
// ... emit the point, THEN:
if let actualRating {
    localCalibrator.observe(
        baseStrength: tracker.posteriorMean, actualRating: Double(actualRating),
        personalizedPrediction: personalized
    )
    projectionCalibrator.observe(
        actualRating: Double(actualRating), rawPerformanceElo: performance.elo,
        usedMaiaRefinement: performance.usedMaiaRefinement, projection: gameProjection
    )
}

docs.title: StatsKernel.estimateEloHistory — the end-to-end pipeline
docs.text:
1. Flatten every collection's games into candidates: timeControl (Lichess
   formula, artifact selection), displaySpeed (chess.com-facing, grouping),
   a lexically-sortable timestamp (UTCDate/Time → EndDate/Time → Date → date).
2. Sort chronologically (ties: source, username, speed, stable game ID).
3. Group by (source, username, displaySpeed) — never share a tracker or
   offset across providers, accounts, or speed pools.
4. Skip displaySpeed == .daily entirely. The v3 corpus held ZERO
   correspondence rows — measured against 3,378 games, the v2 correspondence
   model produced a near-constant 1937 ± 98 against an actual 765. A flat
   offset, not a measurement.
5. Per group, seed StrengthTracker(priorMean: 1_500, priorSigma: 300),
   PersonalizedStrengthCalibrator(), ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator().
   An unannotated game still updates the projection anchor but yields no
   EloPoint. An annotated game: estimate → update tracker → compute
   projection + personalized prediction (Chess.com sources only) → emit
   EloPoint → THEN observe the rating into both calibrators.
6. Merge all groups' points, re-sort globally by timestamp.

EstimatedStrengthCalibration is a 3-state lifecycle: .lichessEquivalent (unmodified tracker output; always the state for non-Chess.com sources) → .chessComCalibrating (Chess.com, < 20 strictly-earlier labels — still Lichess-scale) → .chessComPersonalized (≥ 20 samples: offset-personalized trend, optionally a per-game gameProjection). EloPoint.strengthCI95 defaults, when not explicitly supplied, to strengthMean ± 1.96 × halfWidth(strengthCI).

let aggregate = StatsKernel.compute(from: snapshot)   // includeEloEstimate: Bool = true
let blitzHistory = aggregate.estimatedEloHistory.filter { $0.speed == .blitz }

StatsKernel.compute returns more than estimatedEloHistory: each opening the library has been played gets an OpeningStat — name, games, wins, draws, losses, and an accuracy that stays nil rather than 0 when no game in that opening was annotated, so a chart never reads a never-analyzed opening as if it were played with zero skill.

docs.title: Chart & UI presentation helpers
docs.text:
EloChartPresentation — pure Y-domain/clipping math shared by the SwiftUI Charts and Compose renderers, extracted after a real divergence: Apple's domain unioned shaded intervals, ratings, and percentile-trimmed evidence dots; Android omitted the dots, so points outside the interval band clamped flat against the axis (measured 2.3%–7.1% of points).

displayedInterval(point) = (chessComPersonalized && gameProjection != nil)
                            ? gameProjection.interval68 : point.strengthCI
unclippedPerformance(point) = same condition ? gameProjection.mappedPerformance
                                              : point.performance.elo

domain(points:showsComparableRating:)
  values = every displayedInterval bound (+ actualRating if showsComparableRating)
  performances = unclippedPerformance(...).sorted()
  n>=20: extend by performances[n/20] (5th pct) and performances[n×19/20] (95th pct)
  else:  extend by performances.first/.last
  padding = max(30, (upper−lower) × 0.05)

clipped(_:to:)  inset = max(1, domainWidth × 0.01); clamp into [lower+inset, upper−inset]

StatsChartPresentationPolicy — estimatedStrengthSpeeds = [.bullet, .blitz, .rapid, .classical] (Daily excluded, no calibrated model). normalizedMode(_:) accepts only the literal "estimated"; any other stored value fails safe to "rating". estimatedStrengthChartPoints drops the Lichess-reference warm-up points once any point has gone .chessComPersonalized, so a chart never mixes two rating scales. estimatedStrengthServingCoverage(for:) tallies GamePerformance values by servingPath into .label strings like "Maia-refined: 41 of 50 games (41 exact)".

AccuracyScaleKit — word grade vs. semantic band, no Color mapping (apps switch over Band themselves):

Range descriptor(_:) band(_:) 95–100 "Engine-level" .elite 90–95 "Excellent" .elite 80–90 "Good" .good 70–80 "Solid" .solid 60–70 "Inconsistent" .inconsistent 50–60 "Shaky" .shaky < 50 "Room to grow" .struggling

The top cut point differs between the two

descriptor splits 90–95 from 95+ into two labels; band collapses both into one .elite case at the 90 cutoff. A UI showing the word grade next to a band-derived color chip can legitimately show "Engine-level" and "Excellent" against the identical color.

RecentAccuracyKernel — candidateLimit = 25 is applied to rows with non-empty annotationEvalsJSON before username/color resolution or accuracy decoding, mirroring Apple's SwiftData query (fetch newest 25 annotated rows, then filter). A malformed-but-annotated row still consumes a budget slot even though it yields no Point. pointLimit = 10; results collected newest-first, reversed to oldest-first for left-to-right display.

docs.title: Supporting pure math
docs.text:
MaterialBalance.compute(from:) — kings excluded from both counting and value:

pieceOrder = [.queen, .rook, .bishop, .knight, .pawn]
startingCounts = [Q:1, R:2, B:2, N:2, P:8]     pieceValues = [Q:9, R:5, B:3, N:3, P:1]
capturedByColor[type] = max(0, startingCounts[type] − currentOnBoard[type])
whiteAdvantage        = whiteTotalValue − blackTotalValue

StreakMath — callers map attempts to [Bool], most-recent last: current(flags) is the trailing run of true (reversed scan, stop at first false); best(flags) is the longest run anywhere (forward pass, reset on false).

docs.title: Headless usage today
docs.text: fianchetto-cli already exposes estimate (runs EloEstimator.estimate against an annotated PGN), track (threads estimates through a StrengthTracker), project (drives ChessComGameProjectionCalibrator), accuracy (AccuracyAggregator's per-phase/per-bucket breakdown), and maia (Maia-native move-quality/rank scoring). Not yet exposed as their own subcommands, despite being pure and headless-safe: chart-domain (EloChartPresentation.domain/.clipped, for a non-Swift consumer to compute the same Y-axis bounds the app draws); serving-coverage (StatsChartPresentationPolicy.estimatedStrengthServingCoverage, to report Maia-refined vs. fallback fraction without the chart UI); recent- accuracy (RecentAccuracyKernel.points, scripting the sparkline budget policy); tc-classify (TimeControlClass.classify and StatsKernel.classifySpeed side by side, useful precisely because they can disagree); and calibration-dump (a diagnostic dump of EloCalibrationData's fitted constants — this one needs a small public shim first, since the type is internal and unreachable from outside FianchettoKit today).

docs.title: Endgame mining and the endgame trainer
docs.text:
Two connected subsystems. The trainer generates fresh legal FENs for eight curated archetypes and bounds the tablebase probe/regeneration loop. The mining pipeline turns the user's own games into drill positions and caches them as immutable, content-addressed, sync-safe generations.

Everything here is pure logic: value types — apart from the two caller-confined scratch classes, EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool and EndgameMiningV2ScratchLease — plus (String) -> String? load closures, injected FileManager, no actor isolation and no storage backend.

Layer Types What it decides Extraction PersonalEndgameExtractor, PersonalEndgameSourceAnalysis which position in a game is the endgame decision point Witnesses EndgameMiningManifest, EndgameMiningGenerationCommit that a source was examined, and that a generation is complete V1 storage EndgameMiningShard, EndgameMiningGenerationRecord, EndgameMiningStorageHead how a generation is partitioned into bounded rows V1 reconciliation EndgameMiningGenerationResolver, EndgameMiningReclamationPolicy which visible head wins, and what may be deleted V2 storage EndgameMiningV2SourceResult, EndgameMiningV2ResultShard, EndgameMiningV2IndexPage generation-neutral results in a radix-16 trie V2 writing EndgameMiningV2StorageBuilder, EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool, EndgameMiningV2ScratchLease streaming construction under bounded memory, disk and ownership Trainer EndgamePuzzle, EndgameProbeGuard, EndgameFeedback which drill to show, when to regenerate, what counts as a miss

docs.title: Extraction: what counts as a personal endgame
docs.text:
PersonalEndgameExtractor walks a game's main line and returns at most one position — the first point where the user was to move and the board had dropped into tablebase range while still holding material worth drilling. One position per game keeps the list varied instead of yielding twenty near-duplicates from a single long endgame.

for ply i in 0 ..< mainLine.count:
    position   = mainLine[i].positionBefore        # the decision point
    pieceCount = non-empty squares of position
    require 4 <= pieceCount <= 7                   # else continue
    require mover(ply: i, startIsWhite:) == userColor
    emit one PersonalEndgamePosition and stop

7 is Lichess tablebase coverage; 4 is the least material that is still a drill. The emitted position carries fen (positionBefore.stockfishSafeFEN), gameInfo ("<white> vs <black>"), moveNumber (the position's fullmoveNumber), pieceCount, userColor, and a category material summary read off the board — "K+R vs K+P", "K+Q vs K+R".

PersonalEndgamePosition.id is its fen, so rebuilding the projection from an immutable generation does not hand every row a new identity and make a list diff treat unchanged positions as new. PersonalEndgamePositionData is the Codable form: it flattens userColor to userColorRaw ("white" / "black") so one plain-JSON shape is shared by iOS and Android, and decodes leniently (fen "", gameInfo "", moveNumber 1, pieceCount 4, userColorRaw "white", category "").

currentRevision is 4, and it is one of the three fields of the source key. Bumping it when eligibility or emitted semantics change is what stops an old negative result from suppressing a newer extractor: revision 5 produces different sources, so every game is reconsidered.

docs.title: Source identity without replay
docs.text:
A cache needs a key that is cheap to compute. Constructing every intermediate position merely to discover whether a result is reusable would defeat the purpose, so sourceDigest(input:) hashes the lexical PGN semantics. Tokenization drops comments, variations, NAGs, move numbers and results, so a plain copy and the app's annotated rewrite of the same game hash identically.

PortableSHA256; every field length-prefixed
  (8-byte big-endian UTF-8 length, then the bytes)

domain   "personal-endgame-source:v4"
then     input.white
         input.black
         input.username
         canonicalStartingPositionIdentity(input.startingPositionFEN)
then     decimal count of main-line moves
then     each canonicalized SAN, in order

canonicalStartingPositionIdentity(fen):
    trimmed.isEmpty -> Position.initial().fen
    otherwise       -> Position(fen: trimmed)?.fen ?? trimmed

canonicalLexicalSAN(san):
    remove '+', '#', '!', '?'; trim whitespace
    "0-0" -> "O-O",  "0-0-0" -> "O-O-O"

The normalization is deliberately conservative: if two unusual SAN spellings are not provably equivalent lexically they become separate sources and are replayed, rather than risking an incorrect cache hit. An invalid starting FEN stays byte-identifiable for repair diagnostics.

Note

This digest is an admission witness, not a completion witness. A match at the same extractor revision may reuse a previously validated result; a miss must still complete a diagnostic-free semantic replay before it can publish either positions or noPositions.

docs.title: Completion versus rejection
docs.text:
analyze(stableGameID:from:) validates and replays one exact source once and returns .completed or .rejected. Only .completed carries a PersonalEndgameCompletedExtraction, whose initializer is fileprivate — nothing outside the extractor can mint one, so a permissive empty legacy result cannot retire a source as complete.

Rejection Cause insufficientInput white, black, username or move text is blank invalidStableGameID empty, or not equal to GameIdentity.normalizedIdentifier of its own NFC-precomposed form unresolvedUserColor the saved account name matches neither player invalidMainLine(diagnostic) ChessCore reported a replay diagnostic insufficientMainLine the record parsed but yielded no playable move

PersonalEndgameMainLineDiagnostic carries bounded context — invalidFEN(preview:), unparseableMove(san:plyIndex:), tagsOnlyRecord, moveTreeNodeLimitExceeded(maximumNodes:), other. Previews are truncated before they enter the value: the first 96 unicode scalars, whitespace runs collapsed to single spaces, "…" appended when anything was dropped. Surfacing an error can therefore never echo a whole PGN. The diagnostic itself is a plain value; every case renders a distinct user-facing message through the rejection's errorDescription (PersonalEndgameExtractionCompletionError is the LocalizedError), and unparseableMove reports a 1-based "ply \(max(0, plyIndex) + 1)".

Warning

A rejection is retry-eligible and must never become a durable noPositions manifest. noPositions means "this exact source was examined and intentionally produced nothing"; a rejection means "this source could not be examined".

let input = TacticsInput(
    white: game.white,
    black: game.black,
    moveText: game.moveText,
    tagsJSON: game.tagsJSON,
    annotationEvalsJSON: "",
    username: account
)

switch PersonalEndgameExtractor.analyze(stableGameID: game.stableID, from: input) {
case .completed(let extraction):
    let admission = try EndgameMiningStorageAdmission(
        completedExtraction: extraction,
        whitePlayerName: input.white,
        blackPlayerName: input.black
    )
    stage(try admission.manifest(generation: 1, completedExtraction: extraction))

case .rejected(let error):
    report(error.errorDescription)      // retry-eligible; record nothing durable
}

EndgameMiningStorageAdmission bounds display metadata before it can enter coverage: stableGameID at 512 UTF-8 bytes, white + black player names at 384 UTF-8 bytes combined, else sourceNotStorable. Without that gate one game with a pathological label could make every full-library generation fail forever at the shard writer. Skipped sources should be counted and reconsidered on each rescan; authored game data is never truncated. manifest(...) re-checks that the extraction's source equals the admitted one (commitMismatch) and that the record is shard-storable.

docs.title: Witnesses: manifests, outcomes, coverage
docs.text:
EndgameMiningManifest is one immutable per-source V1 result. Its Source is the triple (stableGameID, sourceDigest, extractorRevision) — the full triple is the key, so one game can be mined for several account identities without collision. sourceDigest must be canonical lowercase SHA-256 (64 hex) and extractorRevision must be positive.

Outcome cardinality — enforced on construction AND on decode:
    (.noPositions, 0 positions)   ok
    (.positions,   1 position)    ok
    anything else                 throw .invalidOutcome

Position validity:
    FEN parses; moveNumber > 0; userColorRaw ∈ {"white","black"};
    actual board piece count ∈ 4...7 and == the declared pieceCount

manifestDigest = H("endgame-mining-manifest:v1", schemaVersion, generation,
                   source triple, outcome.kind, position count,
                   each position's six fields)

The single-position invariant freezes today's extractor into storage so a malformed record cannot turn one bounded shard into an unbounded payload; a multi-position policy must bump both revision and schema.

Coverage and the commit are built in constant memory from a canonically ordered stream, so no library-sized array is ever materialized.

V1 source order (EndgameMiningSourceOrder.precedes):
    stableGameID, then sourceDigest, then extractorRevision

Coverage.Builder: seed "endgame-mining-coverage:v1"; per source append the three
    fields length-prefixed (duplicate -> .duplicateSource,
    out of order -> .sourceOutOfOrder); finish by hashing the decimal count.

Commit Builder: seed "endgame-mining-set:v1"; per manifest append its
    manifestDigest; finish by hashing the decimal count, then require
    rebuiltCoverage == expectedCoverage else .coverageMismatch.

generationDigest = H("endgame-mining-generation:v1", schemaVersion, generation,
                     coverage.sourceCount, coverage.sourceSetDigest,
                     manifestSetDigest)

Because finish() refuses a partial source set, a cancelled prefix can leave unreachable immutable shards but can never become a visible generation. EndgameMiningHead binds to generationDigest; legacyGeneration = 0 names the historical flat cache, and decode admits only (0, nil) or (>= 1, canonical SHA-256).

docs.title: V1 storage layout
docs.text:
Every sync-visible row is bounded and content-addressed, so the encoded payload stays independent of library size.

Object Bound Storage key manifest (inside a shard) 8 KiB — EndgameMiningShard 96 manifests, 900 KiB personalEndgames/shard/v1/<shardDigest> EndgameMiningGenerationRecord 10 922 shards, 768 KiB personalEndgames/generation/v1/<recordDigest> EndgameMiningStorageHead 4 KiB personalEndgames/head/v1 EndgameMiningProjectionReceipt 8 KiB personalEndgames/projectionReceipt/v1 
maximumSourceCount = 10_922 * 96 = 1_048_512

expectedShardCount(sourceCount):
    0                        when sourceCount == 0
    ((sourceCount - 1) / 96) + 1   otherwise

expectedManifestCount(inShardAt: i):
    96                                    for every non-final shard
    sourceCount % 96, or 96 when that remainder is 0, for the last

Since every non-final shard holds exactly 96 manifests, the source count in the commit determines the entire partition — the layout is unique and a repartitioned copy is rejected with invalidCanonicalPartition. The record also binds its parent (EndgameMiningGenerationIdentity, .legacy = (0, nil, nil)) and requires commit.generation == parent.generation + 1. EndgameMiningStorageNamespace marks all of this as infrastructure: keys under personalEndgames/ (or the reserved legacy personalEndgames_) are sync and crash-recovery machinery, so semantic library backups carry only the flat projection.

EndgameMiningGenerationStorageBuilder writes a generation in constant source memory: feed manifests in canonical order, persist each shard append(_:) returns as it crosses a 96-manifest boundary, then publish Completion(finalShard, commit, generationRecord, storageHead) in exactly that order. Every fallible mutation is staged in value copies, so a rejected append leaves the builder reusable and cannot silently drop a full shard.

docs.title: The canonical-JSON contract
docs.text:
EndgameMiningStorageCodec (and its V2 twin) is the only supported entry point, because a bare JSONDecoder enforces neither half of the contract:

encode: JSONEncoder with [.sortedKeys, .withoutEscapingSlashes]
        reject when data.count > maximumBytes  ->  .payloadTooLarge(limit:)

decode: reject empty, or source.utf8.count > maximumBytes — BEFORE decoding, so
        nested arrays cannot be allocated first
        decode, re-encode, require byte-for-byte equality
        otherwise -> .nonCanonicalJSON

The byte-exact re-encode rejects unknown fields, alternate key order, insignificant whitespace and noncanonical escaping. It is also why the same bytes compare equal across platforms.

docs.title: V1 reconciliation
docs.text:
EndgameMiningGenerationResolver.resolve(...) compares all visible head copies against a freshly recomputed source universe and returns .promote or .retainCurrent(reason).

if headJSONCandidates.count > 4_096  ->  .retainCurrent(.candidateLimitExceeded)

decode candidates, drop legacy heads
append the current receipt's head (a receipt is itself a durable head witness, so
    a missing or hidden physical head row cannot lose it)
sort DESCENDING by (generation, generationDigest, generationRecordDigest);
    skip exact repeats

per candidate:
    skip when precedes(candidate, currentHead)            # monotonic floor
    skip when candidate == currentHead and its record coverage ==
         expectedCoverage and the flat cache matches the receipt
    require the record loads, head.accepts(record),
            record.commit.coverage == expectedCoverage
    fully revalidate every shard  ->  .promote

else .retainCurrent(currentReceipt == nil ? .noCompleteGeneration
                                          : .currentGenerationPreferred)

Two rules carry the weight. The receipt is an unconditional monotonic floor: temporary object loss or a changed live source universe may make its projection unusable, but neither authorizes a passive rollback to an older sync-visible generation. And parent identity is audit metadata, not an admission gate — requiring ancestry would permanently fork replicas that advanced opposite sides of a concurrent head race, so deterministic digest tie-breaking is what makes them converge.

EndgameMiningValidatedGeneration (mintable only by the resolver) re-derives the commit while streaming, checking each shard's content address, generation and expected manifest count, and finally requiring builder.finish() == record.commit.

docs.title: V2: generation-neutral results in a radix-16 trie
docs.text:
V1 embeds the scan generation in every manifest digest, so every full scan rewrites every row. V2 removes the generation from result identity, which makes an unchanged source referencable by every later generation.

sourceKeyDigest = H("endgame-mining-source-key:v2", source triple)
resultDigest    = H("endgame-mining-result:v2", schemaVersion, source triple,
                    outcome.kind, each position's six fields, position count)

V2 order: sourceKeyDigest first; on a hash collision fall back to the V1 tuple
          (stableGameID, sourceDigest, extractorRevision)

EndgameMiningV2SourceResult reuses the V1 manifest kernel for semantic validation (constructed at firstManifestGeneration) without keeping that generation in the value or either hash. Results live in a content-addressed trie keyed by hex nibbles of sourceKeyDigest:

leaf: buffer results while count <= 96
97th: split into a radix-16 index page keyed by the nibble at
      depth = prefix.utf8.count, then reapply the rule recursively
depth: a 64-character prefix exhausts the hash -> .hashPrefixExhausted

Result shard: every result's sourceKeyDigest starts with the shard prefix;
    results strictly V2-ordered; no duplicate source.
Index page:   children strictly ascending by nibble; unique child digests;
    <= 16 children; prefix shorter than 64; summed sourceCount > 96, so a page
    can never stand in for a leaf.
Node reference: sourceCount > 0; resultShard <= 96; indexPage > 96.

Only one child per level is ever active, which bounds writer memory at 96 buffered results plus at most 16 child references per level.

Object Bound Storage key EndgameMiningV2SourceResult 8 KiB — (inside a shard or a spool frame) EndgameMiningV2ResultShard 96 results, 900 KiB personalEndgames/result/v2/<shardDigest> EndgameMiningV2IndexPage 16 children, 16 KiB personalEndgames/index/v2/<pageDigest> EndgameMiningV2GenerationRecord 1 048 512 sources, 16 KiB personalEndgames/generation/v2/<recordDigest> EndgameMiningV2StorageHead 4 KiB personalEndgames/head/v2 EndgameMiningV2ProjectionReceipt 8 KiB personalEndgames/projectionReceipt/v2

The generation record is a compact selection record — coverage proof (endgame-mining-coverage:v2), result-set proof (endgame-mining-result-set:v2), and the root reference. It requires generation == parent.generation + 1, coverage.sourceCount == resultSet.resultCount, and either (0 sources, nil root) or (>= 1 sources, root.sourceCount == coverage.sourceCount). hasEquivalentSourceResults(to:) is the publisher's no-op predicate — coverage, result set and root only, ignoring generation and parent.

docs.title: Writing a V2 generation
docs.text:
EndgameMiningV2StorageBuilder.append(_:) is transactional: coverage, result-set and trie state are staged in copies before commit, and it rejects duplicateSource, invalidCanonicalOrder and tooManySources(limit: 1_048_512). Artifacts stream out dependency-first as subtrees complete, so each can be persisted immediately; finish() returns the remaining artifacts ending with the root, plus the generation record and head.

Results must arrive in V2 order. A platform whose enumeration is not already in hash order uses EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool, a caller-scoped disk-backed radix sort that creates and exclusively owns a previously nonexistent directory and removes it after every successful or failed build.

Frame layout (68 bytes of overhead per record):
    4-byte big-endian JSON length | 64-byte source key | canonical JSON

drain(file, expectedCount, prefix, depth):
    expectedCount <= 96:
        read every frame; require the decoded sourceKeyDigest to equal the frame
        header and to start with `prefix`; sort in memory by
        EndgameMiningV2SourceOrder; feed the trie builder
    otherwise:
        require depth < 64
        partition into up to 16 child files by the nibble at `depth`
        a bucket > 96 whose source keys are all identical throws
            .tooManyEquivalentSourceKeys(limit: 96) rather than copying the same
            input through all 64 radix levels
        recurse over "0123456789abcdef" in order
Constant Value maximumDecodedBatchResultCount 96 maximumInMemoryResultCount 192 (a batch plus the writer's retained leaf) maximumSimultaneouslyOpenFileHandles 17 (one reader, sixteen writers) maximumSimultaneouslyResidentScratchFiles 15 · 64 + 17 = 977 maximumSpoolBytes 1 048 512 · (8 192 + 68) = 8 660 709 120 maximumWorkingBytes twice that — a partition holds its source and its copy minimumFreeCapacityReserveBytes 512 MiB workingDirectoryNamePrefix fianchetto-endgame-mining-v2-spool-

Before each write the spool accumulates bytes and re-probes free capacity every 16 MiB, requiring available >= 512 MiB + 16 MiB or throwing insufficientScratchCapacity(minimumAvailableBytes:) — rendered as MiB by ceiling division on 1 048 576. The reserve leaves room for app recovery, database journals and an actionable error instead of consuming the volume to zero.
