States run accepting -> sealed -> draining -> finished | failed; any failure closes and removes the whole directory, and a cleanup failure supersedes the operation error so a retained spool is never mistaken for a clean one. reclaimStaleWorkingDirectories(in:olderThan:...) sweeps abandoned directories at startup (defaults: 256 scanned entries, 8 removals).

let lease = try EndgameMiningV2ScratchLease.acquire(in: scratchParent)
defer { try? lease.release() }

let spool = try EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool(
    directory: EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool.workingDirectoryURL(in: scratchParent)
)

for extraction in completedExtractions {
    try spool.append(EndgameMiningV2SourceResult(completedExtraction: extraction))
    try lease.checkpoint()          // fails closed if this owner was displaced
}

let completion = try spool.build(
    generation: nextGeneration,
    parent: parentIdentity
) { artifact in
    try store.write(artifact.storageKey, artifact.canonicalJSON())
}

// Publish only after every immutable node is durable.
try store.write(completion.generationRecord.storageKey,
                EndgameMiningV2StorageCodec.encodeCanonical(completion.generationRecord))
try store.write(EndgameMiningV2StorageHead.storageKey,
                EndgameMiningV2StorageCodec.encodeCanonical(completion.storageHead))

Warning

The spool is intentionally not Sendable and performs synchronous file I/O. Create, append and build it on one caller-owned worker; never drive it from several actors or threads.

docs.title: Scratch ownership
docs.text:
A spool can legitimately reach several gigabytes, so age-only cleanup is not enough: repeated force-termination can leave several fresh spools before any becomes reclaimable. EndgameMiningV2ScratchLease permits one owner per app-private parent directory.

acquire: up to 4 attempts at exclusive creation of
         "fianchetto-endgame-mining-v2-lease"

if it exists, observe (owner.json bytes, directory mtime, heartbeat):
    the owner is fresh — takeover forbidden — when the reference time is within
    5 minutes OR lies in the future (a clock rollback must never license two
    owners)

otherwise: same-volume rename to
           "fianchetto-endgame-mining-v2-retired-lease-<UUID>", re-observe, and
           require byte-identical metadata (else restore it and report
           .leaseBusy); then re-create the lease and delete the retired copy

checkpoint(): re-read the token every call — mismatch -> .leaseLost;
              rewrite the heartbeat at most every 5 seconds

Predecessor cleanup is bounded to 512 scanned parent entries, 64 spool directories and 16 retired leases; exceeding any of them throws cleanupLimitExceeded instead of scanning an unbounded directory.

docs.title: Reading, merging and projecting
docs.text:
EndgameMiningV2ValidatedGeneration (public init, throwing headMismatch unless head.accepts(record)) rebuilds the coverage and result-set proofs while descending, checking each node's prefix, digest and sourceCount against its reference (recordMismatch otherwise) and bounding the walk:

maximumNodeCount = maximumSourceCount + 64 * (maximumSourceCount / 97 + 1)
                 = 1_048_512 + 64 * 10_810
                 = 1_740_352 visited nodes before .tooManyNodes

forEachReusableResult(currentSources:loadObjectJSON:_:) is the single-pass merge kernel publishers use instead of a library-sized dictionary. It validates currentSources through a V2 coverage builder (rejecting an out-of-order or duplicated universe up front), traverses both streams once in V2 order, invokes the callback on each exact source match, and returns a [Bool] reuse bitmap — every unset entry must be re-extracted. Callbacks can run before a later corrupt dependency is discovered, so callers must stage writes and commit only after the method returns.

De-duplication reproduces V1 output byte-for-byte regardless of trie layout:

V1: walk manifests in canonical source order, keep the FIRST occurrence of a FEN
V2: traverse in hash order; for a duplicate FEN keep the winner with the MINIMUM
    source under EndgameMiningSourceOrder, then sort survivors by that same order

The receipt distinguishes a valid current cache from a partially written one: it requires a non-legacy head and unique FENs, and hashes the head identity, then each position's six fields, then the count (endgame-mining-projection:v1 / :v2).

switch EndgameMiningV2GenerationResolver.resolveProjection(
    currentReceipt: receipt,
    currentProjectionMatchesReceipt: receipt?.accepts(currentPositions) ?? false,
    expectedCoverage: expectedCoverage,
    headJSONCandidates: perReplicaHeadJSON,
    loadGenerationRecordJSON: { store.string(forKey: $0) },
    loadObjectJSON: { store.string(forKey: $0) }
) {
case .promote(let projection):
    // Atomically replace the flat cache and its receipt — never union them.
    try store.replaceMinedEndgames(projection.positions,
                                   receipt: projection.receipt)
case .retainCurrent(let reason):
    log("kept the current projection: \(reason)")
}

resolve and resolveProjection share one ranking kernel — (generation, generationRecordDigest) descending, the same 4 096-candidate limit, the same receipt-as-floor rule — and evaluate runs at most once per unique viable head, so the winning trie is walked exactly once whether the caller wanted strict validation or a materialized projection. Missing or corrupt higher dependencies never hide a lower complete candidate.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
Every full V1 scan creates a new generation, because generation identity is part of the manifest proof. EndgameMiningReclamationPolicy.plan(...) keeps that from growing without bound.

retain: "personalEndgames/head/v1", plus for each distinct non-legacy visible
        head (INCLUDING the current receipt's) its generation-record key and
        every shard key that record names

defer the whole pass (isDeferred) when candidates exceed 4_096, or an active
        record is missing / undecodable / not accepted by its head — a
        not-yet-arrived directory is the only safe way to discover its shards

reclaim only when ALL hold:
        the key starts with "personalEndgames/shard/v1/"
                         or "personalEndgames/generation/v1/"
        it is unretained
        now - lastModified >= 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1_000 ms  (2_592_000_000)

The 30-day floor covers long offline and sync intervals. Platforms may use a longer interval, never a shorter one.

docs.title: Storage epochs
docs.text:
Occasionally a physical namespace must be retired — a container reset — without changing any semantic V2 object. Epochs give identical bytes a permanently distinct address. EndgameMiningV2StorageEpochIdentity is (sequence, descriptorDigest), valid only as (0, nil) (the shipped unscoped keys) or (>= 1, canonical SHA-256). The descriptor (sequence = parent.sequence + 1, 8 KiB, personalEndgames/storageEpoch/v1/<digest>) binds a transition nonce and the exact replica roster under endgame-mining-v2-storage-epoch:v1.

epoch 0: exact identity mapping of the logical key

epoch n: "personalEndgames/v2e/" + descriptorDigest + "/" + kind + "." + digest
         kind ∈ { "r" result shard, "i" index page, "g" generation record }

reverse: exactly 4 slash-separated components; [0] == "personalEndgames",
         [1] == "v2e", [2] == the epoch digest, canonical SHA-256 after the '.'

loadLogicalJSON(for:epoch:loadPhysicalJSON:) is shaped to be handed straight to the graph walks. EndgameMiningV2EpochStorageHead (prefix personalEndgames/head/v2e/ plus a validated EndgameMiningReplicaID — up to 128 bytes of [0-9A-Za-z._-]) and EndgameMiningV2EpochProjectionReceipt both reject a legacy epoch or legacy inner value and hash the canonical inner JSON (endgame-mining-v2-epoch-head:v1, endgame-mining-v2-epoch-projection:v1), so identical inner heads in different epochs are never interchangeable authority.

docs.title: The trainer runtime
docs.text:
EndgamePuzzle pairs an archetype with a training tip. Its FEN is regenerated on every attempt, so the spaced-repetition key is deliberately FEN-independent:

public var masteryKey: String { "\(archetype.rawValue):\(description)" }

The static catalogue holds 12 drills — two K+Q vs K, two K+R vs K, one K+2B vs K, one K+B+N vs K, three K+P vs K, one Lucena, one Philidor, one K+Q vs K+P. Mastery counts persist through BlunderMasteryStore (see Stores).

EndgameProbeGuard bounds the "regenerate when the tablebase says drawn" loop and rejects stale in-flight probes:

beginSetup(isRegen:)  currentToken &+= 1; regenAttempts = 0 unless isRegen
isStale(token:)       nil -> false (unowned mid-puzzle re-probes are fresh);
                      otherwise token != currentToken
decideOnDraw()        regenAttempts < maxRegenAttempts (default 3)
                          -> increment and return .regen
                      otherwise -> .exhausted, permanently, for this puzzle

var probeGuard = EndgameProbeGuard()          // maxRegenAttempts: 3
var fen = puzzle.archetype.randomFEN()
let token = probeGuard.beginSetup()

let probe = try await TablebaseService.shared.probe(fen: fen)
guard !probeGuard.isStale(token: token) else { return }   // a newer setup won

if probe.category == .draw {
    switch probeGuard.decideOnDraw() {
    case .regen:
        fen = puzzle.archetype.randomFEN()
        _ = probeGuard.beginSetup(isRegen: true)   // keeps the attempt count
    case .exhausted:
        present(fen)                               // stop looping
    }
}

EndgameFeedback is the answer verdict: correct(dtm:), closeEnough(dtm:best:), wrong(expected:), tablebaseUnavailable, engineUnavailable, done.

Warning

engineUnavailable means the Stockfish fallback produced no completed score. It is not a chess miss and must not increment attempts or mastery — otherwise a flaky engine silently resets the user's streak.

EndgameProbeGuard owns the trainer's own probe tokens; RunGeneration is the separate general-purpose restartable-work token the long-running schedulers use (Maia backfill, the Android mining run lifecycle). begin() and invalidate() both do current &+= 1 (invalidate revokes without granting), and owns(_:) is exact equality. Capture a token, then publish or clear shared state only while owns(_:) holds: cancellation cannot synchronously stop code already inside a non-cancellable framework call, so a predecessor may reach its cleanup after its replacement has started.

docs.title: Position generation
docs.text:
EndgameArchetype.randomFEN() retries attemptGenerate() up to 200 times, then returns the per-case fallbackFEN (kqVsK → "8/8/8/4k3/8/3Q4/3K4/8 w - - 0 1", philidor → "8/8/4k3/8/4K3/r7/4P3/3R4 b - - 0 1"). Each random-square primitive retries 50 times before returning to the outer loop. Lucena and Philidor are hard-coded template families (5 and 4 templates), varying the file while preserving the technique.

Kings are never adjacent (Chebyshev distance <= 1 is forbidden).
A piece adjacent to the enemy king is admitted only when the friendly king
    also defends it.

K+Q vs K, K+R vs K  black king on files/ranks 2...5; white king at Chebyshev
                    distance 2...4
K+2B vs K, K+B+N    black king on files/ranks drawn from {1, 2, 5, 6};
                    white king at distance 2...5
K+P vs K            pawn on 0-indexed rank 2...5; white king within distance
                    1...2 of the square in front of the pawn and never on
                    rank 0; black king at distance 2...4 from the pawn, not
                    adjacent to the white king, not on a pawn-attacked square
K+Q vs K+P          black pawn on 0-indexed rank 1...2, white to move

Finalization is where "legal" becomes "drillable":

finalize(pos):
    reject when the side NOT to move is in check
        (the previous move would have been illegal)
    reject when the side to move has no legal move
        (mate or stalemate is not a drill)
    emit pos.stockfishSafeFEN

That last line matters: Position() defaults castling rights to all-true and a random endgame layout has no kings or rooks on their home squares. stockfishSafeFEN zeros castling and en-passant state inconsistent with the board, which is what stops these FENs from crashing Stockfish's strict parser downstream.

CustomEndgameConfig covers material outside the curated catalogue. PieceCounts clamps queens, rooks, bishops and knights to 0...maxPerPieceType (4) and pawns to 0...8; totalPieces = 2 + white.totalNonKing + black.totalNonKing, and isValid is totalPieces <= 32. Generation places the black king centrally, then the non-adjacent white king, then non-pawn pieces under the en-prise/defended rule, then pawns on 0-indexed ranks 1...6 with white pawns forbidden from attacking the black king. randomFEN() returns nil after 200 failed attempts; fallbackFEN is "8/8/8/4k3/8/4K3/8/8 w - - 0 1".

Note

Positions above 7 pieces fall outside Lichess tablebase coverage, so the trainer skips win verification for them. See Network clients for TablebaseService.

docs.title: Using it from the command line
docs.text:
Every seam above is already headless, which is what makes it scriptable without an app. fianchetto-cli today ships annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project and track; none of them wrap this pipeline yet. The natural split follows the three proofs:

Proposed subcommand Seam it would expose endgame-mine PersonalEndgameExtractor.analyze + EndgameMiningStorageAdmission + EndgameMiningV2OrderingSpool.build over a PGN corpus, emitting trie artifacts endgame-verify EndgameMiningV2ValidatedGeneration.validate / EndgameMiningGenerationResolver.resolve against a directory of head copies endgame-pack materializeProjection to the flat position cache plus its receipt

Because every digest is PortableSHA256 over length-prefixed UTF-8 and every envelope is byte-exact canonical JSON, golden digest fixtures are the cheapest parity test available: mine a fixed corpus once, record the sourceDigest, resultDigest, shardDigest, recordDigest and projectionDigest values, and assert that the iOS and Android implementations reproduce them byte-for-byte.

docs.title: Engine, Annotation & Maia
docs.text: The engine subsystem: a UCI session layer shared by Stockfish and Reckless, the per-ply classification kernel that turns a raw eval sweep into !!/?? glyphs, two-engine consensus, and the Maia 3 board/policy codec plus the on-device Elo backfill pipeline built on it.

docs.title: Overview — headless kernels, one MainActor-isolated driver
docs.text:
Every file under Engine/ imports only Foundation and/or ChessCore — no CoreML, SwiftUI, or UIKit. EngineBroker and EngineProbe are Swift actors, not observable view-model state. The actual UCI process/bridge and the actual model inference are both supplied by the caller through closures.

That is not the whole isolation story, though: LiveAnalysisDriver and the protocols it publishes through are genuinely @MainActor-isolated, on the type itself — LiveAnalysisDriver.swift:112 (LiveAnalysisContext) and :314 (LiveAnalysisDriver), and LiveAnalysisPublication.swift:295 (LiveAnalysisResultPublishing). This is a real, load-bearing dependency the kit carries, not a doc-comment note about how to call the code. It is deliberate: LiveAnalysisDriver feeds the eval bar, best-move arrow, and "Top lines" panel while the user navigates a game, and it is designed to run on the same actor as the @Observable shell object it writes into, so no cross-actor hop is needed to publish evalCp, bestMoveUCI, or the ranked line list on every engine info line. That is a different case from AnnotationDriver.collectEvals's onProgress parameter, which stays @Sendable and actor-agnostic: a caller touching actor-isolated UI state from that callback still has to marshal onto it itself (Task { @MainActor in … }).

Everything else here — EngineProbe, EngineBroker, AnnotationKernel, ConsensusKernel, Maia3Encoding, and the whole Maia backfill pipeline — carries no actor isolation beyond its own actor types and runs from a plain executable. LiveAnalysisDriver is the one deliberate exception, because it exists specifically to sit directly under a UI's observable state rather than behind a headless seam. That headless boundary for the rest is what lets fianchetto-cli's annotate, estimate, maia, and accuracy subcommands drive these same kernels from a plain executable, with a process-backed UCI engine and a CPU/ONNX Maia backend in place of the app's CoreML bridge.

docs.title: EngineProbe — the UCI transaction layer
docs.text:
EngineProbe is an actor that owns one live engine's raw output stream and turns it into a journal with monotonic cursors (EngineOutputCursor), so a protocol wait can never be satisfied by stale output. It sits directly above ChessCore's UCIEngine transport seam; the caller supplies an EngineFactory — @Sendable (EngineKind, URL) -> (any UCIEngine)? — that builds a concrete engine or returns nil if it can't initialize (e.g. a missing NNUE net). The kit never links an engine package itself.

Output journal. Every emitted line gets a monotonically increasing sequence number. The journal retains up to 4,096 lines under normal operation; once it exceeds 2× capacity (8,192 entries), an amortized compaction removes the oldest 4,096 at once rather than trimming per line. A cursor is valid only while its required sequence is still in the retained window — once it ages out, waits against it resolve to nil (fail closed) instead of resuming against a partial journal.

Protocol barriers.

  • drainSearch(timeoutNanoseconds:) — the single-phase Stockfish barrier: stop + isready, wait for a fresh readyok, and if a search was in flight also wait for its terminal bestmove.
  • beginNewGame(timeoutNanoseconds:) — the two-phase Reckless barrier. Reckless's router ignores ucinewgame while a search is running, so this crosses drainSearch's phase first, then sends ucinewgame + isready and waits for a second readyok.

Both default to 8,000,000,000 ns (8 s), the same timeout start(kind:networkDirectory:) uses for its own startup handshake.

One-shot helpers replace the hand-rolled start→send→wait→stop loop every drill/annotation site used to write:

Helper Returns Notes oneShotBestMove(fen:goCmd:maxIter:) String? MultiPV 1; legality-checked via legalBestMove oneShotScore(fen:goCmd:maxIter:pointOfView:) EngineScoreAdapter.Evaluation? Last rank-1 info before bestmove oneShotEvalCPAndMate(fen:goCmd:maxIter:) (cp: Int?, mate: Int?)? Splits oneShotScore's result oneShotIsMatingInBudget(fen:goCmd:budget:maxIter:) Bool? true iff 0 < mate <= budget oneShotRawLines(prelude:fen:goCmd:maxIter:pollNs:) [String]? Generalized collector; legacy pollNs default 50,000,000 ns (50 ms), timeout = maxIter × pollNs oneShotRecklessRawLines(prelude:fen:goCmd:readyTimeoutNanoseconds:searchTimeoutNanoseconds:) [String]? Fresh beginNewGame barrier; defaults 8 s ready / 20 s search

legalBestMove(in:for:) is the safety net every helper routes through except the generalized oneShotRawLines collector, which leaves parsing to the caller's own parser by design (its doc comment: site-specific parse semantics are not altered) — oneShotRecklessRawLines still gates on it. legalBestMove itself takes the last bestmove line, parses it with UCIParser, and returns nil unless it's actually legal — rejecting trailing junk, uppercase promotion letters, and omitted promotion suffixes.

docs.title: EngineBroker — one live engine per kind
docs.text:
The native engine bridges enforce exactly one live engine per process per EngineKind; a second construction blocks the underlying thread. EngineBroker is the process-wide actor owner that makes that safe under concurrent features, holding one EngineProbe.

Two consumption patterns share the one probe:

  • Exclusive leases (withEngine(networkDirectory:_:)) — short-lived, one-shot consumers (annotation sweeps, drill probes, trap miners), FIFO across borrowers. No start/stop inside the lease — the broker starts lazily on first use and never tears down a healthy engine.
  • The revocable live slot (claimLiveSlot(id:networkDirectory:pause:resume:isValid:) / releaseLiveSlot(_:)) — continuous consumers (live eval bar, second opinion, play-vs-engine search). Last claimant wins: claiming pauses the current holder via its own pause closure and returns an opaque LiveClaim (probe, holderID, epoch), so a stale continuation can never interrupt a replacement. An exclusive lease likewise pauses the live holder first and resumes it once the last queued borrow drains.

Failure is never silent. If the engine can't start, or stops answering its owner barrier (ownerBarrierTimeoutNanoseconds, default 8,000,000,000 ns), the broker attempts exactly one revival — tear the wedged engine down and rebuild through the same EngineFactory — before surfacing a typed, LocalizedError-conforming BrokerError.engineStartFailed / .protocolBarrierFailed. It never substitutes a different engine kind.

let broker = EngineBroker(kind: .stockfish, engineFactory: myEngineFactory)

let bestMove = try await broker.withEngine(networkDirectory: netDir) { probe in
    await probe.oneShotBestMove(fen: position.fen, goCmd: "go movetime 800", maxIter: 200)
}

Warning

Never nest withEngine calls on the same broker — the FIFO lease queue self-deadlocks, since the outer call already holds the only lease the inner call is waiting on.

docs.title: Position evaluation
docs.text:
AnnotationEval is the per-position payload every kernel here consumes (both iOS's PositionEval and Android's PositionEvalResult map onto it): engine-POV bestCp (mate flattens to ±100,000), optional secondBestCp, isMate, a signed mover-POV mateIn (the only place the mate distance survives the flatten), and bestMoveUCI ("" for terminal positions).

PositionEvaluator is the one-method seam the whole pipeline depends on instead of a concrete engine — func evaluate(fen: String) async -> AnnotationEval?. AnnotationDriver.collectEvals(positions:evaluator:onProgress:) walks a game's positions, filling terminal ones from AnnotationKernel.terminalEval(for:) directly and routing the rest through the evaluator; it returns nil on cancellation or if the evaluator ever returns nil (engine went silent aborts the whole sweep).

AnnotationEngineKind (String, CaseIterable, Codable, Sendable) sits beside that seam as the registry of which concrete evaluator a user may pick to drive library annotation — .stockfish (displayName "Stockfish") and .reckless ("Reckless"), persisted under settingsKey, the literal string "annotationEngine":

AnnotationEngineKind.settingsKey            // "annotationEngine"
AnnotationEngineKind.resolve(nil)           // .stockfish
AnnotationEngineKind.resolve("reckless")    // .reckless
AnnotationEngineKind.resolve("maia")        // .stockfish — unknown values fall back

resolve(_:) never fails: nil, an unknown raw value, or a value naming an engine that no longer qualifies all resolve to .stockfish. Membership here is a capability boundary, not a taste — only evaluating search engines, those producing a best move plus a centipawn or mate score per position, belong in this enum. Maia is deliberately absent: a human-move predictor (policy + WDL) cannot produce the centipawn deltas blunder-grading is built on, so it can never conform to PositionEvaluator's contract. Playing against an engine carries no such requirement, which is why PlayConfig.Engine is the wider set .maia / .stockfish / .reckless.

struct StockfishEvaluator: PositionEvaluator {
    let broker: EngineBroker
    let networkDirectory: URL
    let movetimeMs: Int

    func evaluate(fen: String) async -> AnnotationEval? {
        try? await broker.withEngine(networkDirectory: networkDirectory) { probe in
            guard let lines = await probe.oneShotRawLines(
                prelude: ["setoption name MultiPV value 2"],
                fen: fen,
                goCmd: "go movetime \(movetimeMs)",
                maxIter: 400
            ), let position = Position(fen: fen) else { return nil }
            let ranked = UCIInfoParser.bestInfoByRank(lines)
            let bestMoveUCI = EngineProbe.legalBestMove(in: lines, for: position) ?? ""
            return AnnotationKernel.extractEval(fromRankedInfos: ranked, bestMoveUCI: bestMoveUCI)
        }
    }
}

ranked above is a [Int: UCIInfoLine] rank map. UCIInfoLine is not a FianchettoKit type of its own — it's a compatibility typealias for ChessCore.UCIInfo. UCI line parsing is foundational chess logic, so ChessCore owns it; the alias (alongside UCIInfoParser for ChessCore.UCIOutputParser) exists purely so every FianchettoKit call site, and the Android port, kept compiling unchanged after the former kit-local copies were collapsed onto ChessCore's — which had already picked up the better parser (nps parsing, no mandatory pv token, bestmove (none) handling, bestInfoByRank). ChessCore.UCIInfo is a strict superset of the old line type: it keeps depth, multipv, scoreCp, mateIn, nps, pv, bestMoveUCI, centipawns, winProbability, displayText, and whitePovCentipawns, and adds a .score enum view plus .multiPV.

RecklessLine is a different shape over the same kind of MultiPV sweep, built for display and persistence rather than kernel consumption: one Identifiable (on rank, 1 = best), Codable value per ranked line — rank, evalText (pre-formatted White-POV, e.g. "+1.34", "M5"), bestMoveSAN, bestMoveUCI. It deliberately leaves origin/target squares for the caller to derive from bestMoveUCI's prefix/suffix rather than storing them redundantly. It's the canonical replacement for what iOS (AnalysisSession.swift's own RecklessLine) and Android (RecklessTopLine, which split UCI into separate from/to fields) each kept as independent duplicates — the shared form standardizes on bestMoveUCI and adds Codable so a ranked-line list can round-trip through session persistence.

EngineScoreAdapter is the one place a raw ChessCore.UCIInfo.Score becomes a mate-aware, explicitly-oriented Evaluation (centipawns + optional mateIn). PointOfView is .sideToMove (UCI convention) or .opponentOfSideToMove (flipped); flipping negates both fields via a saturating negation (Int.min maps to Int.max, never traps) — guarding a malformed cp Int.min line from turning a POV flip into a crash.

docs.title: The annotation kernel
docs.text: AnnotationKernel is the pure classification core both platforms previously hand-kept in sync: given a sweep of AnnotationEvals it decides, per ply, which glyph (if any) the move earns.

docs.title: Thoroughness scaling
docs.text:
Two knobs read the same user "Annotation thoroughness" pref string ("fast" / "thorough" / anything else including nil):

annotateMovetime(batch:thoroughness:)      // Stockfish, ms per position
  base = batch ? 500 : 1000
  "fast"      -> base * 6  / 10   //  300 / 600 ms
  "thorough"  -> base * 16 / 10   //  800 / 1600 ms
  default/nil -> base             //  500 / 1000 ms

annotateDepth(thoroughness:)               // Reckless, search depth in plies
  "fast" -> 10   "thorough" -> 14   default/nil -> 12

docs.title: Terminal and extracted evals
docs.text:
terminalEval(for: position)
  no legal moves, in check  -> bestCp = -100_000, isMate = true,  mateIn = 0,   bestMoveUCI = ""
  no legal moves, no check  -> bestCp = 0,         isMate = false, mateIn = nil, bestMoveUCI = ""
  has legal moves           -> nil   // non-terminal; caller must probe the engine

extractEval(fromRankedInfos: bestMoveUCI:)     // from a UCIInfoParser.bestInfoByRank map
  rank 1 .mate(m)  -> bestCp = ±100_000 (sign of m), isMate = true,  mateIn = m
  rank 1 .cp(cp)   -> bestCp = cp,                    isMate = false, mateIn = nil
  no rank 1 score  -> nil
  rank 2 .mate/.cp -> secondBestCp set the same way; absent -> nil

Every forced mate collapses bestCp to ±100,000 throughout this subsystem; the true distance survives only in mateIn.

docs.title: classifyGlyph — the annotation decision cascade
docs.text:
Evaluated in order; first match wins:

classifyGlyph(wpDrop:wpBefore:wpAfter:gap:playedBestMove:opponentMissed:involvesSacrifice:absEvalCp:)

Error band (worst first):
  wpDrop >= 0.20   -> blunder
  wpDrop >= 0.10   -> miss (if opponentMissed) else mistake
  wpDrop >= 0.05   -> miss (if opponentMissed) else dubious

Positive band (wpBefore < 0.75 required for brilliant — "not already winning"):
  wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.15 && |absEvalCp| < 50_000
    && wpBefore < 0.75 && involvesSacrifice          -> brilliant
  wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.08
    && (wpBefore < 0.40 || (wpBefore < 0.55 && wpAfter > 0.60)) -> great
  playedBestMove && gap >= 0.03                      -> best
  wpDrop < 0.02 && gap >= 0.03                       -> excellent
  wpDrop < 0.05 && gap >= 0.06                       -> good
  otherwise                                          -> nil   // fine, not remarkable

gap is the MultiPV win-probability gap between best and second-best (0 if no second line). opponentMissed, computed per ply:

opponentMissed = (oppWP - oppWPAfter) >= 0.10 && wpBefore > 0.55
  oppWP      = winProbability(evals[i-1].bestCp)   // opponent's WP two plies back
  oppWPAfter = 1 - wpBefore                        // opponent's WP right after their move

— the previous mover held a 10+ point swing and the current mover is still above 55%, meaning the opponent just failed to capitalize. involvesSacrifice (positionBefore:positionAfter:) feeds the brilliant gate:

for each of the mover's pieces on the post-move board, excluding king and pawn:
  skip unless the opponent attacks the square
  attacked AND undefended by the mover        -> sacrifice
  attacked AND defended, but specifically by
    an opponent PAWN                          -> sacrifice (still a net material loss)

AccuracyAggregator.classifyMoveQuality(wpDrop:playedBestMove:) (see Analysis Math) runs alongside classifyGlyph inside computeAnnotations to derive the separate, coarser 6-band MoveQuality written onto each node: playedBestMove short-circuits to .best; otherwise wpDrop >= 0.20/0.10/0.05/0.02 steps down through blunder/mistake/inaccuracy/good/excellent.

docs.title: computeAnnotations, applyAnnotations, annotateNodes
docs.text:
The pass splits into a pure stage (computeAnnotations(inputs:evals:startIsWhite:) -> [NodeAnnotationResult], Sendable end to end so it can run in Task.detached) and a write stage (applyAnnotations(_:to:game:)) that always clears every node's annotation fields first — so a re-annotation pass starts from a clean slate — then writes the new values. annotateNodes(mainLine:evals:game:startIsWhite:) is the backward-compatible wrapper that does both.

let evals = await AnnotationDriver.collectEvals(
    positions: positions,   // positions[0] = start; positions[i+1] = after mainLine[i]
    evaluator: StockfishEvaluator(broker: broker, networkDirectory: netDir, movetimeMs: 1000)
)
guard let evals else { return }   // cancelled, or the evaluator went silent

AnnotationKernel.annotateNodes(mainLine: mainLine, evals: evals, game: game, startIsWhite: true)

docs.title: The annotation pass kernel
docs.text:
AnnotationPassKernel sits above AnnotationKernel and owns the pass-level recipes both shells previously duplicated. Each decision below is pinned to a lettered "D" number from the 2026-07-31 extraction and covered by a kit parity test.

One-shot eval validation (D11). validatedOneShotEval(_:fen:) -> AnnotationEval? — AnnotationDriver.collectEvals only calls the evaluator for non-terminal positions, so an acceptable eval must name a legal best move. Stockfish's "(none)" normalizes to ""; empty, unparseable, or illegal-in-fen rejects the eval outright (aborts the sweep).

Verify-baseline rebuild (D7 / D8). rebuildVerifyBaseline(nodes:startIsWhite:provenanceJSON:finalPosition:retainedFinalWhiteCp:) -> Result<[AnnotationEval], VerifyBaselineFailure> reconstructs a mover-POV baseline from stored per-node fields (StoredBaselineNode { engineEval, engineBestMoveUCI }) for a "verify with the second engine" pass. D8: refuses to run unless provenanceJSON decodes to a Stockfish AnnotationProvenance (.provenanceNotStockfish). D7: every node must carry a parseable stored eval; one unparseable node hard-fails the entire rebuild (.unparseableStoredEval) rather than quietly substituting cp(0), which could misclassify that move. The parser inverts AnnotationKernel's display format:

parseStoredWhitePovEval(_:)
  "-M<N>" / bare "-M"   -> .mate(-N)     // bare sentinel means N = 1
  "M<N>"  / bare "M"    -> .mate(+N)
  "+1.3" / "-0.5" / "+0.0"  -> .cp(round(value * 100))   // pawns, |value| <= 1_000
  anything else          -> nil

storedWhiteCPScore(_:)                    // decoding the retained final-eval chart value
  non-finite, or |value| > 100_000  -> nil
  |value| == 100_000                -> .mate(value >= 0 ? +1 : -1)
  otherwise                         -> .cp(round(value))

The trailing sentinel (eval "after the last move") prefers the exact terminal eval when the final position is terminal, else the retained chart value — never inventing cp(0), which could falsely reclassify the last move (.missingFinalEval otherwise).

Batch charts and the per-game recipe (D1 / D4). serializeCharts(evals:startIsWhite:) -> AnnotationCharts (evalsJSON, secondBestJSON, mateDistancesJSON, all White-POV). D1: all three charts are always emitted, with explicit JSON null where no second line / no forced mate exists, so a game annotated on either platform satisfies the same isFullyAnnotated contract. runBatchGame(positions:startIsWhite:hasMoves:evaluator:pauseGate:progress:persistCharts:markUnevaluable:) -> BatchGameResult (.persisted, .unevaluable, .persistRejected, .engineSilent, .cancelled). D4: a zero-move / unparseable game calls markUnevaluable() and returns .unevaluable instead of being silently skipped forever, so a batch pass converges.

docs.title: AnnotationProvenance — compatibility rules
docs.text:
AnnotationProvenance (engine, engineRevision, searchKind: .movetimeMilliseconds | .depth, searchLimit, multiPV, includesConsensus, plus schemaVersion/contractVersion pinned to 1) is the durable identity of one annotation run — without it, switching Stockfish ↔ Reckless or changing thoroughness could silently reuse a stale array as current.

Two compatibility checks, deliberately different strictness:

Field satisfies — serve a cached request satisfiesRefreshRequirement — offer an auto-refresh schema/contract version both self and required == current same engine exact match exact match engineRevision exact match ignored — revisions describe, they don't expire searchKind exact match exact match searchLimit self >= required (deeper/longer satisfies weaker) self >= required multiPV exact match exact match includesConsensus superset: includesConsensus \|\| !required.includesConsensus same

AnnotationProvenanceCodec.decode only accepts JSON ≤ 4,096 UTF-8 bytes that is also structurally valid: engineRevision non-empty, ≤ 512 UTF-8 bytes, printable ASCII only (0x20...0x7e); searchLimit in 1...60_000; multiPV in 1...32. A missing, malformed, or future-schema envelope decodes to nil — stale, never silently current.

docs.title: AnnotationDisplay — glyph, name, and color tables
docs.text:
Centralizes what iOS and Android had each copied and let drift once already ("Dubious" vs "Inaccuracy"). Pure String/Double extensions on ChessCore.MoveAnnotation / MoveQuality — no SwiftUI Color.

MoveAnnotation.displayGlyph / .displayName / .displayRGB:

Case Glyph Name RGB brilliant !! Brilliant (0.00, 0.67, 0.67) great △ Great (0.35, 0.55, 0.71) best ✓ Best (0.55, 0.72, 0.30) excellent ✓ Excellent (0.55, 0.72, 0.30) good ! Good (0.45, 0.65, 0.50) interesting !? Interesting (0.45, 0.70, 0.45) dubious ?! Inaccuracy (0.90, 0.64, 0.45) miss ✕ Miss (0.85, 0.55, 0.30) mistake ? Mistake (0.90, 0.50, 0.15) blunder ?? Blunder (0.80, 0.20, 0.20)

MoveQuality.displayName / .displayRGB:

Case Name RGB best Best (0.00, 0.67, 0.45) excellent Excellent (0.30, 0.72, 0.40) good Good (0.60, 0.72, 0.30) inaccuracy Inaccuracy (0.95, 0.70, 0.20) mistake Mistake (0.95, 0.50, 0.20) blunder Blunder (0.80, 0.20, 0.20)

blunder's red — (0.80, 0.20, 0.20) — is identical between the two tables on purpose: a blunder reads the same whether shown via the glyph or the quality system.

docs.title: Two-engine consensus
docs.text:
ConsensusKernel reads two independent strong engines' takes on the same position and reports how much they agree — the basis for the "higher confidence" badge and "critical moment" flags. Both Stockfish and Reckless emit normalized centipawns (Reckless's normalize_to_cp mirrors Stockfish's NormalizeToPawnValue), so AccuracyAggregator.winProbability applies to both on the same scale — no engine-specific calibration needed.

compare(a, b, criticalGap: 0.15)     // EngineRead { cp, isMate, bestMoveUCI }; winProbability clamps mate to 0/1
  gap      = |a.winProbability - b.winProbability|
  sameMove = a.bestMoveUCI == b.bestMoveUCI && bestMoveUCI not empty
  critical = gap >= criticalGap || (!sameMove && gap >= criticalGap * 2 / 3)   // 0.15, or ~0.10 on disagreement
  confidence = sameMove && gap < 0.05 ? .high : critical ? .low : .medium

reconcileAnnotation(_:_:) merges two independently classified glyphs into one consensus glyph via a severity ladder, so a single engine's noise can't produce a false-positive ??/!!:

severity: brilliant=+4  great=+3  best/excellent=+2  good/interesting=+1
          nil=0  dubious=-1  miss/mistake=-2  blunder=-3

reconcileAnnotation(a, b):
  severity(a) == 0 || severity(b) == 0     -> nil   // one engine finds it unremarkable
  sign(severity(a)) != sign(severity(b))   -> nil   // opposite directions, no consensus
  otherwise -> whichever of a, b has the SMALLER |severity|   // what both engines actually support

ConsensusRecord (ply, agree, winProbGap, confidence as a raw string, critical) is the persisted per-ply summary; ConsensusJSON encodes/decodes [ConsensusRecord] as a plain array, returning "[]" / [] on any failure rather than throwing.

docs.title: Maia 3
docs.text:
Maia3Encoding is the pure, engine-agnostic codec for the Maia 3 network — inference (CoreML on Apple, ONNX/LiteRT on Android) stays app-side; only the tensor shapes are shared.

encodeTokens(position:)                          // 768 Float32s = 64 squares x 12 planes
  isBlack = position.activeColor == .black
  for each square (White's rank/file order):
    actualRank   = isBlack ? 7 - rank : rank                       // mirror ranks when Black is to move
    pieceColor   = isBlack ? piece.color.opposite : piece.color    // mirror color too
    featureIndex = pieceFeatureIndex(type) + (pieceColor == .white ? 0 : 6)
    tokens[(rank*8 + file)*12 + featureIndex] = 1.0
  pieceFeatureIndex: pawn=0 knight=1 bishop=2 rook=3 queen=4 king=5

policyIndex(for: move, activeColor:)             // squares mirrored to White's view when Black is active
  regular:    fromSq*64 + toSq                         // 0..4095, sq = rank*8 + file
  promotion:  4096 + fromFile*32 + toFile*4 + promoIdx  // 4096..4351; promoIdx: queen=0 rook=1 bishop=2 knight=3

decodeOutput(moveLogits:valueLogits:position:topK:) throws -> EngineAnalysis requires moveLogits.count >= 4352 or throws .predictionFailed. Its value head reorients the raw side-to-move-POV softmax into an explicit White-POV WDL — [stmLoss, drawProb, stmWin] = softmax(valueLogits[0..2]), then Black-to-move maps to .winDrawLoss(win: stmLoss, draw:, loss: stmWin) and White-to-move to .winDrawLoss(win: stmWin, draw:, loss: stmLoss). Legal moves (.noLegalMoves if none) are gathered by policyIndex, softmaxed only over that legal-move subset (max-subtracted for stability), then sorted and truncated to topK ScoredMove(move, notation, probability) entries.

PlayMoveKernel.weightedRandomMove(from:using:) picks the move actually played from that distribution, generic over RandomNumberGenerator for deterministic tests:

totalProb <= 0  -> moves.first
else: r = uniformRandom(in: 0..<totalProb); walk moves subtracting probability;
      first move where r <= 0 (a CDF walk) -> chosen; walk exhausts -> moves.last

let tokens = Maia3Encoding.encodeTokens(position: position)
let (moveLogits, valueLogits) = try await maiaModel.predict(tokens: tokens, eloSelf: 1500, eloOpponent: 1500)
let analysis = try Maia3Encoding.decodeOutput(moveLogits: moveLogits, valueLogits: valueLogits, position: position, topK: 5)
let chosen = PlayMoveKernel.weightedRandomMove(from: analysis.topMoves)

MaiaRankStyle.tier(forRank:) maps a 0-based prediction rank to a display tier — .best (rank 0), .good (1–2), .moderate (3–4), .poor (≥5, or −1 for outside the top-K) — replacing two byte-identical implementations iOS and Android had each independently written. EloKernel.bestElo(from:) -> Int? picks the single most-likely Elo bucket from a {Elo bucket: average log-likelihood} map by argmax (nil for an empty map).

GameAnalysis and GuessEloResult are the two result shapes the Maia move side of this feeds. GameAnalysis holds an array of nested MoveResult(moveIndex:playerMoveRank:playerMoveProbability:) values — 0-based ranks — and derives three summaries over moveResults: accuracy (share at rank 0), top3Accuracy (share with rank in 0..<3), and averageProbability (mean playerMoveProbability); all three return 0 for an empty array rather than dividing by zero. GuessEloResult carries whiteElo and blackElo as Int?, where nil means no estimate was produced for that side. Both types moved into FianchettoKit from ChessCore in the 2026-06-30 split; neither has a fianchetto-cli surface today — the Maia scoring path is reachable headlessly through fianchetto-cli maia, but the CLI emits its own JSON rows rather than these two struct shapes.

docs.title: The Maia Elo backfill pipeline
docs.text:
Backs fianchetto-cli's estimate subcommand and the on-device background pass: score every qualifying position of the account owner's own moves against an 11-point Elo grid, accumulate log-likelihoods, and persist a versioned evidence envelope a separate estimator turns into a rating.

Eligibility. isEligibleForBackfill = isCandidateForBackfill (statisticsEnabled && hasAnnotationEvals && !hasMaiaVector) && isEligible(tc:). TC eligibility: bullet/blitz/rapid/classical are eligible (classical alone contributes +115.6 Elo in the v4.1 fit); correspondence is not, and is served by the v2 binned-median instead. Position qualification mirrors the Python corpus collector: qualifiesForInference(plyIndex:legalMoveCount:) = plyIndex >= 8 && legalMoveCount > 2 (skip the opening 8 half-moves and forced moves).

Golden fixture

Ruy Lopez, Morphy Defence — 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Re1 b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. c3 O-O (16 plies) yields 8 qualifying positions at plies 8–15, with legal-move counts [27, 30, 25, 30, 25, 30, 27, 33] — pinned against a Python chess-library reference walk of the same game. The White-only walk returns plies [8, 10, 12, 14], Black-only [9, 11, 13, 15]. Scholar's mate (1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. Qxf7#, 7 plies) yields zero — every ply is below the threshold.

Opponent conditioning — Maia was trained on Lichess ratings, so a Chess.com (or unknown-provider) rating can't feed elo_oppo unadjusted:

OpponentConditioning When used Opponent Elo fed to the model .exactLichess source == "lichess" and the rating is inside trainedOpponentEloRange (400...3,200) the game's actual opponent rating .neutralLichessPrior everything else neutralOpponentElo = 1,500

Input fingerprint. ScoringContext.inputFingerprint is a 64-hex-character SHA-256 digest (PortableSHA256.Hasher) binding a persisted vector to the exact move list it was scored from. It hashes three things, each pushed as length-prefixed UTF-8 so no concatenation of adjacent tokens can collide: the current targetEvidenceContractID, then "white"/"black" for the owner's color, then every SAN token of the main line in order (mainLineSAN, from PGNParser.tokenize + .flatMoves over the normalized move text). Including the contract ID in the hash means a contract bump changes every fingerprint too, not just the envelope's contractID field.

Elo grid. Sourced from EloCalibrationData.v41ensembleModel(forRawTC: TimeControlClass.blitz.rawValue), falling back to [600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2400, 2600]. expectedVectorLength == eloGrid.count == 11.

Position encoding fails closed. encodeForInference(qualifying:) requires every position to encode to exactly 768 tokens with a policy index inside 0..<4352; one failure aborts encoding for the whole game (returns nil) rather than dropping that position via compactMap.

Note

Apple and Android originally disagreed three ways here — whole-game abort vs. silent drop, checked vs. unchecked token width, one- vs. two-sided policy-index range — so the same PGN could carry differently-normalized evidence (eligibleMoveCount normalizes the persisted estimate) depending on which platform scored it. Apple's fail-closed rule is now the shared contract.

Evidence envelope. Versioned JSON: targetEvidenceContractID = "maia3-v4.1-owner-moves-elo-sweep-v1", schemaVersion = 1, moveScope = "account-owner-only", plus the owner's color/source/opponent-conditioning, the inputFingerprint above, eligibleMoveCount, and the 11 summed log-likelihoods. targetEvidenceContractID binds persisted evidence to a specific model and serving contract: the current Apple and Android asset hashes are registered alongside this same value in ModelContracts/maia-target-evidence-assets.registry, and Apple's staging pipeline verifies that registry before bundling the model. Bump the contract ID whenever the model's outputs, the Elo grid, the move scope, or the conditioning semantics change, so every stored envelope fails validation and requeues by itself — a registry-only hash update is safe only for byte-level repackaging whose numerical equivalence was established explicitly.

Decoding (decodeTargetEvidenceEnvelope, run before any context check) enforces a full structural ruleset, not just the four headline fields:

  • schemaVersion == 1 and contractID == targetEvidenceContractID
  • moveScope == "account-owner-only"
  • playerColor is "white" or "black"
  • ownerUsername non-empty
  • source is already canonical (re-normalizing it is a no-op)
  • opponentElo finite and > 0
  • inputFingerprint.count == 64
  • every value in logLikes finite

then a status-dependent shape check (status == "scored" requires eligibleMoveCount > 0 and exactly 11 logLikes; a missing status is treated as .scored, since the first generation of envelopes predates the field; "no-qualifying-owner-moves" requires both empty), then a conditioning cross-check (.exactLichess requires source == "lichess"; .neutralLichessPrior requires opponentElo == 1500). Any failure on any of these — not only a schema/contract/scope/side mismatch — makes the stored evidence stale and it requeues automatically.

Legacy bare arrays are rejected here

encodeVector(_:) / decodeVector(_:) still read and write the old unversioned [Double] form for the retired maiaLogLikesJSON field — kept only so old backups and the retired ANE remediation stay source-compatible; new scoring must never write it, and decodeVector only accepts arrays of exactly 11 values. The target-evidence path above never accepts a bare array. Those old vectors were scored over both players' moves, so a restored pre-fix backup must requeue rather than masquerade as corrected evidence.

logSoftmaxAt(logits, idx)        // used by both scorers below
  idx out of range, or any logit non-finite -> nil
  else: logits[idx] - (max(logits) + log(sum(exp(logit - max(logits)))));  result non-finite -> nil

Sequential and parallel scorers. MaiaBackfillGridScorer.score(eloGrid:encodings:opponentElo:inference:) sums logSoftmaxAt across every position, per grid point, via an Inference closure — @Sendable (tokens, eloSelf, eloOpponent) async throws -> [Float]. Any single inference failure throws and aborts the entire vector — a partial vector would bias exactly the point it stopped at and could never be cleanly retried. MaiaBackfillParallelScorer is the many-core twin: it scatters all eloGrid.count × encodings.count units across width = max(1, min(workerCount, units)) strided workers into a NaN-initialized terms array (NaN = "never computed", so the reduce hard-fails on any gap), then reduces per grid point in position order — bit-identical to the sequential scorer regardless of worker scheduling.

Pacing. MaiaBackfillPacingPolicy replaced two independently-drifted magic numbers:

Preset Inter-game delay Inter-slice delay .handheld 1 s 100 ms .desktop 100 ms 0 s (no slicing on the fan-out path)

Per-game skeleton. MaiaBackfillGameScorer.score(_:pacing:workerCount:constraintGate:inferenceForWorker:): parse the main line off-actor → resolve scoringContext (.unresolvedAccountIdentity on failure) → no moves, or none qualifying, yields a terminal "no qualifying owner moves" evidence receipt → encodeForInference once, reused across every grid point (.positionEncodingRejected on failure) → sweep: workerCount > 1 fans out through MaiaBackfillParallelScorer, else one grid point per detached slice with the pacing breather between each (keeps a 30–90 s sweep cancellable and thermally quiet) → encodeTargetEvidence into .evidence(json), or .evidenceEncodingFailed. MaiaBackfillScoringFailure (unparseableMoveText, unresolvedAccountIdentity, positionEncodingRejected, inferenceFailed(String), evidenceEncodingFailed) is the typed reason for every non-evidence outcome; only inferenceFailed reports isTransient == true.

MaiaBackfillRunKernel — the scheduler run loop. candidateLimit = 2_000 rows/batch, candidateEnumerationBatchSize = 256, completedRunRestartInterval = 900 s (15 min). shouldThrottleRestart(force:lastCompletedRunAt:lastCompletedStoreRevision:currentStoreRevision:now:) suppresses a restart only when unforced, a completion stamp exists, the store revision is unchanged, and less than 900 s has elapsed — a new/edited/imported game bypasses it via the revision check. shouldRecordSuccessfulSweepCompletion requires owning the generation, no cancellation, no candidate-limit truncation, no retryable failure, and processedCount == eligibleCount before stamping a completion. BoundedCandidateCursor<Candidate, ID> admits up to limit candidates while skipping already-excludedIDs, flipping reachedLimit once full — the pagination cursor that lets the scheduler page into older rows across batches instead of the newest 2,000 rows starving the rest of the library. SuccessorQueue coalesces forced wakes that arrive mid-sweep into exactly one immediate successor run; cancellation always clears any queued successor.

docs.title: Headless usage
docs.text:
Three closure seams let this whole subsystem — engine, annotation, consensus, Maia — run from a plain executable:

Seam Shape Supplies EngineFactory @Sendable (EngineKind, URL) -> (any UCIEngine)? The concrete UCI engine — process-backed on a CLI, native in the app PositionEvaluator func evaluate(fen:) async -> AnnotationEval? Whatever sits behind annotation — routes through an EngineBroker lease either way MaiaBackfillGridScorer.Inference @Sendable (tokens, eloSelf, eloOpponent) async throws -> [Float] The Maia backend — CoreML, ONNX Runtime, or a remote call

The StockfishEvaluator shown earlier needs nothing beyond a UCIEngine conformer that shells out to a Stockfish binary — no CoreML, SwiftUI, or UIKit. The same shape carries through to Maia: wire inferenceForWorker to an ONNX Runtime session instead of a CoreML MLModel, and every kernel from MaiaBackfillPolicy through MaiaBackfillGameScorer runs unmodified.

docs.title: FileJSONBlobStore & the Persistence Machinery
docs.text: How JSONBlobStore gets a real, Foundation-only body: directory layout and key routing, atomic and durable writes, deterministic fault injection for tests, and the type-aware merge policy that reconciles two replicas that both wrote progress offline.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Stores & the storage seam covers the two-protocol boundary — JSONBlobStore (key → JSON-string get/set) and BlobBackedStore (a single-row Codable keyed by a stable blobKey, with load(from:) / save(to:) supplied by a protocol extension) — and the five stat stores that persist through it. This page covers the one concrete backend that ships in the kit: FileJSONBlobStore, a Sendable struct that stores one JSON file per key under a directory.

It's Foundation-only — no SwiftData, no CloudKit, no UIKit/SwiftUI, no app process. That's the headline: any store or namespace in the kit that talks through the seam — BlobBackedStore conformers like tactics rating, tactics performance, and repertoire drill stats, as well as direct-JSONBlobStore namespaces like blunder mastery — round trips through FileJSONBlobStore unchanged, which means it round trips through a plain command-line tool unchanged too. Construct one, hand it to TacticsRatingStore.load(from:) / .save(to:), and you have working, crash-safe persistence with nothing else running. This is exactly what would let a headless tool persist and reload rating/SRS state between invocations: build one FileJSONBlobStore pointed at a chosen directory and hand it to the same BlobBackedStore calls shown on this page.

fianchetto-cli does not do this today. Its six shipped subcommands — annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project, track — are all JSON-lines pipes over stdin/stdout with no persisted directory. track in particular replays StrengthTracker, a pure value type, over a stream of per-game Elo estimates: its entire state is one var the caller re-assigns on each line, and it never touches a blob store. A store subcommand that would exercise FileJSONBlobStore directly — enumerate keys, dump one key's raw JSON, snapshot a directory — is proposed but not implemented.

let store = FileJSONBlobStore()                   // "blobs" under the
                                                    // documents directory
var rating = TacticsRatingStore.load(from: store)  // decode, or a fresh Self()
_ = rating.recordAttempt(
    puzzleKey: "startFEN:e4",
    difficulty: .medium,
    outcome: .correct,
    in: store                                      // recordAttempt persists too
)

Everything below this line is FileJSONBlobStore-specific: it is not part of the portable JSONBlobStore protocol, and nothing outside this file backend needs to know about it.

docs.title: Directory layout & key routing
docs.text:
A FileJSONBlobStore owns one directory: URL (a "blobs" subdirectory under .documentDirectory for the default init(subdirectory:), or any URL you supply for init(directory:...) — the latter is what a CLI or a test uses to point the store at an arbitrary path). Every key routes through fileURL(forKey:) into exactly one of three namespaces.

Directory constant Value Holds (blob root) — ordinary flat blobs: <key with "/" → "_">.json authoredHeadDirectoryName "authored-heads" compact per-replica authored heads authoredRevisionDirectoryName "authored-revisions" immutable authored revision facts authoredIndexDirectoryName "authored-index" keys prefixed authoredFrontierIndexPrefix authoredWitnessDirectoryName "authored-frontier-witnesses" keys prefixed authoredFrontierWitnessPrefix importCheckpointDirectoryName "import-checkpoints" the one lichessHistoryImportCheckpointKey RepertoireExpansionCheckpointStorage.directoryName "expansion-checkpoints" keys prefixed RepertoireExpansionCheckpointStorage.keyPrefix ("local.repertoireExpansionCheckpoint.v1.") endgameMiningDirectoryName "endgame-mining" derived personal-endgame mining proofs

The routing decision, in order:

fileURL(forKey: key):

  1. EndgameMiningStorageNamespace.isInfrastructureKey(key)
       — key has prefix "personalEndgames/" (or the legacy flat
         "personalEndgames_")
     → split key on "/"; a valid route needs exactly 3 or 4 components,
       each passing the safe-component check below
     → endgame-mining/<c1>/.../<cN-1>/<cN>.json   (every component nests,
       including the leading "personalEndgames" segment)
     → e.g. "personalEndgames/head/v1"
            → endgame-mining/personalEndgames/head/v1.json
        "personalEndgames/head/v1/deviceA"
            → endgame-mining/personalEndgames/head/v1/deviceA.json

  2. AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.kind(of: key)
       .compactHead — exactly 5 dot-separated parts, namespace
         "authoredHead.v1." ("authoredHead.v1.<field>.<game>.<replica>")
           → authored-heads/<field>/<game>/<replica>.json
       .immutableRevision — exactly 8 dot-separated parts, namespace
         "authoredRevision.v1." ("...v1.<field>.<game>.<replica>.<counter>.<sha256>.<proof>")
           → authored-revisions/<field>/<game>/<replica>/<counter>.<sha256>.<proof>.json
       either kind, with a part count that doesn't match
           → a flat legacy file in the same directory (`<key>.json`),
             never a route into a parent directory

  3. anything else → flat "<key with "/" → "_">.json" in the blob root,
     except four fixed-prefix keys routed to their own directory, checked
     in this order:
       key == lichessHistoryImportCheckpointKey        → import-checkpoints/
       RepertoireExpansionCheckpointStorage
         .isCheckpointKey(key)                          → expansion-checkpoints/
         ("local.repertoireExpansionCheckpoint.v1.")
       key.hasPrefix(authoredFrontierIndexPrefix)       → authored-index/
         ("local.authoredFrontierIndex.v1.")
       key.hasPrefix(authoredFrontierWitnessPrefix)     → authored-frontier-witnesses/
         ("local.authoredFrontierWitness.v1.")

fileURL(forKey:) is public and does no filesystem work by itself — only a save prepares the parent directory, and it reports preparation failures rather than creating silently.

An interrupted repertoire-expansion walk's cursor gets the same routed-away treatment as the Lichess import cursor, and for the same reason: it is non-portable per-device state, not authored library state a second device should inherit, so it must stay out of the flat key enumeration a backup inventory walks. Directory routing is only half the guard — RepertoireExpansionCheckpointStorage's own doc comment notes that LibraryStoreKernel.reservedBlobKeys membership does the other half, since the "local." prefix on the key enforces nothing by itself.

docs.title: Path-component safety and depth bound
docs.text:
Every slash-separated component of an endgame-mining key must pass a whitelist before it is allowed to become a directory or file name:

isSafeEndgameMiningPathComponent(component):
  non-empty, not "." or "..", <= 255 UTF-8 bytes, and every byte in:
    0x30–0x39  '0'–'9'
    0x41–0x5A  'A'–'Z'
    0x61–0x7A  'a'–'z'
    0x2D  '-'     0x2E  '.'     0x5F  '_'

maximumEndgameMiningPathComponents = 4: a logical key must split into 3 or 4 components (a singleton head/receipt is 3; a content address or per-replica head is 4), and the recursive directory walk used by storedEndgameMiningObjectsReportingError throws once components.count + 1 >= 4 — it refuses to descend past the depth any valid key could use, independent of how many entries are down there. Bounding depth separately from entry count stops a hostile or corrupted skinny tree from turning a bounded inventory into an unbounded recursive walk.

docs.title: NAME_MAX and legacy-key migration
docs.text:
fallbackFileURLs(forKey:) — the list of legacy candidate paths a read falls back to when the routed URL is missing — filters every candidate to lastPathComponent.utf8.count <= 255 before ever touching the filesystem. NAME_MAX is 255 on both Android app storage and Apple filesystems, and Linux and Darwin surface different errno domains for exceeding it, so the store never issues a call it already knows will fail in a platform-specific way.

At store initialization (init(subdirectory:) and init(directory:...) alike), removeLegacyFlattenedEndgameMiningFiles deletes every regular (not directory, not symlink) personalEndgames_*.json file directly in the blob root — proof files written by a retired slash-to-underscore flat router, one release prior. It fails closed on anything that isn't a plain file, and logs [FileJSONBlobStore] <message> on any cleanup failure rather than throwing from the initializer.

docs.title: Reads, writes, and tri-state results
docs.text:
Method Returns Behavior loadJSON(forKey:) String? the JSONBlobStore conformance; collapses the tri-state result into nil loadJSONReportingError(forKey:) FileJSONBlobReadResult .value(String) / .missing / .failure(String) loadDataReportingError(forKey:) FileJSONBlobDataReadResult byte-preserving variant for recovery evidence saveJSON(_:forKey:) — the JSONBlobStore conformance; fire-and-forget saveJSONReportingError(_:forKey:) String? call-scoped error, nil on success saveDataReportingError(_:forKey:) String? atomic .write(to:options: .atomic) removeJSONReportingError(forKey:) String? a missing file counts as success removeCanonicalEndgameMiningJSONReportingError(forKey:) String? removes only the routed leaf, never a legacy fallback

A plain String?/Bool optional can't tell a caller "genuinely absent" apart from "I/O error that happens to look like absent." Backup and recovery code needs that distinction, so every read has a tri-state counterpart: FileJSONBlobReadResult and its byte-preserving twin FileJSONBlobDataReadResult each have exactly .value / .missing / .failure(String). loadJSON(forKey:) (the ordinary protocol method) still collapses .failure into nil, same as .missing — only the ...ReportingError calls let a caller treat them differently.

saveJSONReportingError/saveDataReportingError return a call-scoped error string rather than setting a process-global "last error" property: two independent progress stores writing concurrently would otherwise race on a shared field, letting one write's success erase another write's failure before anything observes it.

docs.title: Bounded enumeration
Durability: DurableBlobPersistence
docs.text:
saveJSONReportingError/saveDataReportingError are already atomic (a .write(to:options: .atomic) never leaves a half-written file installed at the canonical path). saveJSONDurablyReportingError / saveDataDurablyReportingError add a second, stronger tier: after the ordinary atomic write succeeds, they fsync until the bytes are proven to be on stable storage, not just handed to the OS page cache.

saveJSONDurablyReportingError(json, forKey: key):
  1. saveJSONReportingError(json, forKey: key)         — the ordinary atomic write
  2. synchronizeInstalledBlobDurablyReportingError(forKey: key):
       a. fsync the installed file itself
            Android → installed FileJSONBlobStoreDurabilityBridge.syncAfterAtomicReplace
            elsewhere (incl. a native CLI) → FileHandle(forWritingTo:).synchronize()
       b. if the key routes through the endgame-mining namespace, also fsync
          every ancestor directory from the leaf's parent up to the durable
          blob root, deepest first:
            endgameMiningDurabilityDirectories(forKey:)
              = endgameMiningRouteDirectories(forKey:).reversed()
          (flat blob keys have no ancestor chain — step (b) is a no-op)

Directory fsync is real on Darwin and Glibc; only Windows is a no-op

synchronizeDirectoryDurablyReportingError(_:) — the call each ancestor directory in step (b) goes through — is real work on every platform except Windows. Under #if os(Android) it goes through the installed bridge's syncDirectory closure. Everywhere else, including the native macOS/Linux binary a CLI builds and runs as, it opens the directory itself (open(path, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_CLOEXEC)), calls fsync on that descriptor, and closes it — POSIX exposes the primitive directly, and canImport(Darwin) || canImport(Glibc) is exactly the native-binary case. Only under canImport(WinSDK) does the call return nil (success) without doing anything: Win32 has no documented, unprivileged equivalent to POSIX directory fsync, and FlushFileBuffers requires a writable file handle and does not document directory-entry synchronization, so the source deliberately validates the directory there and stops rather than call an API that doesn't do what the name suggests.

docs.title: The platform bridge
docs.text:
public struct FileJSONBlobStoreDurabilityBridge: Sendable {
    public let syncAfterAtomicReplace: @Sendable (String) -> String?
    public let syncDirectory: @Sendable (String) -> String?

    public init(
        syncAfterAtomicReplace: @escaping @Sendable (String) -> String?,
        syncDirectory: @escaping @Sendable (String) -> String?
    )
}

Both closures take an absolute filesystem path and return nil on success or a short error description. Android's app shell wraps its Kotlin/JNI fsync helper in these two closures and calls FileJSONBlobStore.installDurabilityBridge(_:) once at process bootstrap, before any durable write can occur — the kit itself never links against JNI. A durable save that needs the bridge before it is installed fails explicitly ("Stable-storage verification failed (...): Android durability bridge is unavailable") rather than silently downgrading to a non-durable write. The test initializer's platformDurabilityEnabled: Bool = false parameter exists because native Android test executables have no Java VM to host the bridge; setting it lets a native test opt out of only that adapter while keeping the same atomic-write and fault-injection behavior as production.

docs.title: Atomic same-directory install
docs.text:
replaceInstalledBlobAtomicallyDurablyReportingError(with:forKey:) is the lower-level primitive migration and recovery code use when they've already prepared a complete replacement file next to the routed target, instead of handing raw bytes to saveDataReportingError:

replaceInstalledBlobAtomicallyDurablyReportingError(with: prepared, forKey: key):
  1. reject unless `prepared` and fileURL(forKey: key) share a parent
     directory and are two distinct paths
  2. canImport(WinSDK) → MoveFileExW(source, target,
       MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING | MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH)
     else               → POSIX rename(sourcePath, targetPath)
  3. on success, run the same fsync chain as an ordinary durable save

A single rename/MoveFileExW call is the required primitive, not remove-then-move: a process interruption at any point always leaves either the old file or the complete new file installed at the canonical path — never a missing interval. The two branches exist because they aren't equivalent calls: the UCRT's rename fails with EEXIST when the target already exists, so it can create but never replace, while Win32's MoveFileExW swaps the directory entry in one operation when passed MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH additionally asks Win32 not to return until the move has completed on disk — the strongest documented app-level option on that platform, though the kit's own source comment is careful not to call it equivalent to POSIX's parent-directory fsync.

docs.title: Deterministic fault injection
docs.text:
Persistence-failure tests need "the 3rd read of key X fails" to be a fact, not a flake. FileJSONBlobStore's test-only initializer exposes two layers of injected faults, both defaulted to off so production code pays nothing:

public init(
    directory: URL,
    failingReadsForKeys: Set<String> = [],
    failingWritesForKeys: Set<String> = [],
    failEnumeration: Bool = false,
    failingReadCallNumbers: [String: Set<Int>] = [:],
    malformedReadCallNumbers: [String: Set<Int>] = [:],
    failingWriteCallNumbers: [String: Set<Int>] = [:],
    platformDurabilityEnabled: Bool = false
)

failingReadsForKeys / failingWritesForKeys / failEnumeration are coarse: every access to that key (or every enumeration call) fails, every time. The call-numbered parameters are precise — only a specific, 1-based call number for a specific key faults:

FileJSONBlobInjectedCallFaults.readFault(forKey: key):
  call = (readCalls[key] ?? 0) + 1; readCalls[key] = call
  call ∈ failingReadCallNumbers[key]    → .failure
  call ∈ malformedReadCallNumbers[key]  → .malformedValue
      (the read returns the literal bytes Data("{ injected malformed JSON".utf8))
  otherwise                             → no fault

The counter lives behind an NSLock in a private, reference-typed FileJSONBlobInjectedCallFaults (final class, @unchecked Sendable) — reference semantics so a test that constructs one store and hands it to both the code under test and its own assertions observes a single, shared call order, not two independent counters that could diverge. Leave all three [String: Set<Int>] parameters empty (the default) and injectedCallFaults stays nil — production's init(subdirectory:) never even allocates it, so ordinary reads and writes pay no locking cost.

let store = FileJSONBlobStore(
    directory: scratchDirectory,
    failingReadCallNumbers: ["tacticsRating": [3]],     // 3rd read of this key fails
    malformedReadCallNumbers: ["drillSRS": [1]],        // 1st read returns malformed JSON
    failingWriteCallNumbers: [:]
)

docs.title: Conflict resolution: ProgressBlobSemanticMerger
docs.text:
Two replicas can both write the same progress blob offline — two CloudKit-synced devices, say — and land back at the same key with genuinely different attempts recorded. Plain last-writer-wins would silently discard one replica's real progress. ProgressBlobSemanticMerger is a stateless namespace that performs a deterministic, replica-order-independent union for exactly the keys where that's meaningful; everything else stays on the platform's ordinary LWW path.

public static let mergeableKeys: Set<String> = [
    TacticsRatingStore.blobKey,        // "tacticsRating"
    TacticsPerformanceStore.blobKey,   // "tacticsPerformance"
    DrillSRS.blobKey,                  // "drillSRS"
    RepertoireDrillStats.blobKey,      // "repertoireDrillStats"
    BlunderMasteryStore.blobKey,       // "blunderMastery"
    "endgameHistory",
]
public static func canMerge(key: String) -> Bool

Menu snapshots and other rebuildable caches are deliberately excluded — a generic JSON-object merge on payloads that don't carry stable record identity or a causal reset tombstone would corrupt them rather than reconcile them.

docs.title: Candidate selection and the "more than one" gate
docs.text:
mergedResult(forKey: key, candidates: [ProgressBlobCandidate]):
  ordered      = candidates.sorted(by: updatedAt descending, ties by json ascending)
  contributors = ordered.filter { isConsumerDecodable($0, forKey: key) }
  guard contributors.count > 1 else return nil

isConsumerDecodable decodes the candidate's JSON against the real type for that key (TacticsRatingStore, DrillSRS, …; blunderMastery and endgameHistory both decode as ConsecutiveCorrectProgress). A candidate that fails to decode is simply not counted in contributors — it can't win the merge, but the caller's original candidates list still has it for conflict-evidence purposes. The > 1 gate is what keeps a single decodable candidate's exact bytes and timestamp untouched: zero or one contributor returns nil ("no merge needed"), so a newer-but-malformed sibling can never lend its timestamp to a synthetic one-row union.

docs.title: Per-record tie-break
docs.text:
When two contributing stores supply a record sharing the same Identifiable id — a TacticsAttempt, a rating or SRS Mutation, a RepertoireDrillStats.DrillAttempt — the merger keeps whichever copy's canonical JSON encoding sorts smaller:

canonical(x) = JSONEncoder(outputFormatting: .sortedKeys).encode(x) → UTF-8 String
winner = canonical(a) < canonical(b) ? a : b

This is a lexicographic tie-break on encoded bytes, not "keep the newest" — these per-record types don't reliably carry an independent timestamp to compare, and a byte-canonical order is fully deterministic and replica-order-independent, which is the property a merge needs.

docs.title: Ledger baseline, compaction, and reset tombstones
docs.text:
TacticsRatingStore, DrillSRS, and the shared ConsecutiveCorrectProgress (behind blunderMastery/endgameHistory) all carry an optional mutation-ledger shape (legacyBaseline, mutations, mutationCompactedAt). Only TacticsRatingStore additionally carries a reset tombstone (resetAt, clearsLegacyBaseline, discardedMutationIDs) — DrillSRS and ConsecutiveCorrectProgress have no resetAt field at all, so they have nothing for a sibling replica's reset to dominate. The compaction step below is shared by all three merges:

ledgerStores = stores where legacyBaseline != nil || mutations != nil
               (ratings also count clearsLegacyBaseline == true)

selectedCompactedStore =
    ledgerStores.max(by: mutationCompactedAt ?? .distantPast);
    ties favor the LOWER candidate index
    (candidates are pre-sorted newest-updatedAt-first, so a tie favors the
     replica that was already ahead on updatedAt)
compactedAt = selectedCompactedStore?.mutationCompactedAt

For TacticsRatingStore only, a reset tombstone can still override a compacted baseline:

resetAt = ledgerStores.compactMap(\.resetAt).max()
resetDominatesBaseline = resetAt.map { $0 >= (compactedAt ?? .distantPast) } ?? false

baseline =
    resetDominatesBaseline               → empty .init()          (tombstone wins)
    else selectedCompactedStore.legacyBaseline
    else first ledgerStore.legacyBaseline (candidate order)
    else a baseline synthesized from the single newest decodable
         candidate's already-materialized fields (`stores.first`)
    else empty .init()

DrillSRS and ConsecutiveCorrectProgress have no reset step, and their final fallback (once neither selectedCompactedStore nor any ledger store has a legacyBaseline) is a per-key union over every decodable candidate, not one candidate's whole snapshot:

baseline =
    selectedCompactedStore?.legacyBaseline
    else first ledgerStore.legacyBaseline (candidate order)
    else DrillSRS: union of `entries` over every decodable candidate
         (candidates are pre-sorted newest-first, so the first value seen
         per key wins)
         ConsecutiveCorrectProgress: union of `values` over every decodable
         candidate, keeping the larger count seen per key

Mutations from every ledger store are then unioned by id (same canonical-JSON tie-break as above), filtered against the union of every store's discardedMutationIDs/discardedAttemptIDs, and finally sorted by id.uuidString (orderedMutations) — never by dictionary iteration order, which Swift doesn't guarantee is stable across runs. TacticsPerformanceStore and RepertoireDrillStats have no compaction ledger; they skip straight to the discard-set/reset-cutoff union over attempts.

docs.title: Post-merge caps
SavedGameCollectionRole
docs.text:
Stable identity for the three app-generated saved-game collections:

Case sourceIdentifier defaultCollectionName defaultEventTag .otb "fianchetto.otb" "OTB Games" "Over the Board" .vsEngine "fianchetto.vs-engine" "vs Engine" "Play vs Engine" .boardImports "fianchetto.board-imports" "Board Imports" "Board import"

init?(sourceIdentifier:) trims whitespace/newlines, lowercases, and requires an exact match against one of the three sourceIdentifier strings above — no prefix or fuzzy matching. owns(sourceIdentifier:) is Self(sourceIdentifier:) == self.

Two disjoint legacy sets feed one-time migration/auto-promotion for games saved before roles existed:

Case legacySourceIdentifiers (Android) legacyAppleSourceIdentifiers (Apple) .otb ["local", "pgn"] ["local"] .vsEngine ["pgn"] [] .boardImports [] ["local"]

Note

The two legacy sets share values ("local", "pgn") but not meaning — a "local" Android source and a "local" Apple source promote to different roles. They're two separate properties instead of one shared set for exactly that reason: collapsing them would let an arbitrary Apple PGN import literally named "OTB Games" be mistaken for OTB provenance.

if let role = SavedGameCollectionRole(sourceIdentifier: "fianchetto.otb") {
    print(role.defaultCollectionName)   // "OTB Games"
}

docs.title: SavedGameTags
docs.text:
One shared PGN-tag builder used by every app-generated saved game (OTB, electronic-board OTB, play-vs-engine), so their persisted tags stay structurally identical:

public static func make(
    eventTag: String,
    date: String,
    white: String,
    black: String,
    result: String,
    startFEN: String?,
    termination: String? = nil,
    timeControl: String? = nil
) -> PGNGame.OrderedTags

Event / Date / White / Black / Result are always set, in that insertion order. SetUp / FEN follow, added only when startFEN is non-nil and non-empty; then TimeControl, added only when timeControl is non-nil and non-empty; then Termination, added only when termination is non-nil and non-empty. pgnDateString(from: Date = Date()) formats the date as yyyy.MM.dd using Calendar(identifier: .gregorian) and Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX") — the standard PGN-safe, non-localized date form.

Note

termination and timeControl are recent additions, and termination closes a real gap rather than a cosmetic one: StatsKernel has always read tags["Termination"] straight into EloEstimator.isTimeEnding, so every app-generated game silently told its own rating estimator that no game ever ended on time until something actually populated the tag. Callers should pass GameResultPresentation.terminationTag(for:) — derived from the same typed GameOutcome that produces result — never a hand-written string.

pgnTimeControl(secondsBase:incrementSeconds:) is the matching helper for the timeControl argument: "300+3" for a Fischer-increment clock, "300" with no increment, "-" (the standard's own untimed token) when secondsBase is not positive.

let tags = SavedGameTags.make(
    eventTag: SavedGameCollectionRole.otb.defaultEventTag,
    date: SavedGameTags.pgnDateString(),
    white: "Player",
    black: "Engine",
    result: "1-0",
    startFEN: nil
)

docs.title: OTBGameTags
docs.text:
The single home for the over-the-board (electronic-board) saved-game tag roster, shared by both apps' saveOTBGame:

public static func make(
    eventTag: String,
    date: String,
    outcome: GameOutcome,
    startFEN: String?,
    timeControl: String?
) -> PGNGame.OrderedTags

It delegates straight to SavedGameTags.make, supplying placeholder white: "White" / black: "Black" player tags (editable afterwards through the game's tag editor) and deriving both result and termination from the one outcome: GameOutcome argument — GameResultPresentation .pgnResultToken(for:) and .terminationTag(for:) respectively — never recovered from display prose and never supplied as two tags that could drift apart. startFEN and timeControl pass straight through to SavedGameTags, so the same conditional SetUp/FEN/TimeControl rules apply: a game that started from a non-initial position reloads its SAN correctly, and a clock session that was actually attached is the only thing that writes TimeControl.

let tags = OTBGameTags.make(
    eventTag: BoardBrand.pgnEventTag(rawValue: "chessnutAir"),
    date: SavedGameTags.pgnDateString(),
    outcome: .rules(.checkmate, activeColor: .black),
    startFEN: nil,
    timeControl: SavedGameTags.pgnTimeControl(secondsBase: 300, incrementSeconds: 3)
)

docs.title: SyncVisibleRetentionStorageKeys
docs.text:
Eight content-addressed key-prefix families for personal-endgame retention sync state, built by string concatenation off one shared root:

prefix                     = "personalEndgames/retention/v1/"
rosterPrefix                = prefix + "roster/"
capabilityPrefix            = prefix + "capability/"
rootProofPrefix             = prefix + "root/"
proposalPrefix               = prefix + "proposal/"
acknowledgementPrefix       = prefix + "ack/"
