sealPrefix                   = prefix + "seal/"
sweepAcknowledgementPrefix  = prefix + "sweepAck/"
completionPrefix             = prefix + "completion/"

Because every one of these shares the "personalEndgames/" prefix, any concrete key built from them falls under EndgameMiningStorageNamespace.isInfrastructureKey and routes through the endgame-mining namespace described above, not the flat blob namespace. Values are immutable and content-addressed, so a storage adapter is free to tolerate identical physical duplicates rather than treating them as a conflict.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Stores & the storage seam — the BlobBackedStore conformers (TacticsRatingStore, TacticsPerformanceStore, RepertoireDrillStats) and the direct-JSONBlobStore namespace BlunderMasteryStore that persist through this substrate, and the Elo/SRS math they run.
  • Persistence DTOs — PersistenceDTOs.swift lives in this same Storage/ directory; its DTOs (PersonalTrapData, GameCollectionData, RepertoireData, FingerprintedCacheData, …) are documented there in full rather than repeated here.

docs.title: Library Backup: Format, Streaming Encoder & Exact-Byte Proofs
docs.text: The library-backup subsystem defines the on-disk JSON that the iOS app and the Android (Skip/SkipFuse) port read and write byte-compatibly, plus everything needed to produce, validate, stream, and prove that JSON without ever loading an unbounded amount of it into memory at once.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A backup is one JSON document: games, repertoires, traps, caches, synced progress blobs, and settings. Both platforms must agree on every field name, type, and optionality, because the JSON keys come directly from the Swift struct's stored properties — a renamed or reordered field breaks a lossless cross-platform restore. The source comments describe this format as mirroring a shared docs/BACKUP_FORMAT.md, kept outside this package.

There is exactly one hard rule that everything else in this page exists to enforce:

Warning

Always encode and decode through LibraryBackupCodec, never a bare JSONEncoder/JSONDecoder. A bare JSONEncoder emits reference-date Doubles for every Date instead of ISO-8601 strings and silently corrupts a cross-platform restore. LibraryBackupCodec is also the only place that runs schema-version gating and semantic/resource validation, so a file that a bare encoder would happily write might be a file the app later refuses to restore.

File Role LibraryBackup.swift The envelope model, LibraryBackupCategories, LibraryBackupAncillaryOverlay, and LibraryBackupCodec (config + validate/encode/decode entry points) LibraryBackupStreamingEncoder.swift Bounded-memory incremental encoder (streamSupported, ValidatedStream) LibraryBackupReplayableSource.swift ReplayableSource, the actor-confined streaming input, and the game replay-fingerprint machinery ExactByteProof.swift The {byteCount, sha256} proof type BackupFileProofReader.swift Chunked, change-detecting proof of a file already on disk LibraryBackupSettingPolicy.swift The portable settings kind/rule/registry and RatingChartWindow LibraryBackupAuthoredAdapter.swift Canonicalizes game-owned causal rows against marker-derived identity MaiaBackupEvidenceReplayer.swift Rejoins an offline Maia evidence corpus back onto its source backup StoredBackupOverlayHead.swift Android's compact backup-overlay storage format + migration reader

docs.title: The LibraryBackup envelope
docs.text:
LibraryBackup.currentSchemaVersion is 1. It is a monotonically increasing Int bumped only for a breaking shape change; anything additive is expressed as an Optional field instead, which is the pattern nearly every field below follows.

public struct LibraryBackup: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    public let schemaVersion: Int
    public let exportedAt: Date
    public let collections: [Collection]
    public let personalTraps: [PersonalTrapRow]
    public let trapScanRecords: [TrapScanRecord]
    public let repertoires: [Repertoire]?          // nil = older build, no repertoires yet
    public var auditCaches: [AuditCacheRow]? = nil
    public var punishCaches: [PunishCacheRow]? = nil
    public var syncedBlobs: [SyncedBlobRow]? = nil
    public var syncedBlobConflicts: [SyncedBlobConflictRow]? = nil
    public var settings: [SettingRow]? = nil
}

Only collections, personalTraps, and trapScanRecords are required, non-optional arrays that were present since schema v1. Everything from repertoires onward is Optional with a nil default so that:

  • an older build's export, which never wrote the key, still decodes (Codable treats a missing key as nil for an Optional property with no custom init(from:));
  • a newer reader can tell "zero rows" ([]) apart from "this build didn't know about this category yet" (nil) — syncedBlobConflicts, for example, is lossless recovery data for CloudKit duplicate rows, and a nil there means "no conflicts were even tracked," not "no conflicts existed."

LibraryBackup's memberwise init reflects the same split: repertoires has no default value (callers must pass nil or an array explicitly) while every field after it defaults to nil.

docs.title: Collection, Game, and Enrichment
docs.text:
Collection holds name, source, username, an optional lastSyncDate, orderIndex, dateCreated, and its games: [Game]. One flag does double duty: includeInOpeningBook: Bool also gates which games can receive a Maia-replay ordinal (see below).

Game mirrors StoredGame's persisted, non-derived fields — note that date is a PGN yyyy.MM.dd string, not an ISO-8601 Date, and stays opaque all the way through this subsystem. A Game carries its own portable enrichment fields directly (annotationEvalsJSON, userNotes, maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON, …); Game.Enrichment is the same data factored out as a standalone value so an adapter can reason about "just the enrichment" without touching PGN identity:

public struct Enrichment: Sendable, Equatable {
    public var annotationEvalsJSON: String
    public var secondBestEvalsJSON: String
    public var annotationMateDistancesJSON: String?
    public var annotationProvenanceJSON: String?
    public var userNotes: String
    public var boardArrowsJSON: String?
    public var consensusJSON: String?
    public var maiaLogLikesJSON: String?
    public var maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON: String?

    public func overlayingNonEmpty(from backup: Self) -> Self
}

overlayingNonEmpty(from:) is the merge rule used whenever a backup is reconciled against already-live data: a non-empty incoming (backup) value wins, but nil/empty backup data never erases something already present live. annotationProvenanceJSON is a deliberate exception — it is treated as inseparable from the eval payload it describes, so it is only overlaid when the incoming annotationEvalsJSON or secondBestEvalsJSON is itself non-empty; otherwise a live envelope is preserved rather than falsely attributing existing numbers to the incoming engine/configuration. maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON instead delegates to MaiaBackfillPolicy.preferredTargetEvidence(live:incoming:).

docs.title: LibraryBackupCategories
docs.text:
Selective import/export is driven by an OptionSet whose bit positions are part of the persisted cross-platform contract — a saved restore journal stores rawValue directly, so these must never be renumbered:

Category Bit .games 1 << 0 .repertoires 1 << 1 .traps 1 << 2 .caches 1 << 3 .progress 1 << 4 .settings 1 << 5 .all union of the six above

docs.title: LibraryBackupAncillaryOverlay
docs.text:
A game-free projection of a backup — schemaVersion, exportedAt, and every field from personalTraps onward except collections and repertoires — for an adapter that only needs to enrich a fresh live projection without materializing the whole game graph. init(projecting: LibraryBackup) derives one from a complete backup so platform adapters don't repeat the category field list. Going the other way, var ancillaryEnvelope: LibraryBackup re-wraps it as a LibraryBackup with collections: [] and repertoires: nil, purely so the existing envelope-level validation and merge kernels can run against it unchanged.

Warning

ancillaryEnvelope's result is a game-free compatibility value for reuse of merge kernels, not a complete backup — the doc comment is explicit that it must never be published directly. Authored rows carried by an overlay still require reconciliation against live game ownership before a caller persists or publishes them, exactly as for a complete backup.

docs.title: SettingValue and the setting policy
docs.text:
SettingRow pairs a key: String with a SettingValue, a three-case enum covering the value kinds carried by a backup:

public enum SettingValue: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    case bool(Bool)
    case int(Int)
    case string(String)
}

Its Codable conformance is hand-written rather than synthesized, and it reproduces the exact shape Swift's synthesizer would produce for an associated-value enum: a single-key object whose payload is nested one level down under the key "_0".

SettingValue.string("blue")  →  {"string":{"_0":"blue"}}
SettingValue.int(42)         →  {"int":{"_0":42}}
SettingValue.bool(true)      →  {"bool":{"_0":true}}

The doc comment is explicit about why: Skip/SkipFuse transpilation of a synthesized associated-value-enum Codable conformance is a known portability risk, and the natural alternative shape a naive hand-write might produce — {"string":"blue"} — would fail to decode on iOS. Hand-writing both init(from:) and encode(to:) pins the byte shape deterministically on both platforms; the shape is also asserted directly in tests.

docs.title: The setting registry and policy
docs.text:
LibraryBackupSettingRule is a per-key validation rule with three cases — .bool, .int(minimum:maximum:), .string(maximumUTF8Bytes:) — and an accepts(_:) method that checks a SettingValue against it. LibraryBackupSettingRegistry.definitions curates every key the backup format understands: 20 bool settings, 9 bounded-int settings, and 11 bounded-string settings (40 definitions total), each independent of whatever physical UserDefaults/SharedPreferences key a platform stores it under. A representative slice of the bounded numeric ranges:

Key Rule drillSessionSize .int(minimum: 1, maximum: 100) checkmateIntensity .int(minimum: 0, maximum: 3) missedMateMaxN .int(minimum: 2, maximum: 10) punishTopK .int(minimum: 2, maximum: 8) punishOpponentElo .int(minimum: 800, maximum: 2_400) autoICloudBackupRetention .int(minimum: 1, maximum: 30) masteryThreshold .int(minimum: 2, maximum: 10) tacticsSwingThreshold .int(minimum: 50, maximum: 1_000) stockfishDepthLimitPersisted .int(minimum: 0, maximum: 128)

Every one of the 11 curated string settings (boardTheme, pieceSet, explorerDatabase, annotateThoroughness, annotationEngine, tacticsMode, drillStrictness, evalDisplayFormat, libraryGameSort, ratingChartWindow, otbLastTimeControl) uses the same bound: .string(maximumUTF8Bytes: 256).

LibraryBackupSettingPolicy.accepts(_ row: LibraryBackup.SettingRow) -> Bool is deliberately forward-compatible: a key with no registered definition passes automatically (?? true), so a future build's new setting doesn't fail validation on an older reader; a known key must satisfy its registered rule or the row is rejected — .int(minimum: 2, maximum: 8) on punishTopK rejects a stored 9, for instance, while an unrecognized key like someFutureFlag passes regardless of its value.

docs.title: RatingChartWindow
docs.text:
Older Apple builds stored the rating-history window preference in lowercase; Android stored the display label. RatingChartWindow(storedValue:) bridges both by trimming whitespace and lowercasing before matching a raw value:

Case Raw value shortLabel monthOffset .threeMonths "3m" "3M" -3 .sixMonths "6m" "6M" -6 .oneYear "1y" "1Y" -12 .all "all" "All" nil

LibraryBackupSettingPolicy.normalizedPortableRow(_:) runs accepts(_:) first, then — only for the ratingChartWindow key — replaces whatever spelling arrived with the canonical lowercase raw value via RatingChartWindow(storedValue:). If the stored string doesn't match any case, the row is dropped (returns nil) rather than persisted as a value no segmented-picker UI could represent.

docs.title: Canonical JSON encoding contract
docs.text:
LibraryBackupCodec.makeEncoder() and .makeDecoder() are the single source of truth for wire configuration on both platforms:

encoder.outputFormatting   = [.withoutEscapingSlashes, .sortedKeys]
encoder.dateEncodingStrategy = .iso8601
decoder.dateDecodingStrategy = .iso8601

.sortedKeys is what makes the encoding canonical: without it, swift-foundation emits object keys in hash-seed-dependent order that can vary across processes (and, on an older Foundation runtime, even across separate encode() calls within one process). Any consumer that treats the encoded bytes' SHA-256 as a payload identity — publication dedup/retention being the motivating case — needs that hash to be a true content identity, not an artifact of key ordering.

LibraryBackup.exportedAt is canonicalized at construction time, independent of encoding:

canonicalExportDate(date) = Date(timeIntervalSince1970: date.timeIntervalSince1970.rounded(.down))

Rounding down to the whole second matches .iso8601's whole-second string output, so an exact-byte proof taken over the in-memory value can never imply sub-second precision the JSON itself doesn't carry.

docs.title: Schema-version gate
docs.text:
validateSchemaVersion(schemaVersion):
    schemaVersion < 1                         → throw .invalidSchema(found:)
    schemaVersion > currentSchemaVersion (1)  → throw .unsupportedSchema(found:supported:)
    otherwise                                 → accept

Codable silently ignores unknown JSON fields, which — absent this gate — would let a future-schema backup appear to restore successfully while quietly discarding data it doesn't understand yet. Every decode path in LibraryBackupCodec runs this check before any semantic validation.

docs.title: Resource ceilings
docs.text:
maxPayloadBytes is checked before JSONDecoder ever runs (validatePayloadSize), so a malformed multi-gigabyte file can't multiply its footprint inside the decoder and take down the process. Every other ceiling is enforced after decode, in validateResourceLimits / validateEnvelopeResourceLimits, against the already-structured value:

Ceiling Value maxPayloadBytes (public) 512 × 1024 × 1024 (512 MiB) maxCollections 4,096 maxGames 250,000 maxGamesPerCollection 100,000 maxRepertoires 10,000 maxRepertoireMoves 500,000 maxAuxiliaryRows (traps / trap-scan records) 250,000 maxSyncedBlobRows 1,000,000 maxSyncedBlobConflictRows 500,000 maxSyncedBlobAlternates (total, across all conflict rows) 1,000,000 maxGenericSyncedBlobAlternatesPerKey 10,000 maxSettings 512 maxSmallFieldBytes (names, tags, PGN metadata) 65,536 maxGameTextBytes (move text, evals, notes, Maia payloads) 8 × 1024 × 1024 maxBlobBytes (one synced-blob row/alternate) 16 × 1024 × 1024

A conflict row's own alternate count is bounded per key, and the per-key limit depends on what kind of key it is: an authoredHead.v1.… compact-head key uses the much smaller AuthoredBlobRecordCodec.maximumCompactHeadAlternates (63 — one less than the 64-candidate compact-frontier ceiling, since a sidecar excludes the active row), while every other key uses the generic 10,000-alternate ceiling. maxSyncedBlobRows in particular is sized around a documented rationale: a 250k-game backup can plausibly carry roughly one compact head plus one exact immutable revision per authored field, so 1,000,000 keeps that arithmetic in bounds without letting the old, unrelated 10k-repertoire cap reject a valid compact frontier.

docs.title: The streaming encoder
docs.text: encodeSupported(_:) and makeEncoder().encode(_:) both return one payload-sized Data. For a 250,000-game backup that is a real cost — the caller ends up holding the whole encoded document in memory at once, on top of whatever in-memory model it was built from. LibraryBackupCodec.streamSupported(_:emit:) avoids that: it emits the same bytes encodeSupported(_:) would, incrementally, through a callback.

docs.title: Shell-and-splice
docs.text:
The technique (writeShell) exploits JSONEncoder's determinism on an empty array:

For a value with N array-typed properties:
  1. Build a "shell" copy of the value with every array-typed property
     replaced by [].
  2. encoder.encode(shell) → shellData (one small Data).
  3. For each array property, search shellData for the literal byte
     sequence  "<property>":[]
     — the insertion point is the byte offset just before the closing `]`.
  4. Sort every insertion point by byte offset (multiple arrays on one
     shell — e.g. Collection has only "games", but the top-level envelope
     has up to seven — must be spliced in stream order, not declaration
     order).
  5. Walk shellData once, writing the bytes up to each insertion point,
     then writing that array's real elements one at a time (encoding each
     element individually and joining with a literal `,`), then resuming
     at the shell byte just after that point.

If a marker isn't found — i.e. if JSONEncoder ever stops emitting a bare [] for an empty array — the encoder throws LibraryBackupCodec.StreamingError.incompatibleArrayShell(property:) rather than silently producing wrong JSON. Nested shells compose: the envelope shell splices in "collections":[], and writeCollection runs the identical technique one level down for each collection's "games":[].

docs.title: Chunking and the running hash
docs.text:
Every write — shell bytes, a comma separator, one encoded element — passes through BackupJSONStream.write(_:), which splits it into pieces of at most maximumStreamingChunkBytes (64 * 1_024, 64 KiB) before handing each piece to the caller's emit closure:

for each chunk (≤ 64 KiB):
    byteCount += chunk.count   // via addingReportingOverflow; throws .payloadTooLarge on overflow
                                //   or if byteCount would exceed maxPayloadBytes (512 MiB)
    emit(chunk)                 // caller writes it — e.g. to a staging FileHandle
    hasher.update(chunk)        // folded into a running PortableSHA256.Hasher

Only bytes actually accepted by emit participate in the final ExactByteProof — a throwing sink owns disposal of whatever partial staging target it already wrote.

let handle = try FileHandle(forWritingTo: stagingURL)
defer { try? handle.close() }

let proof = try LibraryBackupCodec.streamSupported(backup) { chunk in
    try handle.write(contentsOf: chunk)
}
// proof.byteCount / proof.sha256 describe exactly what landed in stagingURL —
// publish stagingURL only after this call returns successfully.

Validation runs to completion before the first byte is emitted (validatedStream(for:) calls validateSupported(_:) up front), but a sink failure or a late aggregate payload-size overflow can still leave a partial stream on disk — production callers target a discardable staging file and publish it only once streamSupported returns.

docs.title: Streaming a ReplayableSource
docs.text:
LibraryBackupCodec.ReplayableSource is the other streaming input: an envelope LibraryBackup plus, per collection, a ReplayableSource.Collection(name:source:username:lastSyncDate:includeInOpeningBook:orderIndex:dateCreated:gameCount:replayGames:) whose replayGames: (_ visit: (LibraryBackup.Game) throws -> Void) throws -> Void closure can capture live persistence-actor model objects instead of a fully materialized [Game] array.

ReplayableSource is marked @available(*, unavailable, message: "ReplayableSource is actor-confined") extension LibraryBackupCodec.ReplayableSource: Sendable {} — it is actor-confined by construction and must be built and consumed synchronously by the actor that owns the live models its closures capture. streamSupported(_:emit:) walks it twice in spirit but once in practice: validateReplayableSource(_:) replays every game once to compute a ReplayProofAccumulator digest (the expected proof), then the actual write pass (writeBackup(_:expectedReplayProof:...)) replays the same source again while accumulating a second digest, and the two must match exactly:

ReplayProofAccumulator, seed "library-replay-games:v1":
    hash(collectionCount)
    for each collection: hash(collectionIndex), hash(gameCount)
    for each game:       hash(collectionIndex), hash(gameIndex),
                          then replaySemanticFingerprint's field list (below)

If replaying the source a second time produces a different game count for some collection, StreamingError.replayCollectionCountMismatch(collectionIndex:expected:actual:) is thrown; if the accumulated digest itself differs, StreamingError.replaySourceChanged is thrown. Either way, the write fails into the caller's discardable staging file rather than publishing a document that doesn't match what was validated.

LibraryBackup.Game.replaySemanticFingerprint is the field-framed digest shared by that accumulator and by persistence adapters as one review point for the wire projection:

replaySemanticFingerprint, seed "library-backup-game-replay:v2":
    hash(orderIndex)
    hash(white, black, date, event, result, opening, moveText, tagsJSON,
         gameID, annotationEvalsJSON, secondBestEvalsJSON, userNotes)
    for each of [annotationMateDistancesJSON, annotationProvenanceJSON,
                 boardArrowsJSON, consensusJSON, maiaLogLikesJSON,
                 maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON]:
        present → hash("some"), hash(value)
        nil     → hash("nil")

Every hashed piece goes through update(lengthPrefixedUTF8:) — an 8-byte big-endian length prefix followed by the UTF-8 bytes — not through JSON encoding, so a harmless key-order difference between two encodings of the same value can never look like a semantic change.

docs.title: Exact-byte proofs
docs.text:
ExactByteProof is {byteCount: Int, sha256: String} — Codable, Equatable, Sendable — constructible via init(byteCount:sha256:), init<Bytes: Sequence>(bytes:) where Bytes.Element == UInt8, or init(utf8 source: String), the last two hashing incrementally without retaining a second payload-sized copy. isCanonicalSHA256 requires exactly 64 UTF-8 bytes, each in the ASCII ranges 48...57 ('0'–'9') or 97...102 ('a'–'f') — uppercase hex is rejected. isStructurallyValid additionally requires the bounds themselves to be sane (minimumByteCount >= 0, maximumByteCount >= minimumByteCount) and byteCount to fall within them. Decoding deliberately preserves a structurally invalid proof rather than failing to decode, so a persistence boundary can quarantine a damaged record without being unable to even read it back.

Both ExactByteProof and the streaming encoder's running hash are built on PortableSHA256.Hasher (Support/PortableSHA256.swift) — a small, dependency-free, incremental SHA-256 implementation chosen specifically because CryptoKit is unavailable on the native Android build and Swift's built-in Hasher is intentionally process-randomized, so neither can serve as a stable cross-platform or cross-process content identity.

docs.title: BackupFileProofReader — proving a file already on disk
docs.text:
public enum BackupFileProofReader {
    public static let readChunkBytes = 64 * 1_024

    public static func proof(
        of url: URL,
        expectedProof: ExactByteProof? = nil,
        maximumBytes: Int = LibraryBackupCodec.maxPayloadBytes,
        hooks: ReadHooks = ReadHooks()
    ) throws -> ExactByteProof
}

It reads a local regular file only (SAF/content URLs must first be copied into private storage) in 64 KiB chunks, and detects a file that changed underneath the read even when the change happens to leave the size unchanged mid-read:

1. Reject non-file URLs (.nonFileURL) and missing paths (.missing).
2. attributesOfItem(atPath:)[.size] → initialByteCount   (before opening the handle)
3. Reject non-regular files (.notRegularFile).
4. Read in chunks of min(readChunkBytes, remaining + 1) bytes —
   the "+1" makes a file that grew past maximumBytes overshoot the cap
   and get caught by .payloadTooLarge, instead of silently reading a
   truncated prefix.
5. Fold every chunk into a running PortableSHA256.Hasher; call
   hooks.afterChunk(index, byteCount) after each one (a deterministic,
   test-only seam — production callers use the no-op default).
6. attributesOfItem(atPath:)[.size] → finalByteCount     (after the last read)
7. Require initialByteCount == finalByteCount == (bytes actually read),
   else throw .changedDuringRead.
8. If expectedProof was supplied and it doesn't equal the observed
   proof, throw .proofMismatch(expected:observed:).

The before/after size comparison is the reader's sole detector of a same-size content mutation — the doc comment notes explicitly that Skip's Android Foundation layer exposes no inode/mtime identity to lean on instead.

// After staging a backup file, prove it matches what streamSupported wrote.
let stagedProof = try BackupFileProofReader.proof(
    of: stagingURL,
    expectedProof: streamingProof
)

docs.title: StoredBackupOverlayHead — Android's compact storage path
docs.text:
Instead of retaining a complete portable backup in app storage, the Android port can retain a compact head at the same blob key:

public struct StoredBackupOverlayHead: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public static let formatIdentifier = "fianchetto.android.stored-backup-overlay-head"
    public static let currentFormatVersion = 1

    public let format: String
    public let formatVersion: Int
    public let completeEnvelopeProof: ExactByteProof
    public let overlay: LibraryBackupAncillaryOverlay
}

StoredBackupOverlayReader is the single fail-closed reader for the shared library.fullbackup.v1 blob key (StoredBackupOverlayReader.blobKey), and it distinguishes the legacy shape from the compact one with a format discriminator rather than a try/catch fallback:

decode(data):
    probe = decode({ format: String? })   // container.contains(.format), then a
                                           // non-optional decode(String.self) —
                                           // a *present* null value therefore fails
                                           // to decode rather than being treated as absent
    if probe.format is present:
        format must equal formatIdentifier, else throw .unsupportedFormat
        decode as StoredBackupOverlayHead, validate formatVersion == 1
          and completeEnvelopeProof.isStructurallyValid(...)
        → .compactOverlayHead
    else (no "format" key at all):
        decode as the legacy LibraryBackupAncillaryOverlay envelope
          via decodeSupportedAncillaryOverlay(_:)
        → .legacyCompleteEnvelope

Any mismatch on the compact-head branch — wrong identifier, wrong version, an invalid proof — fails closed rather than being silently retried as a legacy envelope. This is what lets one JSON blob key safely serve both an old install (writes/reads the legacy shape) and a migrated one (writes/reads the compact head) during rollout: the presence of a top-level format key alone decides which namespace a given payload belongs to.

docs.title: Authored-row reconciliation at a glance
docs.text:
Rows keyed under authoredHead.v1.… / authoredRevision.v1.… in syncedBlobs/syncedBlobConflicts are not an opaque progress namespace — they are game-owned causal state (things like move annotations and notes), and LibraryBackupAuthoredAdapter exists because a backup restore must never trust that namespace at face value. Every decode and encode path in LibraryBackupCodec routes through it (validateSupported, decodeSupportedWithAuthoredProjection, validateReplayableSource) before persisting anything.

At a high level, the adapter:

  1. Builds a GameOffset-indexed (collectionIndex, gameIndex) identity candidate for every game in the backup via gameCandidates(in:), using each game's PGN tags and move text.
  2. Resolves those candidates — plus any caller-supplied live AdditionalID candidates — into a canonical alias map through AuthoredGameIdentity.
  3. Canonicalizes every authored SyncedBlobRow/SyncedBlobConflictRow onto that map (canonicalized(_:canonicalLogicalIDByAlias:)).
  4. Runs the shared AuthoredBackupReconciler semantic plan against the canonicalized rows, producing a Projection<AdditionalID> — the ownership, the canonicalized rows, the reconciliation plan, and the resulting allowedLogicalGameIDs.
public static func project(_ backup: LibraryBackup)
    throws -> Projection<NoAdditionalCandidate>

public static func project<AdditionalID: Hashable>(
    _ backup: LibraryBackup,
    additionalCandidates: [AuthoredGameIdentity.LogicalIDCandidate<AdditionalID>]
) throws -> Projection<AdditionalID>

A validated projection can be cheaply reused via reprojectValidated(_:validatedBase:additionalCandidates:) instead of re-running the whole plan against live candidates — but only if a narrow authoredSource(in:) SHA-256 (seed "library-authored-source:v1") still matches exactly. That hash covers only the fields that can affect authored ownership — white/black/date/result/event/opening/moveText/tagsJSON/ gameID/annotationEvalsJSON, plus authored-keyed synced-blob rows and sidecars — and deliberately excludes progress, repertoire, and cache fields, since the doc comment states plainly that "they cannot affect authored ownership." If the backup passed to reprojectValidated doesn't hash to the proof captured at first validation, it throws AdapterError.validatedProjectionSourceMismatch rather than silently skipping re-validation of a backup that was mutated after it was first checked.

This page only sketches the shape of that reconciliation; the identity markers, alias promotion, revision retention, and CAS semantics it builds on are covered in depth in the Authored History & the Mutation Journal page.

docs.title: Maia evidence replay
docs.text:
MaiaBackupEvidenceReplayer rejoins a privacy-reduced, offline Maia inference corpus — produced by a MaiaHarness aggregate step outside this package — back onto the exact backup it was derived from, without ever exporting player names, game IDs, PGN text, URLs, or notes into that corpus in the first place. Each corpus row is a MaiaBackupReplayRecord:

public struct MaiaBackupReplayRecord: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let sourceBackupSHA256: String
    public let sourceGameOrdinal: Int
    public let timeControl: String
    public let trueElo: Int
    public let opponentElo: Double
    public let opponentConditioning: String
    public let targetEvidenceContractID: String
    public let logLikes: [Double]
    public let eligibleMoveCount: Int
    public let positionSequenceSHA256: String
    public let modelArtifactSHA256: String
}

Its CodingKeys map every field to a short snake_case wire name (source_backup_sha256, source_game_ordinal, tc, true_elo, oppo_elo, opponent_conditioning, target_evidence_contract_id, log_likes, n_maia_moves, position_sequence_sha256, model_artifact_sha256) — this is the JSON-lines shape the offline aggregation step actually emits.

let result = try MaiaBackupEvidenceReplayer.enrich(
    sourceBackupData: backupData,
    with: records,
    exportedAt: .now
)
result.backup             // the same backup, with maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON filled in
result.enrichedGameCount  // how many games actually matched a record

sourceGameOrdinal is a global ordinal across every game in every collection with includeInOpeningBook == true, assigned in collection/game iteration order — a collection outside the opening book contributes no ordinals at all, so a game inside it can never be a replay target. enrich enforces, in order: ordinals are strictly increasing with no duplicates (.sourceOrdinalsNotStrictlyIncreasing / .duplicateSourceOrdinal); every record's modelArtifactSHA256 is a canonical lowercase-hex SHA-256 and identical across the whole batch (.modelArtifactMismatch); every ordinal falls inside the backup's actual eligible-game count (.sourceOrdinalOutsideBackup); and every record in the batch is actually consumed (.recordsNotConsumed(expected:actual:)).

Per record, evidenceJSON(for:collection:record:) then independently re-derives the scoring context from the game's own PGN tags — via MaiaBackfillPolicy.scoringContext, GameTagCodec, and TimeControlClass.classify — and cross-checks it against the record before trusting a single number in it:

targetEvidenceContractID == MaiaBackfillPolicy.targetEvidenceContractID       (.contractMismatch)
logLikes.count == MaiaBackfillPolicy.expectedVectorLength,
    all finite, all <= 1e-6 (log-probabilities are non-positive)              (.invalidLikelihoodEvidence)
eligibleMoveCount > 0                                                        (.invalidLikelihoodEvidence)
opponentConditioning ∈ {"exactLichess", "neutralLichessPrior"}               (.unknownOpponentConditioning)
recomputed opponentElo within < 0.001 of record.opponentElo                  (.gameContextMismatch)
recomputed TimeControlClass matches record.timeControl                       (.timeControlMismatch)
recomputed owner-color rating (by context.playerColor) == record.trueElo     (.ownerRatingMismatch)
recomputed qualifying-move count == record.eligibleMoveCount                 (.eligibleMoveCountMismatch)
recomputed positionSequenceSHA256 == record.positionSequenceSHA256           (.positionSequenceMismatch)

positionSequenceSHA256 itself hashes, for every qualifying position, the little-endian bit patterns of Maia3Encoding.encodeTokens(position:) followed by the little-endian Maia3Encoding.policyIndex of the move actually played — so the corpus is bound not just to "this game" but to "this exact sequence of encoded model inputs."

Only when every check agrees does enrich overwrite game.enrichment.maiaTargetEvidenceV1JSON — every other field on that game is preserved byte-for-byte through a hand-rolled copying(_:enrichment:) that deliberately bypasses PreparedGameData's ID-normalizing round trip, so a replay pass can never quietly renormalize a legacy game ID as a side effect of adding evidence to it.

docs.title: Headless-ness & CLI angle
docs.text:
Every type on this page lives under Library/Backup, and the whole subsystem depends on Foundation and ChessCore only — there is no import SwiftUI, no import UIKit, and no @MainActor isolation anywhere in these nine files. LibraryBackupCodec.encodeSupported/decodeSupported, the streaming encoder, BackupFileProofReader, ExactByteProof, the authored adapter, and MaiaBackupEvidenceReplayer are all synchronous, non-isolated, and exercisable from a plain command-line binary or a CI job with no simulator involved.

That makes a handful of fianchetto-cli subcommands a natural fit even though they don't exist today: a backup verify subcommand is barely more than BackupFileProofReader.proof(of:expectedProof:) plus LibraryBackupCodec.decodeSupported; a backup diff subcommand is two decodes and a structural comparison of the resulting LibraryBackup values; and a backup replay-maia subcommand would be a thin argument-parsing wrapper over MaiaBackupEvidenceReplayer.enrich(sourceBackupData:with:exportedAt:), reading a JSON-lines corpus from stdin or a file. None of the three exist today; fianchetto-cli's existing maia subcommand covers other Maia-related surface, but not this join-back step.

docs.title: Library Store Kernel
docs.text: The persistence and transaction core for the whole game library: one LibraryStoreKernel owns load/save lifecycle, mining admission, chunked import, backup/restore, and every dedup/reconciliation pass, all driven off one JSON aggregate (LibraryData). It was hoisted out of the Android shell's LibraryFileStore class (the "T4 class move") so both platforms — and a headless CLI — share the exact same transaction logic instead of maintaining parallel copies that drift.

docs.title: Kernel, context, and ownership
docs.text:
LibraryStoreKernel is @MainActor and imports only Foundation and ChessCore — no SwiftUI, no UIKit, no app-lifecycle dependency anywhere in this subsystem. It publishes UI-visible state through a small protocol seam rather than owning @Observable state itself:

@MainActor
public protocol LibraryStoreContext: AnyObject {
    var data: LibraryData { get set }
    var isLoaded: Bool { get set }
    var saveErrorMessage: String? { get set }
    var minedEndgameRepairMessage: String? { get set }
    var semanticCollectionMigrationNotice: String? { get set }
}

A platform shell's @Observable store conforms automatically (its stored properties are named to match), then wires itself in with kernel.attach(context: myObservableStore), which starts the deferred off-main decode. The ownership direction is deliberate: attach(context:) stores the context weakly and the facade that created the kernel holds the kernel strongly, so the kernel can never keep a platform shell alive. LibraryStorePlatformAdapter(settingsRestorer:settingsSnapshot: repertoireExportDirectory:repertoirePieceArt:) carries the four things the kernel is not allowed to hard-code; a nil settingsRestorer just means platform settings are disabled for that store instance — no JVM-backed UserDefaults bridge required. repertoirePieceArt is a (() -> [String: String])? closure from canonical piece-set key to raw SVG text, wired by whichever shell owns the current piece art and used by the repertoire HTML export's board diagrams; nil selects the exporter's Unicode fallback. It is a seam rather than a defaulted kernel argument for a concrete reason: the piece-set choice is the shell's to make, and the choice of whether it is honored has to stay visible. Apple once honored the user's piece set in an exported repertoire while the store-kernel export path silently fell back to Unicode glyphs — one account, one repertoire, no error anywhere (M11).

File Responsibility LibraryStoreKernel.swift load lifecycle, stats/mining admission bookkeeping, incarnation tokens, persistence batches LibraryStoreKernel+Mutations.swift collection/game CRUD, chunked online import, dedup, repertoire builder, PGN/HTML export LibraryStoreKernel+PGNImport.swift pasted/bulk PGN import with a crash-recovery journal LibraryStoreKernel+LichessImport.swift page-spanning Lichess complete-history import LibraryStoreKernel+Mining.swift mined trap/endgame storage, endgame projection CAS LibraryStoreKernel+Restore.swift backup restore transaction, additive merge, authored two-phase mutation LibraryStoreKernel+BackupProjection.swift live library → exportable LibraryBackup blob LibraryStoreKernel+Queries.swift repertoire gap analysis, totals LibraryStoreOutcomes.swift every typed outcome/capability value the kernel returns or accepts LibraryData.swift the one persisted aggregate value graph

docs.title: The data model — LibraryData
docs.text:
The entire library is one Codable, Sendable, Equatable struct persisted as a single JSON blob under the reserved key "library". Cascade is structural, not referential: Game rows live inside Collection.games, and RepMove rows live inside Repertoire.moves. Deleting a Collection drops every game it contains — there is no foreign-key layer to keep in sync.

public struct LibraryData: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    public var collections: [Collection] = []
    public var repertoires: [Repertoire] = []
    // installation-local: never projected into a portable LibraryBackup
    public var localCollectionIncarnations: [LocalCollectionIncarnation] = []
    public var localGameIncarnations: [LocalGameIncarnation] = []
    public var pendingPGNImport: PendingPGNImport? = nil
    public var pendingAuthoredMutation: PendingAuthoredMutation? = nil
    // locally mined content — coexists with anything imported via LibraryBackup
    public var minedTraps: [PersonalTrapData] = []
    public var minedScanRecords: [PersonalTrapScanRecordData] = []
    public var minedEndgames: [PersonalEndgamePositionData] = []
}

Every nested type (Collection, Game, Repertoire, RepMove) hand-writes its own init(from:) instead of using the synthesized decoder, and every field goes through decodeIfPresent(...) ?? default:

public init(from decoder: Decoder) throws {
    let c = try decoder.container(keyedBy: CodingKeys.self)
    id     = try c.decodeIfPresent(UUID.self,   forKey: .id)     ?? UUID()
    white  = try c.decodeIfPresent(String.self, forKey: .white)  ?? ""
    // ...
    orderIndex  = try c.decodeIfPresent(Int.self,  forKey: .orderIndex)  ?? 0
    dateCreated = try c.decodeIfPresent(Date.self, forKey: .dateCreated) ?? Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 0)
}

The synthesized JSONDecoder throws keyNotFound for a non-optional property even when a default value is declared, so a naive struct would make a library blob written before some new field shipped fail to decode entirely — silently losing the whole library on the next app update. decodeIfPresent ?? default is the back-compat pattern every schema addition in this subsystem must follow.

Some fields are decode-lenient in a stronger sense

minedEndgameProjectionSelection fails toward the conservative state on any decode error: a malformed or unrecognized schema version sets minedEndgameRestoredLegacyAuthoritySelected = true and clears the derived projection, rather than aborting the whole library decode. MinedEndgameProjectionSelection.currentSchemaVersion is 1; the type is a tagged .v1(EndgameMiningProjectionReceipt) / .v2(EndgameMiningV2ProjectionReceipt) enum so exactly one receipt format is authoritative at a time.

docs.title: Game and collection identity
docs.text:
GameIdentity decides whether a game has a real remote reference or needs a deterministic content ID, and GameDedup turns that decision into a fingerprint every import, backup-merge, and reconciliation path shares.

contentPrefix       = "content:v2:"
legacyContentPrefix = "content:v1:"
legacyReferenceTag  = "FianchettoLegacyGameID"

canonicalProviderID(raw):
  lichess:  8–12 ASCII alphanumeric chars, from "lichess:<id>" or a
            lichess.org/www.lichess.org URL's first path segment — excluding
            reserved words (analysis, broadcast, calendar, editor, features,
            insights, password, practice, streamer, study, timeline, training)
            → canonicalized to "lichess:<first 8 chars>"
  chesscom: all-ASCII-digit, from "chesscom:"/"chess.com:" or a chess.com /
            www.chess.com URL matching .../game/{live,daily,arena}/<id> or
            .../{live,daily,arena}/game/<id> (an optional leading "analysis"
            segment is stripped first)
            → canonicalized to "chesscom:<digits>"
  else → nil (Site is just a venue, not an ID)

Lichess's stable component is explicitly the first eight case-sensitive characters, which is why a 12-character URL slug and its 8-character canonical form resolve to one identity.

Degenerate URLs must not trap

A raw PGN Site/Link tag or a deep-link token reaches this parser unvalidated. A bare "https://" splits to an empty component array; the internal host/path split used to subscript that array directly, which trapped — and turned one poisoned row into a crash-on-launch loop, because stableGameID re-evaluates identity on every read and re-hit the same trap every time (perf/stability audit, 2026-07-19). canonicalProviderID's host/path split now uses a guarded .first instead of a subscript, so a value with no usable host simply yields nil.

docs.title: Recovering identity from a persisted row
docs.text:
canonicalProviderID alone only tells you whether a given string is a provider ID. Reading back a persisted row needs more: older builds sometimes copied Site into gameID outright, and rows promoted from content identity to a real remote ID must not orphan the history keyed on the old identity. Three functions carry that weight.

persistedRemoteID(gameID:link:site:) recovers the semantic remote ID without rewriting anything, applying four fallbacks in order:

1. remoteID(link:site:) is non-empty            → that canonical value
2. gameID is a content ID                       → ""
3. gameID canonicalizes as a provider ID        → its canonical form
4. gameID == Link, or gameID == Site            → ""      (see below)
   otherwise                                    → gameID  (backup compatibility)

Rule 4 exists because many PGN producers reuse a single archive, event, or article Link across every game in a file, and older Fianchetto builds persisted any non-empty Link as a per-game ID. Those rows project to content identity at runtime instead of continuing to collapse distinct games together. stableID(gameID:link:site:contentID:) layers on top: the persisted remote ID, else the explicit ID when it is already a content ID, else the lazily evaluated contentID() — the @autoclosure means an ID-bearing row never pays for content hashing.

promotingIdentity(_:gameID:tagsJSON:) records an authoritative remote identity without discarding the durable reference already in gameID. A recognized provider ID is written into the Link tag and gameID is left untouched; an unrecognized external ID replaces gameID instead, and the previous value is stashed under the internal FianchettoLegacyGameID tag (legacyReferenceTag) for later reference repair.

UnambiguousAliasAccumulator is the streaming form of unambiguousAliasMap for auxiliary records (trap and scan rows, which reference a game by an alias rather than owning its identity directly). record(alias:stableID:) normalizes both sides and ignores empties; the first contradicting stableID for an alias removes it from the map and marks it permanently ambiguous. stableID(forAlias:) therefore returns non-nil only when every recorded occurrence named the same game, and canonicalIdentifier(_:) falls back to the normalized spelling when no unambiguous mapping exists. A shared Site value — two different games played at the same tournament, say — ends up attached to no game rather than to an arbitrary one.

GameDedup.compositeKey is the SHA-256 (via PortableSHA256) content fingerprint used when a game has no recognized remote ID:

payload = length-prefixed(white) ++ length-prefixed(black) ++ length-prefixed(date)
        ++ length-prefixed(result) ++ length-prefixed(event) ++ length-prefixed(opening)
        ++ canonical-move-tree ++ sorted-non-mirror-PGN-tags

canonical-move-tree: each PGN token tagged
  0 = move (SAN, optionally suffix-stripped of trailing !/? if
      strippingDerivedAnnotations and at variation depth 0)
  1 = variationStart   2 = variationEnd
  3 = comment (dropped if it reduces to nothing but an engine eval/best-move)
  4 = nag

compositeKey        = "content:v2:" + SHA256(payload)
authoredIdentityKey = "authored-content:v1:" + SHA256(payload, excluding Link + legacy migration tag)
legacyPromotionKey  = "promotion:v1:" + SHA256(main-line-only payload, excluding Link)

authoredIdentityKey additionally excludes the Link tag, so promoting a row from content identity to a real remote ID never orphans its authored history. legacyPromotionKey is deliberately looser (no comments, NAGs, or variations) and is used only to promote one unambiguous legacy local row when a fetch later supplies its recognized remote ID — ordinary import and destructive dedup always use compositeKey.

GameDedup.MatchIndex<Value> is the generic lookup every import/merge/ reconciliation path builds over a collection, and its Resolution is the one vocabulary every one of those paths switches on:

public enum Resolution {
    case none                     // insert a new row
    case unique(Value)            // merge into the existing row
    case ambiguous                // multiple strong-key matches — skip, never guess
    /// Strong key had no match, but the relaxed legacy-promotion fingerprint
    /// named multiple local rows. Callers must not pick one.
    case ambiguousLegacyPromotion
}
let resolution = matchIndex.resolution(
    for: GameDedup.Identity(preparedGame),   // GameDedup.Identity(_: PreparedGameData)
    allowLegacyCompositeFallback: true
)

docs.title: Durable persistence
docs.text:
LibraryAggregatePersistenceWriter is one serial DispatchQueue lane per physical aggregate-library file path. Synchronous edits call writeSynchronously, off-main imports/maintenance call writeAsynchronously, and restore installs pre-encoded JSON via installEncodedJSONSynchronously — all three funnel through the same queue, so an older async snapshot can never install after a newer synchronous save or restore. A private AsyncCompletionGate actor additionally leases the entire prepare→write→publish sequence for async callers, not just the physical write, so a failed async write finishes its MainActor rollback before a second async caller can snapshot or publish. LibraryAggregatePersistenceWriterRegistry hands out one weakly-held writer per standardized file path (capped at 256, GC-swept on overflow).

Bulk import writes the whole library repeatedly, so the chunk size adapts to the import size instead of using a fixed page:

minimumGameImportChunkSize = 1_000
maximumGameImportSaveCount = 4

gameImportChunkSize(for: incomingGameCount):
  quotient  = incomingGameCount / 4
  remainder = incomingGameCount % 4
  size      = quotient + (remainder == 0 ? 0 : 1)
  return max(1_000, size)

A 50,000-game import therefore chunks at 12,500 games/write (4 whole-library replacements); a 400-game import stays at one 1,000-game chunk (1 write) — the floor exists so a small import never chunks into several tiny writes. kernel.saveNewCollectionInChunks(_:) drives this: each chunk boundary is its own atomic aggregate replacement with a closure-based rollback if that specific write fails, and the returned ChunkedGameWriteResult.inserted count reflects only chunks that actually became durable.

docs.title: Capability tokens
docs.text:
Every collection and game carries an opaque incarnation token (CollectionIncarnation / GameIncarnation) that changes only when the row is durably deleted and recreated — even if its public UUID is reused. A retained editor presents its incarnation back to the kernel; if the token no longer matches, the mutation is rejected as .staleOwner instead of quietly overwriting an unrelated row that happens to share a UUID:

guard let incarnation = kernel.gameIncarnation(for: gameID, in: collectionID) else {
    return   // row no longer exists, or is ambiguous
}
let result = await kernel.updateGame(
    incarnation,
    expecting: GameEditableProjection(game: originalSnapshot),
    white: "Carlsen, M", black: "Nakamura, H",
    event: newEvent, date: newDate, site: newSite, userNotes: notes
)
switch result.outcome {
case .saved:             dismissEditor()
case .conflict:          showConflictBanner(result.failureDescription)
case .staleOwner:        showReplacedBanner(result.failureDescription)
case .persistenceFailed: retry()
}

updateGame acquires its own internal ChunkedMutationLease — chunked mutations and semantic-collection migrations use that same lease type as an exclusive, fail-closed guard, not a queued lock: beginChunkedMutation() returns nil immediately to a concurrent caller instead of waiting, so a cancelled task can never strand ownership. PersistenceBatch is the caller-owned counterpart for deferred writes — beginPersistenceBatch() opens a stream, markPersistenceBatchDirty records uncommitted work, and flushPersistenceBatch/finishPersistenceBatch commit it — while ordinary mutation APIs called without a batch token still save immediately, so a long batch can never suppress an unrelated user edit.

Reserved blob key Purpose library the aggregate LibraryData library.preRestoreRecovery.v1 pre-restore undo snapshot library.corruptRecovery.v1 preserved bytes when the aggregate fails to decode minedEndgames legacy flat mined-endgame projection key local.authoredReplicaID.v1 this installation's authored-mutation replica identity

docs.title: Mining admission
docs.text:
Trap, endgame, and combination-puzzle mining share one admission model with three independent purposes:

public enum MiningAdmissionPurpose: Sendable, Equatable {
    case traps, endgames, combinations
}

Three separate monotonic counters gate them: miningSourceCoverageEpoch (advances only after a durable source-changing mutation — an unrelated annotation/cache write does not bump it), trapMiningEligibilityEpoch (advances only when trap scan witnesses are deliberately cleared), and aggregatePersistenceRevision (consulted only for .combinations, since combination inputs include annotation payloads that fall outside the narrower trap/endgame source epoch). Trap mining additionally holds one exclusive session (activeTrapMiningSessionID: UUID?) so two trap miners can never publish scan witnesses concurrently — endgame results are positive FEN rows and stay safely additive, so no equivalent session exists for that purpose.

let decision = kernel.miningAdmissionSnapshot(for: .traps)
guard let snapshot = decision.snapshot else {
    showBanner(decision.failureMessage!)   // e.g. "another mining run is active"
    return
}
defer { kernel.releaseMiningAdmission(snapshot.token) }
let manifests = mineTraps(from: snapshot.library)   // pure, off-main
_ = kernel.replaceMinedTrapProjections(manifests, admissionToken: snapshot.token)
// if validateMiningAdmission(snapshot.token, for: .traps) is no longer
// .isCurrent, the library changed mid-run: results already saved were
// kept, but coverage may be incomplete — mine again

Mined traps dedup on insert by "\(trap.fen):\(trap.correctMoveUCI)", so a re-run that crosses a cancelled boundary never inserts the same trap twice. The materialized endgame projection uses a UUID-keyed compare-and-swap instead — MinedEndgameProjectionAuthority.mutationID changes on every mutation (never reused, so no ABA), and replaceMinedEndgameProjection(...) returns:

public enum MinedEndgameProjectionInstallOutcome: Sendable, Equatable {
    case installed(changed: Bool)
    case superseded      // a newer local authority already replaced this one
    case sourceChanged   // the admitted library source universe moved
    case failed
}

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
A full backup restore is one all-or-nothing transaction with exactly seven ordered, idempotent phases:

public enum LibraryRestoreInterruptionPoint: CaseIterable, Sendable, Equatable {
    case afterJournalAdmission
    case afterRecoverySnapshot
    case afterAuthoredPublication
    case afterAggregateCommit
    case afterAuxiliaryState
    case afterBackupEnvelope
    case afterJournalRetirement
}

rollForwardRestore is the sole executor for both an interactive restore and startup crash recovery — each phase is re-derivable from journal bytes alone, so resuming after a crash replays exactly the same code path a live restore would take. It writes the pre-restore undo snapshot first (library.preRestoreRecovery.v1), then joins the same serial LibraryAggregatePersistenceWriter lane used by ordinary saves before touching the live library key.

mergeBackupData applies an imported LibraryBackup additively, never destructively:

  • Games — matched via GameDedup.MatchIndex<Int> (allowLegacyCompositeFallback: true); a .unique match enriches the existing row through mergePortableFields(from:) (blank fields fill from the backup, non-empty analysis/notes fields are backup-authoritative, existing non-empty scalars are never overwritten); .none inserts a new row; .ambiguous is skipped rather than guessed.
  • Traps — deduped on (sourceGameID, fen, correctMoveUCI, userActualMoveUCI, halfMoveIndex), since two different mining sources can legitimately surface the same position.
  • Trap scan records — deduped on (sourceGameID, manifest identity), keeping whichever incoming/existing record has the newer scannedAt.
  • Endgame positions — unioned by FEN, then the projection selection is reset to the legacy generation-zero authority (minedEndgames stays authoritative until a fresh complete scan republishes its own successor) because a portable backup never carries the local immutable proof graph a typed receipt depends on.

Authored notes and board-mark edits go through a separate four-phase write-ahead protocol (LibraryAuthoredMutationInterruptionPoint) so a crash mid-edit can never leave the aggregate and the causal proof graph disagreeing: afterIntent (the write-ahead intent lands in a durable sidecar) → afterImmutableFacts (append-only causal rows written idempotently) → afterCompactHead (the compact replica head written) → afterAggregateCommit (one aggregate replacement applies desired and installs the identity marker; only then may the sidecar be retired). PendingAuthoredMutation.currentSchemaVersion is 1, and maximumImmutableRows is AuthoredVectorClock.maximumReplicaEntries (32) + 1. kernel.beginAuthoredMutation(incarnation:field:expected:desired: identitySource:) drains any earlier pending intent first, writes this one, then drains again — it never returns with unflushed intent state.

docs.title: PreparedGameData and the legacy "; best <SAN>" rewrite
docs.text:
PreparedGameData is the off-main import DTO every parsed game becomes before it reaches the kernel — init(from:orderIndex:) does the expensive tokenization, tag encoding, and identity resolution once, on whatever task built the batch, instead of paying that cost again on every subsequent read.

Legacy Fianchetto games stored the engine's best move as a bare inline marker directly after the annotated move: "… Nf3 ; best Bc4 …". Standard PGN treats ; as a comment running to end-of-line, but Fianchetto move text is a single line — so ChessCore's tokenizer reads the bare ; as an illegal SAN and drops the entire main line. Making ; run to end-of-line the way standard PGN does is equally wrong here: it would swallow every following move as comment text.

PreparedGameData.normalizeForParsing(_:) is the public entry point to the kernel-local rewrite (normalizingLegacyBestMoveMarkers) that toPGNGame also applies before tokenizing. It turns each bare marker into a bounded brace comment so the surrounding moves still parse and no content is lost:

"… Nf3 ; best Bc4 …"          →   "… Nf3 {; best Bc4} …"
"… {+0.2; best e4} …"         →   unchanged, byte for byte

The SAN is the single whitespace-delimited token after the marker. A "; best" that already sits inside a {...} brace comment is a structured engine annotation and must stay intact — rewriting it there would shift content digests and dedup keys. The literal "; best " text survives inside the new comment, so computeIsAnnotated keeps recognizing these games unchanged after the rewrite. The scan itself uses only character comparison and firstIndex(where:), deliberately avoiding Foundation range search, so it transpiles cleanly to Android via Skip.

docs.title: Import pipelines
docs.text:
importPGN is the single-shot synchronous path for one paste/autosave. importPGNInChunks parses off a detached task, then delegates to saveNewCollectionInChunks. importPreparedPGNCollection(_:fingerprint:) is the durable, crash-recoverable path: it records a PendingPGNImport journal (collectionID, fingerprint, collectionName) in the aggregate itself before writing the first chunk. A retry with the same fingerprint reuses the recorded collectionID and lets ordinary live dedup skip chunks that already made it to disk; a different fingerprint is rejected until the user explicitly keeps or abandons the partial import. The journal and every game chunk it protects live in one atomic FileJSONBlobStore write, so there is no separate preference file that could disagree with the games actually on disk after a crash.

Lichess's complete-history import pages through fetchLichessHistoryPages, and each page commit needs an O(1) proof that the destination collection's identity multiset hasn't silently drifted since the last page. LichessIdentityAccumulator provides that proof without rehashing the whole collection on every page:

rowDigest(gameID, identity) = SHA-256(
    "fianchetto.android.lichess-destination-row.v1"
    ++ lowercased(gameID.uuidString)
    ++ (identity.remoteID.isEmpty
          ? "content" ++ identity.composite ++ identity.legacyPromotion
          : "remote" ++ identity.remoteID)
)
// split the 256-bit digest into 4 big-endian UInt64 limbs (a, b, c, d)
insert(row): accumulator += rowDigest   // 256-bit add, mod 2^256, with carry
remove(row): accumulator -= rowDigest   // 256-bit subtract, with borrow

Insertion and removal are each O(1); the accumulator's final hexDigest proves the exact multiset of rows durable at that page boundary, so a promoted (content → remote ID) row updates the witness in place instead of forcing a full collection rewalk.

docs.title: Reconciliation and lifecycle
docs.text:
LibraryGameReconciliation.plan(games:) is a pure, persistence-agnostic static function — [LibraryBackup.Game] -> Plan — shared by the dedup preview UI, dedup execution, and LibrarySemanticCollectionReconciler's merges. Rows are grouped by a BaseProof (normalized persisted ID, logical dedup key, core PGN fingerprint, and position-sequence proof); within a duplicate group the survivor is chosen by this exact preference order:

1. isAnnotated            (prefer an annotated row)
2. positionRichness        (more populated derived-analysis fields wins)
3. enrichmentRichness       (richer note/Maia enrichment wins)
4. derivedDepth             (more bytes of regenerable analysis wins, on a tie)
5. orderIndex ascending      (earlier input wins remaining ties)
6. deleteIndices.count descending  (prefer the survivor that absorbs more)
7. survivorIndex ascending    (final deterministic tiebreak)

Complexity is O(total input + Σ group reconciliation costs) — projection and exact-base grouping are linear, and only actual duplicate groups pay the (at most cubic) candidate-selection cost. Board arrows are user-authored and are never dropped; a survivor may only absorb a source's redundant engine analysis when the group key is a recognized remote ID (proof the rows are literally the same online game).

LibrarySemanticCollectionReconciler.migrate(role:collections:) canonicalizes the app-generated collections (.otb, .vsEngine, .boardImports roles) into one collection per role, using the planner above for the merge. A destructive merge is permitted only when every candidate collection and game matches the exact generated shape — tag roster exactly {Event, Date, White, Black, Result} (optionally +{SetUp, FEN}), and for .vsEngine an opponent label prefixed with a known engine tag ("Maia ", "Reckless d", "Stockfish d"). Anything customized is left alone and reported through notice(for:) for manual review instead of merged.

CollectionLifecycle gives CloudKit-synchronized collections a signed soft-tombstone protocol:

legacyGeneration = 0

lifecycleVersion >= 0  → active, generation = lifecycleVersion
lifecycleVersion <  0  → deleted, tombstone generation = -lifecycleVersion
                          (Int64.min maps defensively to Int64.max, not a trap)

childDisposition(parent, child):
  active parent:   child == parent → visible
                   child <  parent → stale
                   child >  parent → deferred (out-of-order CloudKit delivery)
  deleted parent:  child <= tombstone → stale
                   child >  tombstone → deferred

CollectionLifecycle's cleanup extension (CollectionCleanupPolicy.swift) adds the durable two-observation state machine that authorizes actually deleting stale children:

maximumCleanupChildrenPerCollection  = 250_000
requiredStableCleanupObservations    = 2

observing  → first import-idle snapshot recorded
cleaning   → a second DISTINCT snapshot matched → this snapshot is now
             authorization; every batch re-verifies isExactSubset(of:)
             before deleting, so cleanup can only shrink toward it
quiescent  → the authorized snapshot has no stale children left

Any structurally invalid snapshot or token (duplicate child tokens, an oversized token, tombstoneVersion >= 0, tombstoneVersion == Int64.min) routes to .blocked — the caller must fail closed and keep every row rather than guess.

docs.title: Derived projections
docs.text:
LibraryStatsCache is a @MainActor process-local cache shared by Stats and Review. It coalesces identical in-flight requests (keyed by persistenceRevision + includeEloEstimate) into one shared Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated) computation, and a monotonic generation counter means only the last-started request for a given Elo mode may publish. lastGoodValue(includeEloEstimate:) keeps returning the previous good AggregateStats while a refresh is in flight or fails, so views never flash empty.

LibraryStatsProjection.snapshot(from:) maps LibraryData onto the shared GameStatsSnapshot that StatsKernel consumes. cachedMoveCount is always projected as -1 (recomputed downstream, never trusted from storage), and repertoire coverage keys go through OpeningBook.epNormalizedKey so transposed lines still register.

LibrarySortKernel.moveCount(fromMoveText:) fixed a real cross-platform bug — counting whitespace-split PGN tokens counts move-number tokens as moves:

moveCount(moveText):
  for each whitespace-split token:
    skip if first char is a digit       (move numbers: "1." / "12...")
    skip if first char is '*'           (result token)
    skip if first char in "{}();$"      (comments / NAGs / structure)
    else: plies += 1
  return (plies + 1) / 2

Name ordering (namePrecedes) deliberately uses String.compare(_:options:[.caseInsensitive, .numeric]) rather than localizedStandardCompare, with a byte-order lhs < rhs fallback on an .orderedSame result — locale-dependent collation would make the same library sort differently on two devices set to different regions, and without the fallback sorted(by:)'s non-stable order would let two devices holding the same games in different arrival order display them differently.

sortsBefore(lhs, rhs, by: key):
  "date-asc" → lhs.date < rhs.date
  "white"    → namePrecedes(lhs.white, rhs.white)
  "black"    → namePrecedes(lhs.black, rhs.black)
  "event"    → namePrecedes(lhs.event, rhs.event)
  "moves"    → lhs.moveCount > rhs.moveCount
  default    → lhs.date > rhs.date          // newest-first

CollectionOwnerResolver.resolve(explicitUsername:games:) infers whose library an unlabeled PGN import belongs to: it requires at least two games, exactly one name common to every game's {white, black} pair, and rejects placeholder names (?, unknown, anonymous, anon, white, black, player, computer) — anything less unambiguous fails closed (nil) rather than guessing, so an opponent or a one-off match PGN is never mistaken for the account owner.

docs.title: Filename and result-code helpers
docs.text:
PgnFilename.make(white:black:date:) builds the sanitized .pgn filename shared by both platforms' export paths:

PgnFilename.make(white:black:date:)
  keep only isLetter || isNumber || "-" || "_" || "."
  PGN date dots → hyphens BEFORE cleaning       "2024.01.15" → "2024-01-15"
  drop a side whose cleaned name is empty       (the "?" placeholder)
  join surviving players with "-vs-", then join to the date with "-"
  stem = raw.prefix(50); empty stem → "game"; append ".pgn"

Dropping the empty side is what stops "White-vs--2024-01-15" — a double hyphen — when one player tag is the PGN placeholder "?".

PGNResultCode.from(_ humanResult: String?) maps a human-readable end-of-game sentence to a PGN result token by ordered substring contains checks:

"White wins" → "1-0" · "Black wins" → "0-1" · "Draw" → "1/2-1/2"
nil or unrecognized → "*"

Prefer PGNResultCode.from(_ outcome: GameOutcome) where a GameOutcome exists

The string-matching overload substring-matches "White wins" out of prose a view composed elsewhere, so it discards the reason for the result entirely (no Termination tag was ever written from it), and it is one re-worded sentence away from silently answering "*" for a decisive game. It stays only because the import paths genuinely have nothing but prose to work from. The GameOutcome-based overload derives the token from the outcome directly and should be used everywhere else.

docs.title: Appendix: GameViewCache
docs.text:
The one presentation-adjacent type in this subsystem. GameViewCache memoizes EBoardSession.buildGameView() because MoveGenerator.legalMoves ran on every call at BLE notification cadence — measured at ~700ms of main-actor block per event on a Samsung Galaxy A17 (Helio G85, debug build), the dominant OTB-view jank source.

cache key   (ObjectIdentifier(game), game.position.fen, game.currentNode?.move.uci)
    FEN covers position, active color, castling rights, en-passant target, clocks
    currentNodeUCI invalidates the ancestor walk on retraction/take-back
    object identity stops a multi-session switch between two games sharing
      FEN + lastUCI from serving a stale ancestor chain
initial lastNodeUCI = "__INVALID__"      (distinct from the legitimate nil)
on a miss   walk the parent chain for at most 6 plies (take-back detection bound)
            castling rook homes from MoveGenerator.legalCastlingUCIs(for:) mapped
            through {"h1": "e1g1", "a1": "e1c1", "h8": "e8g8", "a8": "e8c8"}
            — measured ~3.6x faster than full legal-move generation

GameViewSource is the minimal surface (position, currentNode) that lets the two platforms' distinct Game classes share one cache; ChessCore's Game conforms in this file.

Main-actor only

GameViewCache is non-Sendable by design — it holds game-tree references without a concurrency penalty — and must only be called from the main actor, the same requirement as the EBoardSession that owns it. It compiles headless (Foundation + ChessCore, no SwiftUI/UIKit), but its output drives an interactive board session, so unlike the rest of this page it has essentially no CLI value — it is not part of the nonisolated pure-value surface below.

docs.title: Headless surface and CLI opportunities
docs.text:
Every file in this directory imports only Foundation (plus Dispatch in the persistence writer) and, where chess logic is needed, ChessCore. @MainActor isolation on LibraryStoreKernel itself is not a UI dependency — it is fine to run inside a CLI process's main-actor context — and a large fraction of the subsystem is nonisolated pure value logic that needs no actor at all: GameIdentity, GameDedup, LibraryGameReconciliation.plan(games:), LibrarySemanticCollectionReconciler, LibrarySortKernel, CollectionLifecycle (including its cleanup extension), CollectionOwnerResolver, PgnFilename, and PGNResultCode are all static functions over plain values with no store attached.

That makes several pieces natural fianchetto-cli subcommand targets beyond the estimate/annotate/maia/accuracy/project/track surface already wired to EloEstimator and StatsKernel:

  • A library import/dedupe pair could drive LibraryGameReconciliation.plan(games:) directly for a preview-then-apply flow, with no store instance needed at all — just an array of LibraryBackup.Game.
  • A stats subcommand reusing LibraryStatsProjection.snapshot(from:) + StatsKernel.compute is the same code path fianchetto-cli's project and track subcommands already exercise for headless Elo estimation, so a library-backed stats command would need no new math — only a LibraryData loaded from a JSON file.
  • GameIdentity's full identity surface — canonicalProviderID, persistedRemoteID, promotingIdentity, stableID — is not the one-line helper canonicalProviderID alone might suggest; see Game and collection identity. Paired with PgnFilename.make, it is well suited to a small identify/export-filename utility subcommand for scripting around PGN archives.

docs.title: Network Clients
docs.text:
Three REST clients: a Lichess tablebase probe, the Lichess opening explorer, and Chess.com / Lichess game import. All identify as User-Agent: "Fianchetto-ChessApp/1.0" and surface failures as ChessAPIError.

dataResult portability shim

All three clients call an internal URLSession.dataResult(for:) / dataResult(from:) pair instead of the native async data(for:) / bytes(for:), wrapping the completion-handler dataTask in a checked continuation. FianchettoKit's own floor is iOS 18 / macOS 15 — already past the iOS 15 / macOS 12 the native async APIs require — so this isn't an OS back-deployment; it's kept for Android portability, since the completion-handler dataTask is broadly available on swift-corelibs-foundation (including Android's SkipFoundation), where the async bytes(for:) is not. A lock-guarded state object (URLSessionDataResultState) guarantees the continuation resumes exactly once even when cancellation races task creation or a completion callback fires after cancellation.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
public enum ChessAPIError: LocalizedError {
    case invalidUsername     // 404
    case networkError(String)
    case noGamesFound
    case rateLimited         // 429
    case unauthorized        // 401
}

ChessAPIError is LocalizedError with user-facing errorDescriptions (e.g. unauthorized → "Authentication required — add your Lichess API token…").

docs.title: TablebaseService — Syzygy probe
docs.text:
A cached actor over the Lichess tablebase endpoint (https://tablebase.lichess.ovh/standard). Results are cached by FEN, with no eviction — unlike LichessExplorer's 200-entry cap — since a session probes a comparatively small set of distinct endgame FENs.

public actor TablebaseService {
    public static let shared: TablebaseService
    public init()
    public static func pieceCount(for position: Position) -> Int
    public func probe(fen: String) async throws -> TablebaseResult
    public func clearCache()
}

import ChessCore
import FianchettoKit

if TablebaseService.pieceCount(for: position) <= 7 {   // tablebase is <= 7 pieces
    let result = try await TablebaseService.shared.probe(fen: position.stockfishSafeFEN)
    print(result.category)            // .win / .loss / .draw / .cursedWin / ...
    print(result.dtm ?? -1, result.dtz ?? -1)
    print(result.bestMove ?? "—")

    for move in result.moves {
        switch move.userVerdict {
        case .keepsWin: print("\(move.uci) keeps the win")
        case .draws:    print("\(move.uci) only draws")
        case .losesWin: print("\(move.uci) throws the win")
        case .unknown:  break
        }
    }
}

Use userVerdict, not category

Lichess reports each move's category from the opponent's perspective — the side to move after your move. So a move whose category is loss means the opponent is losing after your move, i.e. your move keeps the win. TablebaseMove.userVerdict is the single source of truth for the from-your-POV mapping; route every consumer through it instead of mapping categories inline.

public struct TablebaseResult: Sendable {
    public let category: Category    // win, loss, draw, cursedWin, blessedLoss, unknown
    public let dtm: Int?             // depth to mate
    public let dtz: Int?             // depth to zeroing
    public let bestMove: String?
    public let moves: [TablebaseMove]
}

public struct TablebaseMove: Sendable, Identifiable {
    public let uci: String
    public let san: String?
    public let category: TablebaseResult.Category
    public let dtm: Int?
    public let dtz: Int?
    public var userVerdict: UserVerdict   // .keepsWin | .draws | .losesWin | .unknown
}

Category.isDecisive is true for .win, .loss, .cursedWin, and .blessedLoss (not .draw or .unknown).

docs.title: LichessExplorer — opening explorer
docs.text:
A cached actor over the Lichess opening explorer. Pick the database and (for the Lichess database) the rating bands.

public actor LichessExplorer {
    public static let shared: LichessExplorer
    public init()
    public func explore(fen: String,
                        database: ExplorerDatabase = .lichess,
                        ratings: [Int] = [1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2500],
                        speeds: [String] = ["blitz", "rapid", "classical"],
                        token: String? = nil) async throws -> ExplorerResult
    public func clearCache()
}

public enum ExplorerDatabase: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable, Sendable {
    case lichess = "Lichess"   // https://explorer.lichess.org/lichess
    case masters = "Masters"   // https://explorer.lichess.org/masters
}

let result = try await LichessExplorer.shared.explore(
    fen: position.fen,
    database: .lichess,
    ratings: [1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2500],
    speeds: ["blitz", "rapid", "classical"],
    token: nil                 // optional Lichess API token (Bearer)
)

print(result.totalGames, result.white, result.draws, result.black)
for move in result.moves.prefix(5) {
    print(move.san, move.totalGames, move.averageRating ?? 0)
}

Results are cached per "<database>:<fen>", or "<database>:<fen>:r=<ratings>:s=<speeds>" for the Lichess database (.masters ignores ratings/speeds, so its key drops them). ratings is filtered against the allowed set {1000, 1200, 1400, 1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2500}, falling back to the default list if nothing survives; speeds is filtered against ["bullet", "blitz", "rapid", "classical", "correspondence"] the same way. The cache holds at most 200 entries with oldest-first eviction; only non-empty results (white + draws + black > 0) are cached, and a malformed top-level JSON body throws .networkError rather than caching an empty result. A 401 surfaces as .unauthorized; a 429 as .rateLimited.

docs.title: ChessAPIService — game import
docs.text:
A fully nonisolated, Sendable class whose fetch+parse pipeline runs off the main actor. Its fetch methods are @concurrent — under the project's Approachable Concurrency settings, a plain nonisolated async method would run on the caller's actor, silently pulling a multi-month Chess.com sweep or a byte-by-byte Lichess decode back onto the main thread. The optional progress callback is @MainActor @Sendable and fires once per archive month, not per byte.

public final class ChessAPIService: Sendable {
    public init()

    @concurrent public func fetchChessComGames(
        username: String, since: Date? = nil, filters: ImportFilters? = nil,
        onProgress: (@MainActor @Sendable (Int, Int) -> Void)? = nil
    ) async throws -> ChessComFetchResult

    @concurrent public func fetchLichessGames(
        username: String, since: Date? = nil, token: String? = nil,
        filters: ImportFilters? = nil
    ) async throws -> [PGNGame]

    @concurrent public func fetchLichessGameSnapshot(
        username: String, since: Date? = nil, token: String? = nil,
        filters: ImportFilters? = nil
    ) async throws -> LichessFetchResult

    @concurrent public func fetchLichessHistoryPages(
        username: String, since: Date? = nil, token: String? = nil,
        filters: ImportFilters? = nil,
        pageSize: Int = ChessAPIService.defaultLichessHistoryPageSize,
        resumingFrom cursor: LichessHistoryPageCursor? = nil,
        onPage: @Sendable (LichessHistoryPage) async throws -> Void
    ) async throws -> LichessHistoryCompletion
}

The service owns two URLSessions: session (30 s per-request / 180 s total-resource timeout) for the Chess.com archive walk, and streamSession (60 s per-request / 7,200 s / 2 h total-resource timeout) for the Lichess export, a single long-lived stream rather than bounded requests. A second, internal init(session:streamSession:) exists only as a test seam.

LichessExplorer and TablebaseService each own their own private session too, but with a simpler budget: a flat 10 s per-request timeout and no timeoutIntervalForResource override at all. Neither client needs a resource-timeout ceiling — each request is one bounded lookup (an opening-book query, a FEN probe), never a multi-month sweep or an hours-long stream, so the per-request idle timer alone is enough to bound it.
