This capability is not currently exposed headlessly — fianchetto-cli ships exactly six subcommands (annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project, track) and none of them touch import. An import-shaped subcommand is only a proposal on the CLI's own expansion notes; everything below is the underlying policy such a command would eventually have to drive.

docs.title: Chess.com — monthly archive sweep
docs.text:
fetchChessComGames walks GET https://api.chess.com/pub/player/<username>/games/archives, filters and reverses the archive list to newest-first, then fetches and parses each archive's /pgn text. Per-archive failures are collected, never abort the sweep:

archives = GET .../games/archives -> { "archives": [String] }
kept     = chessComArchiveURLs(archives, notBefore: since)
walk     = kept.reversed()                     // newest month first

for each archive URL in walk:
    require url.scheme == "https" && url.host == "api.chess.com"   // else: failedArchives += url; continue
    pgn = GET url + "/pgn"
    games = PGNParser.parse(pgn)
    require isStructurallyValidChessComArchive(games)               // else: failedArchives += url; continue
    allGames += games
    onProgress(index + 1, total)   // @MainActor, once per archive

public struct ChessComFetchResult: Sendable {
    public let games: [PGNGame]
    public let failedArchives: [String]     // archive URLs that errored
    public var isPartial: Bool { !failedArchives.isEmpty }
}

.invalidUsername is thrown only for a 404 on the archive list; .rateLimited can surface from either that request or any per-archive PGN request. .noGamesFound is thrown only when finalGames.isEmpty && failedArchives.isEmpty — a genuinely empty account, never a partial sweep. CancellationError and any ChessAPIError thrown mid-sweep propagate immediately; every other per-archive failure is recorded and the sweep continues.

Archive-month boundary filter. Chess.com's archive URLs are UTC-calendar- month paths (.../YYYY/MM). chessComArchiveURLs(_:notBefore:) builds its own Calendar pinned to TimeZone(secondsFromGMT: 0)! — never Calendar.current — because deriving the boundary from the device's local time zone can make a positive-UTC-offset device consider itself already in the next month and permanently skip the still-current UTC archive:

given since: (sinceYear, sinceMonth) = UTC calendar components of since
keep archive iff:
    trailing "/year/month" path components are unparseable   // KEEP — malformed URLs are
                                                                // reported as failures, not silently dropped
    OR year > sinceYear
    OR (year == sinceYear AND month >= sinceMonth)

Structural validation gate. PGNParser is deliberately permissive for hand-authored imports — any non-empty token text becomes a PGNGame — so a network archive needs a stricter boundary: an HTML error page or truncated body must not be mistaken for a successful, if game-less, month. isStructurallyValidChessComArchive requires the parsed archive to be non-empty and every game to have non-empty trimmed White/Black tags and a Result tag drawn from {"1-0", "0-1", "1/2-1/2", "*"}.

Client-side filters. Chess.com has no server-side filter API, so ImportFilters are applied per game, after parsing — see the mapping table under ImportFilters below.

docs.title: Lichess one-shot fetch — fetchLichessGames / fetchLichessGameSnapshot
docs.text:
fetchLichessGames is a thin convenience over fetchLichessGameSnapshot that throws .noGamesFound when games is empty. Prefer the snapshot form for anything persisting an incremental cursor — an empty terminal-game list is a valid snapshot (it can mean "no new games" or "the only matching game is still in progress"), which the convenience form can't distinguish from a truly empty account.

public struct LichessFetchResult: Sendable {
    public let games: [PGNGame]                    // terminal games only
    public let earliestOngoingGameDate: Date?
    public let serverDate: Date?
    public var hasOngoingGames: Bool { earliestOngoingGameDate != nil }
    public func safeSyncWatermark(fetchStartedAt: Date) -> Date?
}

Both methods first issue a separate ongoing-game probe: the same account/filters request, but with since, until, max, sort, rated, perfType, color, opening, and pgnInJson/ongoing/finished stripped and re-added as pgnInJson=true&ongoing=true&finished=false. Excluding the caller's cursor and filters means the probe always reflects the account's true earliest in-progress game. Only after the probe completes is the requested finished-history slice fetched and merged with the probe's records.

Safe sync watermark — the rewind rule. Lichess delays ongoing games by up to 60 s in the export, so a cursor computed purely from request time can land after a game that started before the response but isn't visible in it yet:

lichessSafeSyncWatermark(fetchStartedAt, serverDate, earliestOngoingGameDate):
    if serverDate == nil: return nil                       // no trustworthy clock — do not advance
    candidate = min(fetchStartedAt, serverDate) - 61s       // 60s export delay + 1s overlap margin
    if earliestOngoingGameDate != nil
       && earliestOngoingGameDate <= candidate:
        return earliestOngoingGameDate - 1s                 // rewind the cursor to just before that game
    return candidate

LichessFetchResult.safeSyncWatermark(fetchStartedAt:) and LichessHistoryCompletion.safeSyncWatermark() both forward to this one private algorithm — the completion form treats snapshotUntilMilliseconds / 1000 as fetchStartedAt.

Never derive a Lichess watermark by any other means

A missing serverDate must disable cursor advance entirely — that's why the function returns nil instead of falling back to the local clock. Publishing a locally-computed cursor when the remote clock is unknown is exactly the failure OnlineImportWatermarkPolicy (below) exists to rule out.

docs.title: ImportFilters / ImportTimeControl / ImportColor
docs.text:
The shared filter vocabulary across both platforms. All fields default to nil (no restriction).

public struct ImportFilters: Sendable {
    public var ratedOnly: Bool?              // nil = any, true = rated only, false = unrated only
    public var timeControls: Set<ImportTimeControl>?   // nil/empty = all classes
    public var color: ImportColor?           // nil/.any = either color
    public var since: Date?                  // nil = no lower bound
    public init(ratedOnly: Bool? = nil, timeControls: Set<ImportTimeControl>? = nil,
                color: ImportColor? = nil, since: Date? = nil)
    public var isActive: Bool   // true iff any field imposes a real restriction
}

public enum ImportTimeControl: String, CaseIterable, Codable, Sendable, Hashable {
    case bullet, blitz, rapid, classical
    public var displayName: String
    public var chessComTimeClass: String   // "standard" for .classical, else rawValue
}

public enum ImportColor: String, CaseIterable, Codable, Sendable {
    case any, white, black
    public var displayName: String
}

ImportTimeControl raw values match Lichess perfType values exactly, while Chess.com names classical games "standard" in its TimeClass tag — the one case chessComTimeClass translates.

Filter field Chess.com mapping Lichess mapping ratedOnly !event.contains("(Unrated)") (client-side) rated=true\|false query param timeControls TimeClass tag vs. chessComTimeClass (client-side) perfType=<comma-joined sorted raw values> color White/Black tag vs. username (client-side) color=white\|black (omitted for .any) since Date tag "YYYY.MM.DD" vs. since (client-side) since=<ms>, = max(since, filters.since)

Lichess applies filters server-side via query parameters built by the shared lichessBaseRequest; Chess.com applies them client-side, after parsing.

docs.title: Lichess bounded history walk — fetchLichessHistoryPages
docs.text:
The producer for a complete, resumable, newest-first account history. It has no total game cap — a full page always produces a strictly older continuation, and the walk ends only when Lichess returns a short page. pageSize must be in 1...maximumLichessHistoryPageSize (5,000) or it throws .invalidPageSize; the default is defaultLichessHistoryPageSize (1,000).

if resuming from a cursor:
    validate cursor.hasValidIntegrityAndShape
    validate cursor.matches(requestSignature, pageSize)   // else .resumeCursorRequestMismatch
    snapshotUntilMilliseconds = cursor.snapshotUntilMilliseconds   // fixed, carried forward unchanged
    nextUntilMilliseconds     = cursor.nextUntilMilliseconds
    previousPageIDs           = Set(cursor.overlapGameIDs)
else:
    probe ongoing games once (no filters/cursor) -> serverDate, earliestOngoingGameDate
    snapshotUntilMilliseconds = floor((serverDate ?? now).timeIntervalSince1970 * 1000)
    nextUntilMilliseconds     = snapshotUntilMilliseconds
    previousPageIDs           = {}

loop:
    GET .../games/user/<username>?until=nextUntilMilliseconds&max=pageSize&sort=dateDesc&finished=true&...filters
    (novelRecords, nextUntil?, nextOverlapIDs) = LichessNewestFirstPageAccumulator(
        pageSize, currentUntilMilliseconds: nextUntilMilliseconds, previousPageIDs
    ).consume(page)
    games  = terminal games in novelRecords
    cursor = nextUntil.map { LichessHistoryPageCursor(snapshotUntilMilliseconds, nextUntilMilliseconds: $0,
                                                        ..., overlapGameIDs: nextOverlapIDs) }
    await onPage(LichessHistoryPage(games, resumeCursor: cursor))   // durability handshake
    if cursor == nil: return LichessHistoryCompletion(...)          // short/partial page = terminal
    nextUntilMilliseconds = cursor.nextUntilMilliseconds
    previousPageIDs        = Set(cursor.overlapGameIDs)

One-millisecond overlap rule. A full page (page.count == pageSize) can't assume the next page starts strictly after this page's oldest game — Lichess may treat until inclusively, and games can share a millisecond-resolution createdAt. LichessNewestFirstPageAccumulator handles this by computing nextUntil = pageMinimum(createdAtMilliseconds) + 1 and requiring nextUntil < currentUntilMilliseconds, else it throws .cursorDidNotAdvance — the guard against an infinite loop or a silently-skipped timestamp cluster. The previous page's full ID set is carried forward as previousPageIDs/overlapGameIDs so records reappearing at the shared boundary millisecond are filtered from novelRecords instead of re-yielded. A short page (page.count != pageSize) is unambiguously the end of history: nextUntilMilliseconds is nil.

onPage is a durability handshake: persist page.games and then page.resumeCursor before returning. Nothing older is requested until that closure returns, so replaying an already-acknowledged page after a crash between those two writes is safe — stable Lichess IDs make re-persisting idempotent.

let completion = try await service.fetchLichessHistoryPages(
    username: "DrNykterstein",
    token: lichessToken,          // optional; changes throughput, not which games match
    pageSize: 5_000,
    resumingFrom: savedCursor     // nil on a fresh import
) { page in
    try await persistGamesAndThenCursor(page.games, cursor: page.resumeCursor)
}
print(completion.acknowledgedGameCount, "acknowledged games")
if let watermark = completion.safeSyncWatermark() {
    // safe to advance the account's incremental-sync cursor
}

public struct LichessHistoryPage: Sendable {
    public let games: [PGNGame]
    public let resumeCursor: LichessHistoryPageCursor?
    public var isTerminal: Bool { resumeCursor == nil }
}

public struct LichessHistoryPageCursor: Sendable, Codable, Equatable {
    public let schemaVersion: Int                  // = lichessHistoryCursorSchemaVersion (1)
    public let snapshotUntilMilliseconds: Int64     // fixed upper bound of the whole walk
    public let nextUntilMilliseconds: Int64
    public let serverDate: Date?
    public let earliestOngoingGameDate: Date?
    public let overlapGameIDs: [String]             // boundary-page IDs, for de-dup on resume
    public let integritySHA256: String              // checksum, not a secret-keyed auth proof
    public func isValid(for identity: LichessHistoryImportIdentity) -> Bool
}

public struct LichessHistoryCompletion: Sendable {
    public let snapshotUntilMilliseconds: Int64
    public let serverDate: Date?
    public let earliestOngoingGameDate: Date?
    public let acknowledgedPageCount: Int
    public let acknowledgedGameCount: Int
    public var hasOngoingGames: Bool { earliestOngoingGameDate != nil }
    public func safeSyncWatermark() -> Date?
}

Request-signature and integrity-proof hashing. Because the cursor is Codable and meant to be persisted, it carries two SHA-256 digests (via PortableSHA256.Hasher, each domain-separated by a literal version string):

lichessHistoryRequestSignature = SHA256(
    "fianchetto.lichess-history-request-signature.v1",
    normalizedUsername, String(pageSize),
    <every base-request query item, sorted by (name, value)>   // order-independent
)

lichessHistoryCursorIntegrityProof = SHA256(
    "fianchetto.lichess-history-page-cursor.integrity.v1",
    schemaVersion, snapshotUntilMilliseconds, nextUntilMilliseconds,
    dateField(serverDate), dateField(earliestOngoingGameDate),   // "none" | "some:<hex bitPattern>"
    requestSignature, pageSize, overlapGameIDs.count, <each overlapGameIDs entry>
)

dateField encodes a Date as "none" or "some:" plus the hex bitPattern of timeIntervalSinceReferenceDate — the exact IEEE-754 bits — so a Codable round-trip is lossless while sub-millisecond mutation is still detected. Both digests are integrity checksums, not secret-keyed authenticity proofs.

isValid(for:) re-derives the expected request signature from a LichessHistoryImportIdentity (below) and checks it, the integrity proof, and the schema version — with the API token deliberately excluded, since a token changes throughput, not which public games match. hasValidIntegrityAndShape additionally requires: schemaVersion == lichessHistoryCursorSchemaVersion (1); snapshotUntilMilliseconds > 0; nextUntilMilliseconds > 0; nextUntilMilliseconds < snapshotUntilMilliseconds; overlapGameIDs non-empty, with no duplicates or empty strings, and count <= pageSize.

docs.title: Crash-safe resumption — LichessHistoryImportIdentity + LichessHistoryImportCheckpoint
docs.text:
A cursor alone is enough to resume a walk mid-flight, but crash recovery also needs to know whose walk a saved cursor belongs to and how much of it has reached durable storage. LichessHistoryImportIdentity is the canonical request identity — the API token is excluded for the same reason as above:

public struct LichessHistoryImportIdentity: Codable, Hashable, Sendable {
    public static let currentSchemaVersion = 1

    public let schemaVersion: Int
    public let normalizedUsername: String
    public let ratedOnly: Bool?
    public let timeControlRawValues: [String]     // sorted
    public let colorRawValue: String?              // nil unless white/black (.any collapses to nil)
    public let sinceMilliseconds: Int64?
    public let pageSize: Int

    public init?(username: String, since: Date? = nil, filters: ImportFilters? = nil,
                 pageSize: Int = ChessAPIService.defaultLichessHistoryPageSize)

    public var isValid: Bool
    public var filters: ImportFilters?      // reconstructed, or nil if not .isActive
    public var storageToken: String         // SHA-256 digest — a stable cache/file key, not a secret
}

The failable initializer normalizes the username (trim + lowercase) and rejects an out-of-range pageSize or a since that doesn't scale losslessly to milliseconds within Int64. storageToken is a domain-separated SHA-256 digest ("fianchetto.lichess-history-import-identity.v1"), a stable filesystem/blob-store key derived from the request shape.

public struct LichessHistoryImportCheckpoint: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public static let currentSchemaVersion = 1

    public let schemaVersion: Int
    public let identity: LichessHistoryImportIdentity
    public let cursor: ChessAPIService.LichessHistoryPageCursor
    public let acknowledgedPageCount: Int
    public let acknowledgedGameCount: Int
    public let insertedGameCount: Int

    public init(identity:cursor:acknowledgedPageCount:acknowledgedGameCount:insertedGameCount:)
    public func isValid(for expectedIdentity: LichessHistoryImportIdentity) -> Bool
}

isValid(for:) requires: schema match; identity.isValid and exact equality to the caller's freshly-recomputed expected identity (so a changed username, filter, or page size invalidates a stale checkpoint rather than silently resuming the wrong request); cursor.isValid(for: identity); acknowledgedPageCount > 0; acknowledgedGameCount >= 0; and insertedGameCount in 0...acknowledgedGameCount (a page can be acknowledged with fewer games actually inserted after dedup).

guard let identity = LichessHistoryImportIdentity(
    username: "DrNykterstein", filters: filters, pageSize: 5_000
) else { return }   // invalid username/pageSize/since

if let saved = loadCheckpoint(for: identity.storageToken), saved.isValid(for: identity) {
    // resume: pass saved.cursor as `resumingFrom:`
} else {
    // start fresh: resumingFrom: nil
}

docs.title: Update Games: the shared incremental-sync policy
docs.text: "Update Games" — re-fetching only what changed since the last successful import — has one policy shared verbatim between platforms: a source-agnostic watermark rule plus GameUpdatePlanner, the namespace that drives a single update pass end to end.

docs.title: OnlineImportWatermarkPolicy.safeSyncWatermark
docs.text:
public enum OnlineImportWatermarkPolicy {
    public static func safeSyncWatermark(
        candidateSyncDate: Date?, isPartial: Bool,
        filtersAreActive: Bool, allFetchedGamesSelected: Bool
    ) -> Date?
}

safeSyncWatermark(candidateSyncDate, isPartial, filtersAreActive, allFetchedGamesSelected):
    if isPartial || filtersAreActive || !allFetchedGamesSelected:
        return nil                       // watermark must not advance
    return candidateSyncDate

Extracted after two app shells independently reimplemented this rule with diverging, less-safe parameter sets. Getting it wrong doesn't crash: it silently makes remote history permanently unreachable, because the next incremental sync starts from the stamped cursor and never looks back. candidateSyncDate must be the request's start time, not the save time, or games published mid-fetch would be skipped; isPartial catches a Chess.com sweep with failed archive months; filtersAreActive catches a filtered batch that can't describe an unfiltered "everything since X" replay; allFetchedGamesSelected catches a shell offering per-game import selection.

docs.title: GameUpdatePlanner
docs.text:
public enum GameUpdatePlanner {
    public static func sinceDate(fullSweep: Bool, lastSyncDate: Date?) -> Date?
    public static func remoteGameID(of game: PGNGame) -> String

    public static func fetch(
        api: ChessAPIService, source: String, username: String, since: Date?,
        lichessToken: String?, onProgress: (@MainActor @Sendable (Int, Int) -> Void)? = nil
    ) async throws -> UpdateFetchResult

    public static func newGames(in fetched: [PGNGame], existing: GameDedup.KeySet) -> [PGNGame]
    public static func newGamesCheckingCancellation(in fetched: [PGNGame], existing: GameDedup.KeySet) throws -> [PGNGame]

    public static func syncStamp(isPartial: Bool, now: Date = Date()) -> Date?
    public static func syncStamp(for result: UpdateFetchResult, source: String, requestStartedAt: Date) -> Date?

    public static func resultMessage(imported: Int, failedMonths: Int) -> String?
}

sinceDate picks the fetch lower bound: a full sweep passes nil (re-walks everything, relying on dedup); an incremental update resumes from lastSyncDate. remoteGameID(of:) forwards to GameIdentity.remoteID(link:site:): an explicit PGN Link tag wins outright; a Site tag is accepted only when it's a recognized Chess.com/ Lichess game URL, so a generic PGN venue falls through to content identity.

fetch is the unified source dispatch:

if source == "lichess":
    fetchStartedAt    = now
    snapshot          = api.fetchLichessGameSnapshot(username, since, token: lichessToken)
    requestedSyncDate = syncStamp(isPartial: false, now: fetchStartedAt)
    safeSyncDate      = snapshot.safeSyncWatermark(fetchStartedAt: requestedSyncDate)
    return UpdateFetchResult(games: snapshot.games, failedArchiveCount: 0,
                              mustRetainSyncWatermark: safeSyncDate == nil,
                              exactSyncWatermark: safeSyncDate)
else:   // chess.com
    result = api.fetchChessComGames(username, since, onProgress: onProgress)
    return UpdateFetchResult(games: result.games, failedArchiveCount: result.failedArchives.count)

// either branch: a caught ChessAPIError.noGamesFound normalizes to an EMPTY
// UpdateFetchResult (not rethrown), but only when `since != nil` (incremental,
// not a first import — where no games really is an error)

public struct UpdateFetchResult: Sendable {
    public let games: [PGNGame]
    public let failedArchiveCount: Int
    public let mustRetainSyncWatermark: Bool   // default false; true when Lichess found no trustworthy boundary
    public let exactSyncWatermark: Date?       // Lichess's authoritative cursor; may rewind (see above)
    public var isPartial: Bool { failedArchiveCount > 0 }
}

newGames dedup. For each fetched game, register it into a GameDedup.KeySet — deduping against both existing and the same fetched batch — preferring a remote ID (remoteGameID(of:)) when present, else the 6-field GameDedup.compositeKey (white, black, date, result, event, opening, plus token-text move export and JSON-encoded tags) as an @autoclosure, so an ID-bearing game never pays for PGN serialization or move-text hashing. newGamesCheckingCancellation is the same policy with a cancellation check before each composite-key fingerprint, so a retired full-history update doesn't keep hashing thousands of games off-screen.

syncStamp — two overloads:

syncStamp(isPartial, now):
    if isPartial: return nil
    return floor(now.timeIntervalSince1970 seconds)   // round DOWN — HTTP Date is second-granular;
                                                        // a fractional client time would compare LATER
                                                        // than the authoritative server boundary

syncStamp(for: result, source, requestStartedAt):
    if source == "lichess": return result.exactSyncWatermark   // verbatim — Lichess's own server-clock cursor
    return syncStamp(isPartial: result.isPartial, now: requestStartedAt)   // chess.com path

resultMessage is the single source of the user-facing outcome string:

imported > 0 failedMonths > 0 Message false false "No new games found." false true "No new games found. {n} month(s) failed to download — retry later." true true "Imported {n}; {m} month(s) failed — retry later." true false nil (plain success — the count change is the feedback) 
let since = GameUpdatePlanner.sinceDate(fullSweep: false, lastSyncDate: collection.lastSyncDate)
let requestStartedAt = Date()

let result = try await GameUpdatePlanner.fetch(
    api: service, source: collection.source, username: collection.username,
    since: since, lichessToken: lichessToken
) { done, total in print("archive \(done)/\(total)") }

let fresh = try GameUpdatePlanner.newGamesCheckingCancellation(in: result.games, existing: existingKeys)
try await persist(fresh)

if !result.mustRetainSyncWatermark,
   let stamp = GameUpdatePlanner.syncStamp(for: result, source: collection.source, requestStartedAt: requestStartedAt) {
    collection.lastSyncDate = stamp
}

if let message = GameUpdatePlanner.resultMessage(imported: fresh.count, failedMonths: result.failedArchiveCount) {
    showBanner(message)
}

docs.title: NDJSON streaming internals
docs.text:
Internal (non-public) types backing the Lichess fetch paths. Briefly, for contributors working inside FianchettoKit/Network — none of this is public API.

LichessGameStreamDecoder frames Lichess's NDJSON export one byte at a time via consume(_ byte:) throws -> LichessGameRecord? and finish() throws -> LichessGameRecord?, buffering only the current line's raw bytes and releasing a LichessGameRecord as soon as a 0x0A newline arrives (trailing 0x0D stripped, empty lines ignored). A line over maximumLineByteCount (default defaultMaximumLineByteCount = 8 * 1024 * 1024, 8 MiB) throws .lineTooLarge.

Each line decodes as {id, createdAt: Int64, status: String, pgn: String?}. status.lowercased() is checked against a fixed set:

finalStatuses = {
    "aborted", "mate", "resign", "stalemate", "timeout", "draw",
    "outoftime", "cheat", "nostart", "unknownfinish",
    "insufficientmaterialclaim", "variantend"
}

A status not in that set — including a future Lichess status the decoder hasn't been updated for — yields finishedGame == nil (isOngoing == true): fail toward "not yet final" rather than risk a persisted in-progress snapshot. For a final status, pgn must be non-nil and parse to exactly one game with non-empty White/Black/Result tags, or the line throws .invalidPGN. Both byte-driven decode paths check Task cancellation every 4,096 bytes rather than every byte.

Two private static helpers on ChessAPIService turn a raw record list into a LichessFetchResult:

finishedLichessGames(in records: [LichessGameRecord]) -> [PGNGame]
    keep record.finishedGame where record.id has not been seen before
    // first occurrence of an id wins; a later duplicate is dropped even if
    // it too carries a finishedGame

earliestOngoingGameDate(in records: [LichessGameRecord]) -> Date?
    min over records where isOngoing of
        Date(timeIntervalSince1970: createdAtMilliseconds / 1_000)

The keep-first-id rule matters because the ongoing probe and the requested finished-history slice are two separate requests merged into one record list; if the same id appears in both, only the first copy encountered should survive into games rather than being counted, or silently overwritten, twice.

Two accumulators sit on top of the decoder, one per pagination strategy:

Type Used by Overlap rule LichessGamePageAccumulator fetchLichessGamesPaged — oldest-first, Android/Linux/Windows fallback (default page size 1,000) full page → nextSince = pageMaximum(createdAt) - 1; throws .cursorDidNotAdvance if pageMaximum <= previousMaximumCreatedAt LichessNewestFirstPageAccumulator fetchLichessHistoryPages — bounded newest-first walk full page → nextUntil = pageMinimum(createdAt) + 1, must be < currentUntilMilliseconds else .cursorDidNotAdvance

Both dedup by stable record id and throw .pageTooLarge if the server returns more records than requested. The Android/Linux/Windows fallback exists because Android's AsyncBytes adapter silently converts a stream read error into ordinary end-of-stream, and swift-corelibs-foundation has no async bytes(for:) at all — all three platforms use finite, overlapping completion-handler pages, which preserve transport errors and bound memory.

lichessServerDate(from:) parses the HTTP Date header as an RFC 7231 IMF-fixdate (DateFormatter, locale en_US_POSIX, zone GMT+0, format "EEE',' dd MMM yyyy HH':'mm':'ss 'GMT'"). A missing or unparseable header deliberately yields nil, disabling cursor advance per the safe-watermark rule above.

docs.title: Public vs. internal surface
docs.text:
Public Module-internal ChessAPIService + nested ChessComFetchResult, LichessFetchResult, LichessHistoryPageCursor, LichessHistoryPage, LichessHistoryCompletion LichessGameStreamDecoder, LichessGameRecord, LichessGameStreamDecodingError ChessAPIError, ChessPlatform, ImportTimeControl, ImportColor, ImportFilters LichessNewestFirstPageAccumulator, LichessGamePageAccumulator, LichessGamePageDecision LichessGamePaginationError — Equatable, so it is directly assertable in tests ChessAPIService.chessComArchiveURLs(_:notBefore:) LichessHistoryImportIdentity, LichessHistoryImportCheckpoint lichessNewestFirstPageComponents(from:untilMilliseconds:pageSize:), lichessOngoingProbeComponents(from:) OnlineImportWatermarkPolicy, UpdateFetchResult, GameUpdatePlanner the init(session:streamSession:) transport test seam LichessExplorer, ExplorerResult, ExplorerMove, ExplorerDatabase, TablebaseService, TablebaseResult, TablebaseMove URLSession.dataResult(for:) / dataResult(from:), URLSessionDataResultState

LichessFetchResult's memberwise init is internal, so an out-of-module caller can only obtain one from a real fetch. UpdateFetchResult has a public memberwise init, which is what lets GameUpdatePlanner tests run against hand-built fetch results with no network involved at all.

docs.title: Error handling pattern
docs.text:
do {
    _ = try await service.fetchLichessGames(username: name, token: token)
} catch ChessAPIError.unauthorized {
    // prompt for an API token
} catch ChessAPIError.invalidUsername {
    // 404 — no such user
} catch ChessAPIError.rateLimited {
    // 429 — back off
} catch ChessAPIError.noGamesFound {
    // empty result
} catch {
    // ChessAPIError.networkError(message) or a transport error
}

docs.title: Play, Review & Voice
docs.text: The Play clock/result flow, the Review pane's derived stats, spoken-move input, and cross-platform leaf utilities (hashing, formatting, licensing data). Everything here is Foundation + ChessCore only — no SwiftUI, @Observable, Timer, or app-lifecycle types — so it runs the same in a unit test, in the iOS/Android apps, or headlessly from a CLI. See Headless-by-construction for the import table.

docs.title: ClockCore — the clock state machine
docs.text:
Deadline-based, not per-tick. ClockCore banks each side's remaining time privately (whiteBanked/blackBanked) plus one optional activeSince: ContinuousClock.Instant? marking when the side to move started thinking. Every read computes banked − (now − activeSince) against ContinuousClock; nothing ticks the clock, and a read that arrives 40 seconds late (backgrounding, a paused compositor, a headless test with no frame clock) still comes back correct with no recovery code anywhere. whiteRemaining, blackRemaining, isRunning, isExpired, and loser are retained spellings — kept for the eleven Apple call sites that already read them — but they are now computed projections over the banked state, not independent mutable fields that could drift out of sync with it. ClockCore itself imports only Foundation and ChessCore: no Timer, no @Observable. A shell's own display loop decides how often to look; the clock doesn't care.

RunState replaces a single isRunning Bool, because the old stop() conflated three situations that resume differently: .idle (never started), .running, .pausedByPlayer (a person pressed pause — the only state resume() accepts), and .stopped(StopReason), terminal. StopReason is .flagged(PieceColor) (latched at the deadline, never un-latches on its own) or .gameEnded (an outcome — checkmate, resignation, an agreed draw — after which no flag can fall, even if resume() is called).

The mutating surface:

Member Behavior start(color:at:) Begins the clock with color to move; refuses if a side is already flagged. pause(at:) A person paused: banks the elapsed time, moves to .pausedByPlayer. Returns false if nothing was running. resume(at:) Resumes from .pausedByPlayer or .idle only — refuses a clock stopped by a flag or an outcome. stop() Retained spelling; maps to pause() (its legacy call sites all meant "a person paused"). stopForOutcome(at:) Terminal stop for a chess/adjudication reason. resume() will not undo it. switchTurn(at:) Banks the mover's elapsed time, pays the increment, hands the turn over, and records a per-ply history frame. No-op unless running. tapAdvance(side:at:) The OTB button rule: the first tap starts the opponent's clock; thereafter only the side to move may press; a tap from the wrong side changes nothing. Returns whether the tap did anything. rewind(plies:at:) Undoes a takeback: restores banked time and the side to move from history. The increment is revoked; the thinking time is not refunded. poll(at:) Latches a flag that has fallen, attributed and banked at the deadline rather than at the read instant. Idempotent; call before any read that must not see a clock "still running" past its deadline. reset() Restores both sides to the initial time, white to move, not running, history discarded.

And the reads:

Member Behavior deadline() The instant the active side's flag falls, or nil if nothing is running — lets a shell schedule one wakeup instead of polling. flagged(at:) The side whose flag has fallen, derived from the deadline while running, read off the latch once poll has fired. renderRevision(at:) A value that changes exactly when a rendered clock string could look different — packs a structural counter with each side's display bucket (tenths below TimeInterval.clockTenthsThreshold, whole seconds above it), so a shell redraws on real state changes and not on every frame. text(_:at:) The rendered string for a side, via the kit's one clock formatter (TimeInterval.clockString), using the same threshold renderRevision buckets against — so the two cannot drift apart the way two hand-rolled per-face computations once did. 
var clock = ClockCore(minutes: 5, increment: 3)   // 5+3 blitz
clock.tapAdvance(side: .black)   // black's first tap starts WHITE's clock
clock.tapAdvance(side: .white)   // white moved: elapsed time banked, +3s paid, black to move
_ = clock.poll()                 // latch a flag if the deadline has already passed
if let loser = clock.flagged() { print("\(loser) flagged") }
print(clock.text(.white))        // e.g. "4:58"

Three siblings, not one type

ClockSnapshot is the packed [Int64] wire shape a shell polls (fields, flags, whiteMillis, blackMillis, activeSide, incrementMillis, flaggedSide, plyCount, renderRevision) — a primitive array rather than JSON because a clock is read roughly ten times a second and crossing JNI as primitives costs ~11.7 ns against JSON's ~98 µs. ClockDefaults.defaultBaseSeconds (600) is the base time control assumed when a game carries no clock at all — an untimed replay still needs something to classify pressure against. ClockPressureBand is that classification: .healthy/.low/.critical via band(remainingSeconds:baseSeconds:), with the low/critical thresholds themselves relative to the base control — controls under quickControlSeconds (180s) go critical under 10s and low under 30s; longer controls go critical under 30s and low under 60s.

docs.title: TimePreset & TimeControlSelection
docs.text:
TimePreset's raw value is the "<minutes>+<increment>" notation:

Category Cases (raw value) Bullet bullet1_0 (1+0), bullet2_1 (2+1) Blitz blitz3_0 (3+0), blitz3_2 (3+2), blitz5_0 (5+0), blitz5_3 (5+3) Rapid rapid10_0 (10+0), rapid15_10 (15+10) Classical classical30_0 (30+0)

TimeControlSelection (.noClock / .preset(TimePreset) / .custom(minutes:increment:)) codecs the persisted @AppStorage value. Apple and Android once wrote different strings for the same choice — Apple "preset:5+0", Android the bare rawValue "5+0" — so a preference saved on one platform silently read as "nothing saved" on the other (no crash or log; the picker just falls back to default). Canonical form is Apple's now, since Apple had already shipped those strings; the decoder accepts both:

encoded:  .noClock -> "none"   .preset(p) -> "preset:<p.rawValue>"   .custom(m,i) -> "custom:<m>:<i>"

decode(raw): ""                  -> nil       (no stored preference)
             "none"               -> .noClock
             "custom:<m>:<i>"     -> parsed as Double then truncated to Int
                                     (old Apple entries can read "5.0:3.0")
             "preset:<rawValue>"  -> .preset(TimePreset(rawValue:))
             "<rawValue>" (bare)  -> .preset(TimePreset(rawValue:))   // legacy Android
             anything else        -> nil

UserDefaults.standard.set(TimeControlSelection.preset(.blitz5_3).encoded, forKey: "timeControl")
switch TimeControlSelection.decode(stored) {
case .preset(let p):          ClockCore(minutes: p.minutes, increment: p.increment)
case .custom(let m, let i):   ClockCore(minutes: m, increment: i)
case .noClock, nil:           break   // untimed, or no stored preference
}

docs.title: CheckmateCelebrationPolicy & CheckmateCelebrationState
docs.text:
A pure decision function from a stored Intensity (off=0, subtle=1, standard=2, festive=3 — Intensity(storedValue:) falls back to .standard, not .off, for any unrecognized integer) plus two accessibility flags, to a Decision:

decision(storedIntensity, reduceMotion, hapticsEnabled):
    intensity = Intensity(storedValue: storedIntensity)
    showsConfetti      = intensity.rawValue >= Intensity.standard.rawValue(2) && !reduceMotion
    playsFestiveHaptic = intensity == .festive && hapticsEnabled
    showsGrandFanfare  = intensity == .festive && !reduceMotion
    playsGrandFinale   = intensity == .festive     // NOT gated on reduceMotion or haptics

playsGrandFinale is the non-screen finale (sound gated separately by the view's sound preference, plus a connected e-board LED/beep) — independent of Reduced Motion because it isn't screen motion.

CheckmateCelebrationState keeps hasCelebrated plus three monotonic trigger counters (confettiTrigger, festiveHapticTrigger, grandFanfareTrigger). celebrateOnce(storedIntensity:reduceMotion:hapticsEnabled:) -> Decision? is a no-op (nil) once hasCelebrated; on first call it flips hasCelebrated, computes the Decision, and bumps whichever counters that decision calls for via &+= 1 (wrapping, never rolled back — resetForNewGame() clears only hasCelebrated, since resetting a trigger to zero can itself re-fire the platform API bound to it).

playsGrandFinale has no trigger counter

grandFanfareTrigger tracks showsGrandFanfare (festive and not Reduced Motion), not playsGrandFinale (festive, full stop). A caller wanting the finale effect must read decision.playsGrandFinale directly off celebrateOnce's return value — no counter observes it later.

docs.title: GameResultPresentation — terminal-state text
docs.text:
text(for state: GameState, activeColor: PieceColor) -> String?, isDraw(_ state: GameState) -> Bool:

GameState text(for:activeColor:) isDraw .checkmate "Checkmate — White wins" / "...Black wins" false .stalemate "Stalemate — Draw" true .draw "Draw by 50-move rule" true .insufficientMaterial "Draw — insufficient material" true .repetition "Draw by threefold repetition" true .playing, .check nil false

The checkmate winner is who is not to move: activeColor == .white ? "Black" : "White" — at checkmate activeColor is the side with no reply.

docs.title: ReviewSnapshotBuilder — the Review pane's derived state
docs.text:
The off-view computer for every stat the Review pane shows, carved out of what were @MainActor computed properties re-evaluated on every body invalidation (including scroll). nonisolated; every function is a pure static transform over a mainline, an eval array, and PGN tags.

public static func build(
    mainLine: [MoveNode], annotationEvals: [Double], loadedTags: PGNGame.OrderedTags?,
    whiteMoves: RepertoireBookKernel.RepertoireMoves = [:],
    blackMoves: RepertoireBookKernel.RepertoireMoves = [:]
) async -> ReviewSnapshot

ReviewSnapshot carries perGameAccuracy, criticalMoments, brilliantMoments, topSwings, tablebaseEntryNode, openingExitNode + openingExitName, missedWinMoment, repertoireFit. build(...) fills it in a fixed order, calling await Task.yield() after each of the first seven assignments (not the eighth — the function returns right after):

1 criticalMoments->yield  2 brilliantMoments->yield  3 tablebaseEntryNode->yield
4 missedWinMoment->yield  5 topSwings->yield          6 perGameAccuracy->yield
7 openingExit(node+name)->yield   8 repertoireFit (no yield — return)

Only TablebaseService.pieceCount(for:) is touched — synchronous and local, never TablebaseService's network probe(fen:).

  • Critical/brilliant — criticalMoments filters .mistake/.blunder, sorts blunders before mistakes then by ascending plyIndex, prefix(6). brilliantMoments filters annotation == .brilliant || .great, keeps mainline order, prefix(6).
  • Tablebase entry — first mainline node whose positionAfter has pieceCount(for:) <= 7.
  • Opening exit — walks from move 1 through OpeningBook.shared, stopping at the first non-book position; nil if move 1 is already out of book (a contiguous-prefix walk, not "any book move anywhere").
  • Win-probability swings — needs ≥2 evals. Converts before/after White-POV eval via AccuracyAggregator.winProbability(cp:) (see Analysis math), flips for a Black mover: delta = (wpAfter - wpBefore) * 100 (mover-relative points). swing.delta = abs(delta); directionForMover keeps the sign. Top 6 by magnitude.
  • Missed-win moment — needs ≥20 evals and a Result tag. Scans plies [20, count) (skips the first 10 full moves), tracking White's and Black's peak eval independently so one side's early missed chance isn't hidden behind the other's later, larger, converted advantage: 
    white qualifies iff result != "1-0"  and  200 <= whitePeak.cp      < 5000
black qualifies iff result != "0-1"  and  200 <= abs(blackPeak.cp) < 5000
pick the qualifying side with larger abs(cp);  movedAt = (index / 2) + 1
  • Per-game accuracy — combines White's and Black's independent AccuracyAggregator.GameAccuracy sample-count-weighted, not a flat 50/50 average (an odd-ply game gives one side an extra move, which a flat average silently dropped): weightedMean = (lhs·lhsCount + rhs·rhsCount) / (lhsCount+rhsCount), applied independently to overall, every Phase, and every move-number bucket, each with its own paired sample counts.
  • Repertoire fit — examines min(mainLine.count, 20) plies (≈10 full moves each side), counting RepertoireBookKernel.isRepertoireMove hits per color. "The user's side" is whichever color has hits >= the other's (ties favor White); nil when both sides have 0 hits.
let snapshot = await ReviewSnapshotBuilder.build(
    mainLine: game.mainLine, annotationEvals: EvalJSON.decode(game.evalsJSON),
    loadedTags: game.tags, whiteMoves: book.whiteMoves, blackMoves: book.blackMoves
)
if let mw = snapshot.missedWinMoment {
    print("missed win at move \(mw.movedAt): \(mw.asWhite ? "White" : "Black") had +\(Int(mw.evalCp))cp")
}

docs.title: BoardMarkDocument — the board-mark wire format
docs.text:
Canonical, size-bounded JSON for user-drawn arrows/circles, shared by both platforms.

currentVersion = 1                        maximumTotalMarks = 16_384
maximumEncodedBytes = 1_048_576 (1 MiB)   maximumPositionKeyBytes = 512
maximumPositions = 4_096                  maximumMarksPerPosition = 128

decodeStrict(_:)'s validity gate: version == 1, byPosition.count <= 4_096; per position key, non-empty and <= 512 UTF-8 bytes with <= 128 marks, a running total <= 16_384 marks, and no duplicate (kind,from,to) id; every mark's fromIndex/toIndex in 0..<64, with kind == .arrow requiring fromIndex != toIndex and kind == .circle requiring fromIndex == toIndex. A missing kind on decode (legacy Apple documents) defaults to .arrow.

The interesting design decision is what happens on failure: a document this build doesn't recognize (future version, or a failed bound) is not discarded or normalized to empty. decodePreserving(_:) keeps its exact original source bytes as an opaque payload, and encoded() returns those bytes back byte-for-byte — a recognized empty drawing still encodes to "" (the historical blank sentinel), but only an unrecognized document round-trips verbatim.

var doc = BoardMarkDocument.decodePreserving(storedJSON)
if doc.isRecognized {
    doc.byPosition[position.positionKey, default: []]
        .append(BoardMark(fromIndex: e2, toIndex: e4, color: .green, kind: .arrow))
}
let roundTripped = doc.encoded()   // unrecognized storedJSON comes back byte-identical

encoded() sorts keys and doesn't escape slashes ([.sortedKeys, .withoutEscapingSlashes]) so two builds of the same drawing are byte-identical — usable as digest input into PortableSHA256.

docs.title: SpokenMoveParser — spoken utterance to legal move
docs.text:
Two entry points are public — normalize(_:profile:) -> [String] and match(_:position:profile:) -> [VoiceMoveCandidate] — the normalization pipeline behind them is internal. match generates candidate strings, tries each against the position's legal moves, dedupes by resulting SAN: 0 candidates = no match, 1 = clear match, >1 = disambiguation. normalize runs the candidate through nine sequential stages, accumulating everything it produces (not stopping at the first plausible one):

1 Whole-phrase rewrites   — lexicon.rawPhraseRewrites applied in order to raw lowercased text
2 Collapsed literal        — the phrase with all spaces removed, as-is
3 Piece-name prefix         — "knight c3": strip piece word, apply capture verbs (-> "x") + fillers inline
4 Castle phrases              — substring match; bare "castle"/"castles" emits BOTH "O-O" and "O-O-O"
5 Capture-verb split            — "e takes d5" -> split on verb into <piece><file>x<dest>
6 Filler-word removal             — " to " removed mid-phrase: "e2 to e4" -> "e2e4"
7 File/rank homophone substitution — fileHomophones then rankHomophones over the whole string
8 Promotion suffix                  — trailing "queen"/"rook"/"bishop"/"knight" -> "=Q"/"=R"/"=B"/"=N"
9 Confusable-letter variants          — file/piece swaps, only for 2–5 char SAN-length candidates

let candidates = SpokenMoveParser.match("knight to f3", position: position, profile: .apple)
switch candidates.count {
case 0: showNoMatchToast()
case 1: apply(candidates[0].move)
default: presentDisambiguation(candidates)   // e.g. Nf3 vs Ngf3
}

Lexicon & profiles. Every recognizer quirk is a data row, not a code branch: RecognizerProfile.lexicon = .core.merged(with: overlay). .apple's overlay is empty (on-device, well-trained on chess vocabulary); .google's is rawPhraseRewrites: [("before","b4"), ("84","e4")], pieceWords: [("brook","R")]. merged(with:) appends overlay rows after core's, so core stays higher-priority in ordered matching. Two orderings inside .core are load-bearing:

fileHomophones: "gee " MUST precede "ee " — "gee" contains "ee"; rows apply
    sequentially, so "ee " first would turn "gee six" into "ge six"
rankHomophones: " fore" (leading space) MUST precede "for" — without the
    guard, "before" -> "be4" (a spurious b4 the PGN parser accepts); with
    it, " fore" isn't a substring of "before" at all, so "before" is left
    alone and the later "for" rule turns it into unparseable "be4e"

docs.title: VoiceAttemptOwnership — async recognition race safety
docs.text:
A generic ownership/provenance state machine so only the newest in-flight recognition attempt can publish state or run cleanup, since platform recognizers shut down asynchronously and a stale one can call back after a newer attempt has started. VoiceAttemptOwnership<SessionID, PositionProof, Confirmation> tracks one activeAttempt: VoiceAttemptProvenance? through four private phases (recognizing → awaitingConfirmation → consumed, with invalidationRequested reachable from either of the first two on a session/position mismatch):

registerConfirmation and consumeConfirmation traffic in VoiceAttemptResult<SessionID, PositionProof, Confirmation> — the matched payload welded permanently to the VoiceAttemptProvenance that produced it. It exists so a UI can hold and present a match without smuggling in a different attempt's context: consumeConfirmation compares the presented result's provenance against the owner's own stored result and, on a match, returns the owner's copy rather than trusting whatever payload the caller handed back.

begin(token, sessionID, positionProof): accepted only if token.processSequence
    STRICTLY EXCEEDS every token this owner has ever accepted (monotonic); a
    newer attempt immediately makes the prior attempt's provenance stale.
acceptsCallback: true only if activeAttempt == provenance AND phase == .recognizing.
    A session/position mismatch marks the attempt invalidationRequested
    PERMANENTLY, so a later return to an equal FEN can't revive it.
registerConfirmation: first match wins — freezes phase to .awaitingConfirmation
    so a second matched result from the same attempt can't overwrite the first.
consumeConfirmation: compares the presented result's provenance against the
    OWNER-HELD pendingConfirmation (not the caller-supplied payload) and
    returns the owner's copy — compare-and-consume, exactly once.
clear(ifOwnedBy: p): compare-and-clear — only clears if activeAttempt == p, so
    stale cleanup from an old attempt can't clear a newer one's state.

var ownership = VoiceAttemptOwnership<UUID, String, VoiceMoveCandidate>()
guard let provenance = ownership.begin(
    token: VoiceAttemptToken(processSequence: nextSequence()),
    sessionID: sessionID, positionProof: position.fen
) else { return }   // a newer attempt already started; this one is stale

recognizer.recognize(utterance) { candidate in
    guard ownership.acceptsCallback(for: provenance, currentSessionID: sessionID,
                                     currentPositionProof: position.fen) else { return }
    _ = ownership.registerConfirmation(candidate, for: provenance,
                                        currentSessionID: sessionID, currentPositionProof: position.fen)
}

docs.title: VoiceTranscriptLog — privacy-minimal tuning ring buffer
docs.text:
BlobBackedStore (see the storage seam), blobKey = "voiceTranscriptLog", cap = 200 (oldest dropped on append(_:)). Each VoiceTranscriptEntry carries a timestamp, transcript, alternatives, FEN, a VoiceOutcome (.matched(san:) / .disambiguation(candidates:) / .noMatch), and the recognizer profile string.

append(_:) itself doesn't filter by outcome — it just appends and trims. "Log only .noMatch/.disambiguation by default, treat .matched as opt-in" is a call-site convention documented on the type to keep the persisted log's privacy surface small, not something the ring buffer enforces. VoiceOutcome hand-writes its own Codable with a kind discriminator field instead of Swift's default enum-with-payload encoding, so the on-disk shape is stable and explicit. The tuning loop this exists for: speak on device → collect misses from the log → add one SpokenMoveLexicon overlay row + one corpus test case → rebuild — no engine code changes.

docs.title: AccessibilityPhrasing — spoken labels
docs.text:
Function Notes material(captured:advantage:sideName:) e.g. "White: captured queen, 2 pawns, plus 3"; empty capture → "White: " (kept for parity) spokenDuration(_ seconds:) "3 minutes 42 seconds" / "42 seconds" (minutes omitted under 60s) squareHint(isSelected:isLegalTarget:isOwnPiece:) priority: selected > legal target > own piece > "" signalBarCount(rssi:) BLE bars, 1–4 evalAdvantageWord(whiteProbability:) "White" / "Black" / "Even" selectedLabel(_:isSelected:) appends ", selected" — Android's .isSelected trait crashes the a11y tree walk, so selection is spoken via the label 
signalBarCount(rssi):  < -85 -> 1   [-85,-75) -> 2   [-75,-60) -> 3   else -> 4
evalAdvantageWord(p):  p > 0.52 -> "White"   p < 0.48 -> "Black"   else -> "Even"   (dead band)

docs.title: PortableSHA256 — dependency-free SHA-256
docs.text:
A from-scratch FIPS 180-4 SHA-256, because CryptoKit is unavailable on native Android and Swift's Hasher is intentionally process-randomized. 64 round constants (0x428a2f98 ... 0xc67178f2), the 8-word IV (0x6a09e667, 0xbb67ae85, 0x3c6ef372, 0xa54ff53a, 0x510e527f, 0x9b05688c, 0x1f83d9ab, 0x5be0cd19), 64-byte blocks, standard Merkle–Damgård padding (0x80 then zero-pad to 56 mod 64, then an 8-byte big-endian bit length), 32-byte digest. Hasher is incremental (update(_:)/update(byte:)/update(utf8:), finalize() -> [UInt8], hexDigest() -> String); hexDigest(utf8:) is the one-shot form.

update(lengthPrefixedUTF8:) prepends an 8-byte big-endian byte count (of the UTF-8 encoding) before the string's own bytes — "the shared canonical framing used by authored causal and frontier proofs," per its doc comment — so a hash commits to a string's exact length rather than leaving where one field ends and the next begins ambiguous:

var hasher = PortableSHA256.Hasher()
hasher.update(lengthPrefixedUTF8: fen)
hasher.update(lengthPrefixedUTF8: san)
let digest = hasher.hexDigest()

docs.title: RunGeneration — the epoch-counter idiom
docs.text:
begin() -> UInt64 and invalidate() both do current &+= 1 (wrapping); owns(_ token:) -> Bool is current == token. begin() hands the new value back as a token to own; invalidate() discards it — no token satisfies owns(_:) again until begin() is called.

var generation = RunGeneration()
func startAnalysis() {
    let token = generation.begin()
    Task {
        let result = try await engine.analyze(position)
        guard generation.owns(token) else { return }   // stale — a newer run started
        self.evaluation = result
    }
}

The same "reject stale async work" shape as VoiceAttemptOwnership, stripped to a single counter for call sites that don't need provenance.

docs.title: DurationFormatting — the rounding fix
docs.text:
drillDuration(seconds):
    totalTenths = Int((seconds * 10).rounded())          // ONE rounding, up front
    totalTenths < 600 (< 60s):  "\(totalTenths/10).\(totalTenths%10)s"      // "9.4s"
    else: totalSeconds = Int(seconds.rounded())           // rounded again, not truncated
          "\(totalSeconds/60)m \(zero-padded totalSeconds%60)s"             // "1m 05s"

The bug this replaced: Apple used String(format: "%.1fs") (rounds); Android hand-rolled the idea (SkipFoundation doesn't reliably support String(format:)) but mixed a truncating Int(seconds) with a separately rounded tenths digit — at 9.97s that produced "9.0s", a whole second wrong, invisible except right at a rounding boundary. Rounding once, up front, in tenths, lets a value that carries into the next second or minute do so correctly. The shells also disagreed on padding above a minute ("3m 5s" vs "3m 05s"); the shared formatter always zero-pads.

docs.title: PieceSet — the piece-set picker
docs.text:
10 cases: cburnett, merida, inkwell, crownline, scandi, minimal, leipzig, mpchess, staunty, maestro — the raw values are the literal @AppStorage keys both apps write ("pieceSet" on iOS, "pref.pieceSet" on Android) and must never change.

assetName(for: piece):  cburnett      -> "{w|b}{K|Q|R|B|N|P}"          // "wK", "bP"
                         other 9 sets -> "{rawValue}_{w|b}{K|Q|R|B|N|P}" // "merida_wK"

selectableCases is a curated 7-set picker subset, in owner-curated order — [.cburnett, .merida, .staunty, .maestro, .leipzig, .mpchess, .inkwell] — filtered against pendingPermission (currently empty, so a no-op filter as of the 2026-07-20 sadsnake1 grant). Crownline, Scandi, and Minimal stay fully wired (assets, export switch, persisted selections) but are hidden to keep the list short; pickerCases(including:) adds a current selection back in even when it isn't in selectableCases, so an existing choice never renders as empty.

docs.title: SharedUtilities — the grab-bag
docs.text:
Small pure helpers deduplicated out of code reimplemented identically in several places.

Type / extension Purpose PercentFormat.whole(_:) Double (0...1) → "73%", "—" for non-finite Array.capLast(_:) trims to the most recent max elements Position.fenStartsWithWhite(_:) parses FEN side-to-move; defaults true on malformed input EvalJSON codec for the eval-array JSON blob (below) PieceColor.mover(ply:startIsWhite:) ((i%2==0)==startIsWhite) ? .white : .black TimeInterval.clockString(showHours:showTenths:) countdown display, e.g. "1:35", "0:09.7" TimeInterval.moveTimeString() move-timing display: "5.3s" / "45s" / "2:05" / "1:02:05" PieceType.materialSummary(_:) "K+Q+R+P" / "K+2N+P" from a piece-count map EvalFormat centipawn/mate display formatting (below) GameResultParser PGN result string → .win/.draw/.loss/.unknown DrillLeniency "close enough to best" grading for drills (below) OnlineGameSourceIdentity.canonical(_:) normalizes "lichess"/"chesscom"/"chess.com"; else nil GameCollectionName parses "Online: lichess/<user>" / "<user> (Lichess)" names Piece.unicodeSymbol Unicode chess glyph, e.g. "♞" 
EvalJSON mate sentinel is exactly ±100_000 cp. Downstream mate detection is
abs(cp) >= 100_000 — callers must NOT pre-clamp a mate score smaller before
it reaches this array.

EvalFormat.formatCentipawns(cp:isMate:) renders "+1.34"/"-0.21" or "M5"/"-M3"; formatEvalDisplay(cp:mateIn:style:)'s "winprob" style converts through AccuracyAggregator.winProbability(cp:) and rounds .toNearestOrAwayFromZero (0.505 → 51%).

DrillLeniency.leniencyAccept(bestCp,bestIsMate,playedCp,playedIsMate,marginCp):
  if bestIsMate:
      guard bestCp > 0 else return false          // best move that's mate AGAINST mover shouldn't occur
      return playedIsMate ? (playedCp > 0) : (playedCp >= 500)
  else:
      if playedIsMate:  return playedCp > 0        // upgraded to / kept a real mate
      if bestCp >= 500: return playedCp >= 200      // best already decisive -> any clear win
      else:              return playedCp >= bestCp - marginCp   // within margin (typically 50-150cp)

A played move that hands the opponent a mate (playedIsMate && playedCp < 0) is correctly rejected by the playedCp > 0 check — an earlier kernel version accepted any playedIsMate, mis-grading a blunder-into-mate as a solve. GameResultParser.parseGameResult(_:userColor:) recognizes only "1-0", "0-1", "1/2-1/2"; everything else ("*", "½-½", malformed, or a decisive result with nil userColor) is .unknown.

PercentFormat.whole(0.734)                                          // "73%"
GameResultParser.parseGameResult(tags["Result"] ?? "*", userColor: .white)
DrillLeniency.leniencyAccept(bestCp: 620, bestIsMate: false,
                              playedCp: 410, playedIsMate: false, marginCp: 100)  // true: bestCp >= 500, playedCp(410) >= 200

docs.title: AboutContent — licensing data
docs.text:
@_spi(FianchettoApp) — this whole type compiles into FianchettoKit's public interface but stays invisible unless a consumer writes @_spi(FianchettoApp) import FianchettoKit, same as an internal symbol otherwise. That boundary exists because it's release-compliance copy owned by the app target (license text, corresponding-source pointers), not a general FianchettoKit API.

acknowledgements: [Acknowledgement] (17 entries, each {title, detail, license, url}) covers the three bundled engines (Stockfish — GPLv3, Maia 3 — AGPLv3 used with author permission, Reckless — AGPLv3), all 10 PieceSet credits (license varies by set: GPLv2+ for Cburnett/Merida, CC BY-NC 4.0 for Inkwell/Crownline/Scandi/Minimal, Freeware for Leipzig, GPLv3+ for MPChess, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for Staunty/Maestro), the opening book (CC0), Lichess Practice puzzles (AGPLv3), a design-inspiration credit for En-Croissant, and a trademark/no-affiliation notice for the Square Off Pro BLE integration. androidAcknowledgements adds one row for ONNX Runtime (MIT), since Android ships Microsoft's runtime for on-device Maia inference. correspondingSourceNotice, gplV3Fallback, and onnxRuntimeMITLicense are the full license/notice strings shown alongside.

docs.text:
Type File Imports ClockCore Play/ClockCore.swift Foundation, ChessCore TimePreset, TimeControlSelection Play/TimePreset.swift (none) CheckmateCelebrationPolicy, CheckmateCelebrationState Play/CheckmateCelebrationPolicy.swift (none) GameResultPresentation Play/GameResultPresentation.swift ChessCore ReviewSnapshotBuilder Review/ReviewSnapshotBuilder.swift Foundation, ChessCore BoardMarkDocument, BoardMark, BoardMarkKind, BoardMarkColor Review/BoardMarkDocument.swift Foundation SpokenMoveParser, SpokenMoveLexicon, RecognizerProfile Voice/SpokenMoveParser.swift Foundation, ChessCore VoiceAttemptOwnership + tokens Voice/VoiceAttemptOwnership.swift (none) VoiceTranscriptLog, VoiceOutcome Voice/VoiceTranscriptLog.swift Foundation AccessibilityPhrasing Voice/AccessibilityPhrasing.swift Foundation, ChessCore PortableSHA256 Support/PortableSHA256.swift (none) RunGeneration Support/RunGeneration.swift (none) DurationFormatting Support/DurationFormatting.swift Foundation PieceSet Support/PieceSet.swift ChessCore SharedUtilities types Support/SharedUtilities.swift Foundation, ChessCore AboutContent Support/AboutContent.swift (none, @_spi)

No type here reads a file, touches the network, or depends on a UI framework — ReviewSnapshotBuilder and VoiceAttemptOwnership are the only two with async/isolation-shaped API, and both are pure value transforms underneath.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
ReviewSnapshotBuilder and SpokenMoveParser are natural fits for two subcommands fianchetto-cli doesn't have yet: a review command running build(...) over a parsed PGN mainline and printing critical moments, swings, accuracy, and repertoire fit as JSON; and a voice-parse command feeding a transcript plus a FEN through SpokenMoveParser.match(_:position:profile:) and printing the resulting SAN candidates — the same shape fianchetto-cli's existing six subcommands (annotate, estimate, maia, accuracy, project, track) already use to run ChessCore analysis and FianchettoKit's stat stores headlessly.

  • Stores & the storage seam — the BlobBackedStore/JSONBlobStore seam VoiceTranscriptLog persists through.
  • Analysis math — AccuracyAggregator.winProbability(cp:) and moveAccuracy(...), which ReviewSnapshotBuilder and EvalFormat build on.
  • Network clients — TablebaseService.pieceCount(for:), the one network-client call ReviewSnapshotBuilder touches.

docs.title: Importing user-supplied puzzles
docs.text:
BUILT — the design record, not a recommendation. Raised 2026-08-19 (users should be able to bring puzzles from Lichess or other public sources) and shipped: this package carries PuzzleLink, PuzzleLinkImport, LichessPuzzleLinkDecoder, LichessPuzzleCSVParser, ImportedPuzzleRecord, ImportedPuzzleWidening and PuzzleImportCopy, and the Apple app drives them through its Fianchetto/Engine/PuzzleLinkImportService.swift. Both the recommendation below and the by-link/by-file scope are what the code does.

This page lived in the Apple app repository as docs/PUZZLE_IMPORT.md until 2026-08-22. Six files in this package cited it and none of them could resolve it, because the design it records governs code that is here, not there.

The reasoning is kept because it is why the import is shaped this way — the set -versus-line problem in particular does not stop being true. The open questions at the end stand as written; they were never blocking.

docs.title: The gap is not the file format
docs.text:
The instinct is to ask "PGN or something else?". That is the second question.

A puzzle's answer is a SET; every interchange format stores a LINE.

Fianchetto already knows this. PuzzleNode in FianchettoKit/Sources/FianchettoKit/Train/Combinations/CombinationPuzzleKernel.swift models a solver node as:

case solverToMove(
    accepted: Set<String>,      // every move that keeps the win within tolerance
    expected: String,           // the one used for hints and length display
    continuations: [String: PuzzleNode]
)
case opponentToMove(replies: [String: PuzzleNode], mainReply: String)

That is a richer representation than any public puzzle source publishes. It carries several equally-correct solver moves, scripted opponent replies, and — via unresolvedBranches — an explicit record of where the tree does not yet answer. The mined-combination pipeline builds these by probing an engine.

So the import problem is not "parse a file". It is: a source gives us one line, and a drillable puzzle needs a tree. Everything below follows from that.

docs.title: PGN
docs.text:
Carries: the position (FEN + SetUp tags), a mainline, variations (RAVs), comments, NAGs.

Does not carry, under any convention a parser can rely on:

  • Which line is the answer. A RAV is "another line". Nothing distinguishes an equally good solution from a plausible try that loses. Treating RAVs as accepted answers would teach users that inferior moves are correct.
  • Who solves. Puzzle sources conventionally start the position before an opponent move, which is then played for you. PGN has no tag for that.
  • Where the puzzle ends. A game's PGN continues past the tactic.
  • Rating, themes, provenance, licence.

PGN is a game format. A puzzle is a game fragment plus a claim about it, and the claim is the part PGN has nowhere to put.

docs.title: The Lichess puzzle database
docs.text:
A CSV export, published CC0. Columns are approximately PuzzleId, FEN, Moves, Rating, RatingDeviation, Popularity, NbPlays, Themes, GameUrl, OpeningTags.

Verify before building. The column list and the licence above are from memory and must be confirmed against the current export before any parser is written. Getting the licence wrong is the expensive mistake here, not getting a column wrong.

Its convention is explicit and machine-readable, which PGN's is not: the FEN is the position before the opponent's move, the first entry in Moves is played for the user, and the rest alternate. It also carries the metadata we have no source for today — a rating and themes.

Its limitation is the mirror of PGN's: exactly one accepted move per solver node and one scripted opponent reply. High fidelity about a solution, silent about alternatives.

We already hold a Lichess personal-access token (Fianchetto/Models/LichessTokenStore.swift), so the account plumbing exists; the puzzle database itself is a public file and needs no token.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
1. Do not invent a third puzzle model. Import targets the existing CombinationPuzzle tree. Endgames keep their own archetype model (FianchettoKit/Sources/FianchettoKit/Train/Endgames/EndgameTrainerKernel.swift) because they are generated, not authored — imported puzzles are authored, and that is the combination shape.

2. Accept the Lichess CSV as the first-class source. Its conventions are stated rather than inferred, and its metadata is real. Map one line into the tree as accepted = [theMove], with every solver node past the first recorded in unresolvedBranches — because we genuinely have not probed the alternatives. That field already means exactly this, and using it keeps the honesty automatic.

3. Support PGN, but only with a declared convention. Ask the user which side solves and where the puzzle starts, rather than guessing. Treat RAVs as candidates, never as accepted answers.

4. Widen accepted with the engine, reusing the miner's tolerance rule. This is the step that converts a lossy single-line import into a real puzzle, and it is the reason not to write a second grading path: if imported puzzles graded answers differently from mined ones, the same move would be correct in one drill and wrong in another. One rule, one place.

5. Make provenance and licence required fields, not optional metadata. CC0 for the Lichess database, unknown for a user's own PGN. A puzzle whose licence we cannot state is one we must not redistribute in a backup, a shared repertoire, or anything else that leaves the device.

6. Put the whole thing in FianchettoKit, so the Apple, CMP desktop, Android and CLI faces import identically. A per-face importer is four subtly different answers to "is this move correct?".

docs.title: Imported puzzles join the existing vendored set
docs.text:
Owner decision, 2026-08-19. They are not a separate pool and not a separate row.

A first draft of this document called the imported rating "a rating we cannot compare to ours". That was wrong, and backwards. TacticsRatingStore is a PAIRED Elo: every puzzle carries its own rating, and a scored attempt moves the user rating and the puzzle rating by equal-and-opposite amounts. A puzzle rating is not decoration — it is the input that decides how much a solve is worth.

Our seeds are a three-bucket heuristic:

case .easy:   return 1200
case .medium: return 1500
case .hard:   return 1800

A Lichess puzzle rating is on the same Elo scale and is derived from millions of real attempts. So an imported puzzle should seed its rating from the imported value, and it will be better calibrated than the puzzles we mined ourselves. Importing is a rating upgrade, not a rating hazard.

Three consequences worth stating before anyone builds this:

  • The pool becomes mixed-precision, and that is fine. Both numbers are only priors; the Elo update corrects them from real attempts either way. An imported puzzle simply starts closer to the truth.
  • Filter on rating deviation, not just rating. Lichess publishes Glicko-2 with an RD, and our model has no RD field. Dropping it means treating a barely-attempted puzzle's shaky rating as confidently as a settled one. Importing only puzzles below an RD threshold is a cheap quality gate and the cheapest place to get this right.
  • An imported puzzle's rating will drift away from Lichess's, because our attempts move it. That is correct and wanted: it becomes our rating, for our users. It also means the imported value is a SEED and must never be re-synced from source later, which would silently discard real evidence.

docs.title: Scope: by link or by file, never a bundled database
docs.text:
Owner decision, 2026-08-20, and it narrows the feature considerably.

We do not ship any of the Lichess database, and we do not offer it. No bulk import, no themed subset, no rating band. The earlier framing in this document — "how much of the database?" — asked the wrong question. What users get is the ability to bring puzzles THEY have:

  • By link. A user shares a puzzle URL into the app. This is the natural companion to the existing Share Extension, and it is the primary path.
  • By file. A user opens a file they already hold.

WHY THIS IS THE BETTER SHAPE, beyond scope. A bundled database would make every licence and provenance question OURS to answer for content we redistribute; a link or a file the user supplies keeps us a reader of what they already have. It also removes the "how much" question entirely, and with it the RD-threshold quality filter this document previously recommended — a filter only matters when you are choosing puzzles on the user's behalf, and now we never are.

WHAT SURVIVES from the CSV work: the parser is still how a supplied FILE is read, and ImportedPuzzleRecord's required provenance/licence fields matter MORE under this model, not less — a puzzle arriving by link carries whatever the source says, and "unknown" must stay an explicit, auditable answer rather than an absence.

Engine probing is REQUIRED, and it is affordable. Owner decision: modest probing, which is fast because the position is fixed and the solution is typical. This is what widens accepted from the source's single line into the set a drill can fairly grade — see recommendation 4 above. One line imported and never probed is a puzzle that marks a correct alternative wrong.

docs.title: Open questions for the owner
docs.text:
• What does a link import do when the source is unreachable or the URL is not a puzzle? It must fail visibly rather than importing an empty puzzle.
  • Does a link import require network at drill time, or is the puzzle materialised once and stored? Materialised once is the offline-first answer and matches the rest of the app.
  • Do imported puzzles show their provenance in the drill? They are now indistinguishable from ours in the pool, which is the point — but a user who hits a puzzle they dislike may reasonably want to know where it came from.

docs.title: Repertoire Gap Analysis: Book Coverage, Personal-Game Sourcing, and the Maia Opponent Model
docs.text: The Repertoire subsystem is the pure chess-algebra layer behind opening prep: finding the holes in a repertoire, scoring the moves already in it, aggregating a player's own games into a personal book, and exporting/importing the result as PGN. Everything here is portable value types and enum namespaces over ChessCore's Position/Move — the app owns the SwiftData rows, the @Observable state, and the Stockfish/Maia run loops that feed engine results back in.

docs.title: Three kinds of gap — and a fourth question
docs.text:
"Gap" means three distinct things in this subsystem, produced by three independent kernels that never overlap:

Kernel Finds Driven by RepertoireBookKernel.computeGaps Positions with no prepared reply at all — book continuations and the player's own faced games that the repertoire doesn't answer OpeningBook + an optional PersonalGamesSnapshot RepertoireAuditKernel Moves the repertoire does prepare, that are objectively weak Stockfish (engine-free kernel; the app supplies the eval) RepertoireOpponentModelKernel Replies inside the repertoire's own tree that a human opponent is likely to play, with no prepared answer Maia's move-probability policy

The first two are inward-looking — they audit what's written down. A repertoire can pass both (no unfinished lines, no weak moves) and still collapse the first time an opponent plays a natural-but-unbooked move on move 6, because nothing ever asked "what will a human actually do here?" That's the question RepertoireOpponentModelKernel answers, using the same Maia policy RepertoireAuditKernel already consults for maiaRank/maiaTopSAN.

A fourth question sits beside the three, and it is the only one that looks at games the user actually played: RepertoireDeviationKernel asks when you sat down and played, did you follow this, and what happened when you didn't. It has its own section below, as do the verdict types every scan shares (RepertoireScanOutcome/RepertoireScanStatus), the evidence-and-claim rules that decide what a face may print about a number, the guided-expansion walk, the leech aggregation, the editing policy, and the per-repertoire health digest that sums the whole surface up.

docs.title: Core data model
docs.text:
Every kernel in this subsystem shares one representation of "what's prepared":

public typealias RepertoireMoves = [String: [String: String?]]
// positionKey → san → comment?

The positionKey is always OpeningBook.epNormalizedKey — never a raw FEN — so transpositions collapse into one dictionary entry regardless of move order:

epNormalizedKey(pos) = first 4 space-separated FEN fields, with the
                       en-passant field replaced by
                       pos.capturableEnPassantTarget?.algebraic ?? "-"

A raw FEN records an en-passant target after every double pawn push, even when no enemy pawn can actually capture there — a "phantom" EP square. Dropping it means 1.d4 e6 2.c4 d5 and 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 — different move orders reaching the same Queen's Gambit Declined position — hash to the identical key. Every gap walk, every coverage index, and the personal book all key off this one function, so a Slav repertoire can recognize a Semi-Slav transposition it never literally walked.

The lookup surface over RepertoireMoves is small:

public struct MoveInfo: Sendable, Hashable {
    public let san: String
    public let comment: String?
    public var annotation: String? = nil
}

RepertoireBookKernel.moves(at: position, in: repMoves)              // [MoveInfo], SAN-sorted
RepertoireBookKernel.isRepertoireMove("Nf3", at: position, in: repMoves)  // Bool
RepertoireBookKernel.crossSuggestions(at: position, own: white, opposite: black)

crossSuggestions surfaces moves the other colour has prepared at the same position that this colour hasn't — "you also study this from the other side."

docs.title: OpeningBook: the shared opening database
docs.text:
OpeningBook wraps a precomputed ECO dataset (entries: position → Entry, continuations: position → [BookMove]), loaded once from JSON or plist and installed process-wide:

OpeningBook.configureShared(precomputedData: data, isPlist: false)  // discardable Bool
let book = OpeningBook.shared

configureShared only installs a book that decoded to at least one entry — a failed or empty load leaves the previous shared value untouched, so a missing resource fails loudly rather than making every lookup silently return nil/"Unknown".

Phantom-EP fallback. Because the book is keyed by raw FEN internally, entry(for:) retries with the EP-normalized key before giving up:

entry(for: position):
    raw = positionKey(position)                 // pos.positionKey, un-normalized
    if entries[raw] exists → return it
    normalized = epNormalizedKey(position)
    if normalized == raw → return nil            // nothing to drop
    return entries[normalized]                   // fallback only ADDS hits, never overrides

continuations(for:) runs the same fallback and additionally resolves each book SAN's openingName/eco from the position it leads to (not just the raw book row), so a continuation lands on its own canonical name rather than its parent's. Results are cached by a private NSLock-guarded ContinuationsCache — countLimit = 4096, evicting ~10% of entries (storage.count / 10, at least 1) on overflow rather than tracking true LRU, since opening-book lookups are dominated by a small set of hot positions anyway. Empty results are cached too, so a non-book position doesn't repeat the dictionary probe.

ECO canonical-name resolution. Loading a book runs a BFS from the initial position over its own continuation graph, assigning a ply depth to every reachable entry:

for each ECO code:
    canonical name = the entry with the MINIMUM BFS ply depth
    ties broken lexicographically by name

orphan entries unreached by BFS get depth Int.max
    (chosen only when they're the sole entry for their ECO code)

This replaced an older shortest-name-string heuristic, which picked "Amazon Attack" (13 chars, ply 3) over "Queen's Pawn Game" (17 chars, ply 2) for D00 — shorter text, but a deeper, less representative line.

findPath(to:) is a separate, uncapped BFS reconstructing the shortest book SAN path to a target epNormalizedKey — used to retroactively derive anchorLineSAN for repertoires anchored before that field existed. It walks the whole graph before giving up on an unreachable target, so it's opt-in (searchBook: on RepertoireBookKernel.anchorPly) and only enabled on off-main scans that already traverse the book.

docs.title: Gap walk algorithm: computeGaps
docs.text:
computeGaps is a pre-order walk of the repertoire's own move tree, looking for two things at once: user-turn positions with nothing prepared, and opponent-turn positions where the book (or the player's own games) lists a reply the repertoire doesn't have.

It uses an explicit stack, not recursion — cooperative-pool threads have roughly 512KB stacks, and a line at the subsystem's 10⁴-position design target overflowed the recursive form. The stack holds two item kinds so that book-gap emission can be deferred until every child subtree has finished:

enum WalkItem {
    case visit(position: Position, moveSequence: [String], lastNamed: (name: String, eco: String?)?)
    case emitBookGaps(position: Position, moveSequence: [String], key: String, lastNamed: (name: String, eco: String?)?)
}

Children are pushed reversed so sorted-SAN order pops first (matching recursive pre-order exactly), and on an opponent-turn node .emitBookGaps is pushed beneath the children — so it only runs after every rep-move subtree below it has already claimed its visited entries. This preserves "first-reached-wins" transposition semantics and gap suppression order identically to what a recursive walk would produce.

Three sources feed the gap list:
